items.title: Formation and Eruption of a Vortex-driven Magnetic Flux Rope in the Simulated Quiet Sun
items.abstract: Abstract Magnetic flux ropes (MFRs) are key structures for understanding flares and coronal mass ejections in active regions, but their characteristics in the quiet Sun remain poorly understood. With a radiative MHD simulation spanning from the upper convection zone to the corona, we analyze the formation and eruption of a supergranular-scale flux rope. We use a clustering method to group the closed field lines by their connectivity. The clusters are gathered further into eight persistent cluster assemblies (CAs) that correspond to a flux rope and ambient magnetic structures. A persistent counterclockwise vortex is maintained at the converging point of the supergranules, i.e., the positive footpoint of the flux rope. The vortex continuously injects helicity into a magnetic flux tube and wraps ambient magnetic structures around the central flux tube. On a timescale of one hour, the flux tube evolves to a strongly twisted flux rope and erupts. The eruption exhibits similar current sheet structures as inferred from the flux rope eruption in active regions; however, the mass ejection and heating are much weaker and give rise to very insignificant observable features. The synthetic EUV images show mostly dimming features caused by density rarefaction in the expanding flux rope. This work helps elucidate the dynamic and complex evolution of flux ropes formed in the quiet Sun and suggests that similar events in the real Sun may have been underestimated due to their stealth behavior.

items.title: DESI Interacting Dwarfs Survey: Multiple Evolutionary Channels of Dwarf Galaxies Driven by Major Dwarf Interactions
items.abstract: Abstract Dwarf–dwarf interactions are a major driver of galaxy evolution in the early Universe, but observational constraints on their impact across mass, separation, and environment remain scarce. Using the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) Early Data Release (EDR), this study constructs the largest sample of dwarf galaxy pairs, spanning stellar masses 6.5 ≤ log ( M ⋆ / M ⊙ ) ≤ 9.5 and redshifts 0.015 ≤ z ≤ 1.5. We analyze the evolution of star formation rates and multiwavelength colors ( NUV − r , U – V , V – J , r – K , and g – r ) as a function of projected separation, stellar mass, and external tidal environment. Low-mass/low-redshift pairs exhibit interaction-triggered star formation at intermediate separations. At the smallest separations (≲10 kpc), these systems display divergent behavior: isolated pairs show the onset of dust-obscured star formation, those embedded in weak external tidal fields undergo extended, dust-unobscured star formation, while those embedded in strong external tidal fields experience rapid quenching of star formation. High-mass/low-redshift pairs follow a more uniform evolutionary track, with generally weaker dependence on environment. Interaction-triggered star formation occurs at intermediate separations, followed by increased dust obscuration and rapid quenching at the smallest separations. At higher redshifts, high-mass dwarf systems display an initial suppression of star formation, followed by renewed activity at smaller separations, consistent with early-stage gas removal and later interaction-driven inflows. These results demonstrate that dwarf–dwarf interactions do not follow a single evolutionary pathway. Instead, we reveal a complex picture of dwarf galaxy evolution, with significant implications for dust-obscured star formation, abrupt quenching, and the formation of compact, dusty, intensely star-forming systems.

items.title: Bias and Inference in Spatial Interaction Models with Suppressed Origin–Destination Data
items.abstract: Maximum entropy methods are used to infer the true trip-distribution matrix in cases where parts of the data are suppressed due to privacy concerns. Large proportions of the suppressed data are found to be inferred correctly when the marginal totals in the trip distribution are known. Entropy-based approaches are further found to outperform a strategy of ignoring suppressed information in cases with suppressed marginal totals and/or a higher cut-off value of suppressing cell information. Our methods are demonstrated to reduce the systematic bias in estimates of the distance deterrence parameter to such small numbers that it is effectively zero, preventing potentially serious bias in estimates and predictions resulting from standard spatial interaction models. Another useful contribution is to identify what scenarios an entropy-maximization approach benefits from incorporating information on times series and/or information on distances in the transportation network.

items.title: Coupling light with matter for identifying dominant subnetworks
items.abstract: We introduce DOMINO, a light-matter computing platform that exploits the full complex amplitude of coupled condensate networks to solve maximum-weight clique problems and reveal hidden indirect correlations in large graphs. By embedding network structure directly into a gain-controlled polaritonic (or photonic) oscillator array, DOMINO performs analog optimization, directly solving the maximum-weight clique problem via the gain-controlled minimisation, through a physically enforced global-intensity constraint, allowing the system to converge rapidly to dominant subnetworks while simultaneously extracting phase, encoded co- and counter-regulation patterns. This gain-based mechanism unlocks capabilities inaccessible to conventional Ising-type simulators: all degrees of freedom (amplitude and phase) participate in the computation, dramatically expanding the class of problems that can be efficiently encoded. Our approach is inherently ultrafast, energy-efficient, and naturally robust to noise, requiring no digital post-processing. Applied to real gene-gene coexpression data, DOMINO reliably identifies biologically meaningful transcription-regulator modules and exposes latent regulatory relationships. Because the method applies generically to any weighted network, it establishes a scalable physical route to solving high-value graph-analytic tasks across biology, finance, social systems, and engineered networks.

items.title: Aging-related cellular and molecular changes reveal a role for Bglap3+ neurons in MEC spatial cognition
items.abstract: Abstract Aging-related cognitive decline, including impairments in spatial orientation and memory, has been linked to dysfunction within the hippocampus and medial entorhinal cortex (MEC). However, the cellular and molecular alterations underlying MEC aging remain poorly understood. Here we show that old mice exhibit a reduced proportion of grid cells and decreased spatial stability. Transcriptomic profiling of the MEC using 10x Genomics Visium technology reveals 1664 differentially expressed genes between young and old mice. Among these, Bglap3 is identified as a marker gene for a subpopulation of Layer III neurons that showed an age-associated reduction in cell number. Chemogenetic silencing of Bglap3 + neurons in young mice impairs spatial tuning of MEC neurons. Together, these findings elucidate cellular and molecular mechanisms contributing to age-related MEC dysfunction and suggest that the loss of Bglap3 + neurons may underlie spatial coding deficits in aging.

items.title: Cobalt(III) Schiff Base Complexes as Irreversible Inhibitors of the Metallo-β-Lactamase NDM-1
items.abstract: Abstract Antibiotic resistance is a critical public health concern, with approximately 2.8 million Americans infected with antibiotic-resistant bacteria annually and over 35,000 deaths in the United States alone. Of particular concern are Enterobacterales that express metallo-β-lactamases (MBLs), bacteria that cause nosocomial infections and exhibit resistance to most β-lactam drugs. The zinc-containing active sites of MBLs differ from those of serine β-lactamases, making current clinical inhibitors ineffective. No FDA-approved MBL inhibitors exist, leaving a critical gap in therapeutics for MBL-expressing Enterobacterales infections. Herein, we biochemically and spectroscopically demonstrate irreversible inhibition of the metallo-β-lactamase NDM-1 by a subset of cobalt(III) Schiff base complexes (Co(III)-sb). Crystallography and 59Co NMR experiments show that inactivation efficiency is dependent on axial and equatorial ligand identity. While Co(III)-sb exhibits NDM-1 inhibition, chemical modification is required to enable complexes to cross the Gram-negative envelope. These findings establish Co(III)-sb complexes as a novel scaffold for the development of MBL inhibitors.

items.title: EnzyREx: deep learning enables reaction-based comprehensive enzyme screening
items.abstract: Abstract Background Enzymes accelerate biochemical reactions in living organisms, thus playing an important role in metabolism. Although metabolic pathway databases are growing, many metabolic reactions, termed orphan enzymes, have not been annotated to gene sequences, which hinders functional annotation in genomic analysis. Moreover, protein databases contain many proteins of unknown function. Owing to this gap between known proteins and enzymatic reactions, various proteins of unknown function may be orphan enzymes; however, available tools cannot adequately predict these links. Results In this study, we developed DeepRES, an AI-based framework for comprehensive enzyme screening, to explore novel enzyme candidates from proteins of unknown function for reactions of interest. DeepRES implements enzyme screening via two steps: classification of enzymes and non-enzymes and prediction of catalytic capabilities for enzyme‒reaction pairs. The two deep learning models comprising DeepRES showed comparable or superior performance to that of existing software. We performed screening of 1,255 orphan enzymes involved in the microbiome using DeepRES and successfully identified candidate proteins for 897 orphan enzymes. We then used those candidates as references for genomic analysis and explored novel biosynthetic gene clusters from microbial genomes to obtain promising candidate gene clusters, including those related to anthocyanin degradation. Conclusions Comprehensive enzyme screening via DeepRES, which is the first computational tool designed to associate orphan enzymes with proteins of unknown function, is expected to facilitate high-throughput identification of orphan enzyme-encoding genes. Furthermore, DeepRES can be easily integrated into the current genomic analysis pipeline to extend the functional annotation.

items.title: Incubation and Beyond: A Comparative Analysis of ASF Projects Sustainability Impacts on Software Quality
items.abstract: Abstract Context: Free and Open Source Software (FOSS) communities’ sustainability, meaning to remain operational without signs of weakening or interruptions to its development, is fundamental for the resilience and continuity of society’s digital infrastructure. Many of our digital services and products either leverage or entirely rely on FOSS somewhere in their software stack. However, FOSS sustainability is a multifaceted concept, and the impact of its decline on community products is less known. Objective: In this study, we sought to understand how the different aspects of FOSS sustainability impact software quality from a developmental trajectory perspective. Specifically, we aim to investigate whether and how incubation of FOSS projects or bypassing incubation correlates with software quality outcomes. Method: We selected 342 FOSS projects from the Apache Software Foundation that have either graduated, retired, or bypassed their incubator program (development trajectory phases specific for Apache FOSS projects). We used 16 sustainability metrics to examine their impact on eight software quality metrics (defect density, code coverage, medium risk complexity, very high risk complexity, number of large files, very large function size count, code duplication percentage, and most complex function LOC). We analyzed the decline in the sustainability metrics and their relationship with our selected software quality metrics using Bayesian data analysis, which incorporates probability distributions to represent the regression coefficients and intercepts. Results: We found that our selected sustainability metrics exhibit distinct relationships with software quality across different project trajectories. Graduated projects demonstrated the strongest sustainability-software quality (SWQ) relationship. In contrast, retired projects exhibited weaker relationships, despite receiving similar governance support during incubation. Bypassed projects, while not outperforming graduated ones, showed comparable sustainability-SWQ relationships. Conclusion: While structured incubation strengthens sustainability and SWQ in graduated projects, retired projects struggle to maintain strong sustainability-SWQ relationships, indicating that additional factors internal and specific to projects influence sustainability. This effect was evident among bypassed projects; their self-reliant sustainability practices yielded stronger sustainability-software quality (SWQ) compared to the retired ones.

items.title: Human Resource Management and AI: Building A Collaborative Contextual Transparency Database
items.abstract: While calls for AI transparency are growing, most approaches still treat transparency as a technical property detached from the contexts in which systems are used. We argue instead that AI transparency emerges through social and technologically-situated professional practice. To study this, we develop a database-driven method for contextual AI transparency in recruiting, drawing on 100+ interviews with HR practitioners and iterative practitioner evaluations to construct a database of HR technologies capturing product functionality, claims, assumptions, and AI clarity. Our findings show that transparency is not a fixed system attribute, but a relational outcome shaped by how tools are represented and used in practice. By examining gaps between claims, assumptions, and functionality, we surface forms of opacity overlooked by technical notions of explainability. We contribute a database-building method for analysis of AI systems, empirical insights into transparency in HR technologies, and design implications for practice-centered approaches to AI transparency.

items.title: Influence of support system on country bean production during summer season
items.abstract: Abstract Country bean ( Lablab purpureus L.) is a valuable leguminous vegetable crop with nutritional and economic significance in tropical and subtropical regions. The present study was to evaluate the performance of three photo-insensitive country bean genotypes, namely Sikribi Sheem-1 (V1), Sikribi Sheem-2 (V2) and SB003 (V3), which were grown under three different support systems called horizontal trellis (S1), vertical trellis (staking, S2) and sloped trellis (A-shaped trellis, S3). The results showed that internode length varied significantly among treatments, with Sikribi Sheem-1 under vertical trellis (17.57 cm) exhibiting the greatest length, indicating increased canopy spread and photosynthetic efficiency. However, other vegetative features showed insignificant variation. Flowering occurred earliest in Sikribi Sheem-1 under an A-shaped frame (40.00 days) and latest under a horizontal trellis (45.67 days). Genotype support interaction significantly influenced pod number per plant and pod yield. The highest values were recorded in Sikribi Sheem-1 under vertical trellis (288.83 pods per plant and 1.34 kg per plant), whereas SB003 under staking and A-shaped frame produced the longest pods (9.93 and 9.80 cm) and highest dry matter (22.30%). Pearson correlation analysis revealed strong positive correlations among pod yield, number of pods per plant, number of branches per plant, and pod morphology, highlighting the critical factors for high productivity. Then, Principal Component Analysis (PCA) split growth, physiological, and yield-contributing traits into distinct groups, explaining 62.8% of total variation, whereas heatmap clustering illustrated co-association patterns among traits and treatments. These findings demonstrate that Sikribi Sheem-1 with vertical trellis or staking is the most effective combination for optimizing plant architecture, enhancing assimilate partitioning, improving canopy efficiency, and providing an effective, low-cost strategy to maximize yield and pod quality of climbing country bean under summer cultivation.

items.title: Minority Collective Action for User-Side Fairness
items.abstract: Machine learning models often preserve biases present in training data, leading to unfair treatment of certain minority groups. Despite an array of existing firm-side bias-mitigation techniques, these methods typically incur utility costs and require organizational buy-in. Recognizing that many models rely on user-contributed data, end-users can induce fairness through the framework of Algorithmic Collective Action. In this setting, a coordinated minority group strategically relabels its own data to enhance fairness without altering the firm’s training process. We design practical, model-agnostic, minority-only collective-action methods and validate them on real-world datasets. Our findings show that a subgroup of the minority can substantially reduce unfairness with little impact on overall prediction error.

items.title: Sex differences in parietal alpha power during sustained attention are related to conflict monitoring performance in mild cognitive impairment.
items.abstract: BackgroundSex differences in cognition among individuals with dementias and prodromal stages such as amnestic mild cognitive impairment (aMCI) manifest in variations in severity and prevalence, but underlying brain activity patterns remain unclear. This study is a secondary endpoint study of the Cogmax project.ObjectiveWe examined sex differences in parietal alpha power during an attention task (Simple Vigilance Task, SVT) and its association with conflict monitoring (Stroop Color-Word Test Part 3, T score) in individuals with aMCI.MethodsThe SVT served as the EEG recording condition because of its low cognitive demands and visually driven structure, while the Stroop task provided an independent neuropsychological measure of conflict monitoring. Seventy-seven participants (23 females; 54 males) were included. We analyzed average power spectral density (PSD) across occipital and parietal electrodes (O1-Pz-O2-P7-P8) using multitaper Fourier transform. Normalized alpha power was calculated as integrated 7-11 Hz relative to total 0.1-40 Hz PSD.ResultsAll participants showed high accuracy on the SVT, indicating stable attentional engagement. Covariate-adjusted permutation tests, robust to unbalanced sample sizes, showed that females exhibited higher parietal alpha power and higher Stroop Part 3 T-scores than males. However, when Stroop performance was included as a covariate, the sex difference in alpha power became nonsignificant. A positive correlation between Stroop 3 scores and parietal alpha power was observed in females but not in males, suggesting a sex-specific relationship.ConclusionsParietal alpha activity may be associated with conflict monitoring performance in aMCI, particularly among females, providing evidence for sex-related neural differences in aMCI.

items.title: Hagen-Poiseuille distributed-pressure model of osmotically-driven cytoplasmic flow in severed axons.
items.abstract: Repair (sealing) of traumatic plasmalemmal lesions involves the formation, movement, and accumulation of vesicles at the injury site by active transport and by passive bulk flow of cytoplasm. We show that hypotonic and hypertonic salines affect the direction and rate of vesicle movement in severed crayfish medial giant axons (CMGAs), presumably because osmotically-driven changes in intracellular pressure alter bulk cytoplasmic flow along the axon and at the lesion site. We develop a general Hagen-Poiseuille pressure-cable biophysical model of bulk cytoplasmic flow to predict direction and relative rate of cytoplasmic influx and efflux for CMGAs and other axons modeled as fluid-filled cylinders with distributed osmotic water permeability. Although our general-model applies to axons of any length, this model simplifies for a short-cable model in which the axonal length is much shorter than the hydraulic length constant, i.e., axons like CMGAs. Both General- and Shortcable-Models predict that hypotonic extracellular conditions drive transmembrane water flux into an axon, elevating intracellular pressure that is relieved by cytoplasmic efflux at the injury site. Conversely, hypertonic conditions drive transmembrane water flux out of the axon that is relieved by extracellular fluid influx at the severed end. Our data from CMGAs show that active transport involving molecular motors associated with microtubules and actin in CMGAs is the predominant contributor to vesicle movement towards severed end. Bulk cytoplasmic flow - as assessed by the movement of vesicles and cellular debris that persist when active transport is inhibited - is a lesser contribution to vesicle movement whose extent depends on the difference between extracellular and intracellular osmolarity. Our Hagen-Poiseuille distributed-pressure Model accurately predicts the direction and approximate rate of movement of vesicles and cellular debris under all osmotic conditions tested. Our Model should also account for vesicle behavior in other axons and cylindrical cytoplasmic processes of various diameters and lengths.

items.title: Lower recorded prevalence of Alzheimer's disease in natalizumab-exposed older adults with multiple sclerosis: A hypothesis-generating observation.
items.abstract: Adaptive immune mechanisms, including CD8 T cell-mediated neuroinflammation, are increasingly implicated in Alzheimer's disease. We examined whether exposure to natalizumab, an α4-integrin antagonist that restricts leukocyte trafficking into the central nervous system, was associated with Alzheimer's disease prevalence among older adults with multiple sclerosis. Using Epic Cosmos electronic health record data, we identified 875,226 individuals with MS, of whom 9095 had an Alzheimer's disease diagnosis after age 65 years. Alzheimer's disease prevalence differed significantly across disease-modifying therapies, with natalizumab-treated patients demonstrating the lowest prevalence (0.13%; 95% confidence interval: 0.10-0.17%). These findings demonstrate a lower recorded prevalence of late-life Alzheimer's disease among natalizumab-exposed patients; however, given the aggregated nature of the data, this observation should be considered descriptive and hypothesis-generating.

items.title: Handedness literacy in teachers: Data from Greece, Serbia, and Belgium.
items.abstract: Handedness literacy, a term coined here to refer to one's knowledge about and understanding of handedness, is an understudied yet crucial component of educational neuroscience. It is distinct from attitudes toward left-handers, but it can inform the practical and psychosocial support teachers provide to their left-handed students, thereby promoting better classroom ergonomics and reducing stigma. This study investigated teachers' handedness literacy for the first time, focusing on educators from Greece (n = 273), Serbia (n = 365), and Belgium (n = 213). Qualitative responses from Greek and Serbian educators differed in emphasis (neurobiological versus practical), but generally revealed supportive attitudes towards left-handers. Quantitative analysis from all three countries highlighted factual misunderstandings, with many educators incorrectly associating left-handedness with increased intelligence, or expressing substantial uncertainty about whether left-handedness is a feature of autism and dyslexia. Contrary to our hypothesis, left-handed educators did not demonstrate superior handedness literacy compared to their right-handed counterparts. Additionally, teachers across countries consistently overestimated the proportion of left-handers in the population, possibly conflating left-handedness with general non-right-handedness. Most teachers further acknowledged the need for improved handedness literacy. Findings underline the critical importance of integrating formal training about handedness into teacher education and professional development programs.

items.title: Haemorrhagic Transformation in Breakthrough Ischemic Stroke: Clinical Characteristics, Outcomes, and Anticoagulation Resumption Timing-Insights from the ASPERA-R Study.
items.abstract: The timing of anticoagulation resumption in patients who experience ischemic stroke despite ongoing anticoagulation and develop haemorrhagic transformation (HT) remains uncertain. We aimed to describe the characteristics and outcomes of patients with HT after a breakthrough ischemic stroke and to explore the association between anticoagulation resumption timing and the model-predicted balance of recurrent ischemic and bleeding risks in this high-risk population. We analysed data from patients with breakthrough ischemic stroke receiving anticoagulation therapy from the multicentre ASPERA-R registry. Analyses focused on patients with HT. HT was defined according to the Heidelberg Bleeding Classification based on brain imaging within 24 hours and categorized as haemorrhagic infarction (HI) or parenchymal hematoma (PH). Anticoagulation resumption and its timing were determined by treating clinicians and were not randomized. Landmark Cox regression models were used to evaluate recurrent ischemic events and moderate-to-severe bleeding after anticoagulation resumption. Restricted cubic spline models and exploratory net clinical benefit analyses integrating ischemic and bleeding risks were used to assess the relationship between anticoagulation resumption timing and model-predicted combined risk, overall and across clinically relevant subgroups. Among 1,555 patients with breakthrough ischemic stroke, 269 (17.3%) developed HT, of whom 170 (63.2%) resumed anticoagulation and contributed to the restart-timing analyses. At 90 days, patients with HT had higher crude rates of recurrent ischemic events (27.1% vs 13.8%), moderate-to-severe bleeding (7.4% vs 2.8%), and mortality (34.2% vs 17.7%) compared with patients without HT. In landmark analyses, HT was not associated with recurrent ischemic events (HR 1.42, 95% CI 0.85-2.37) but remained strongly associated with moderate-to-severe bleeding (HR 3.39, 95% CI 1.61-7.13). Exploratory net clinical benefit analyses showed that the model-predicted combined risk reached its nadir at approximately 10 days after stroke in the overall HT population, with substantial uncertainty around this estimate. HT is a marker of poor prognosis in patients with breakthrough ischemic stroke, with an increased risk of bleeding after anticoagulation resumption. Among selected patients who resumed anticoagulation, exploratory modelling suggested that the combined predicted ischemic and bleeding risk reached its nadir at approximately 10 days after stroke. Given the non-randomized treatment timing and potential for treatment-selection bias, this estimate is hypothesis-generating and requires prospective validation.

items.title: Conventional transcutaneous spinal stimulation waveforms recruit sensory pathways more effectively than burst-modulated high-frequency waveforms.
items.abstract: Transcutaneous spinal stimulation (TSS) can improve motor function in people with paresis, although outcomes remain inconsistent across studies. Different stimulation parameters may influence the effectiveness and sensory fiber selectivity of TSS. Here, we systematically compared the ability of ten TSS waveforms applied over the T11-L1 vertebral levels to evoke a soleus muscle response in people with intact neurological function (n = 12). Burst-modulated high-frequency waveforms (2 kHz, 5 kHz, 10 kHz) were compared with a conventional square waveform of the same total cathodal phase duration (400 μ s); a longer conventional waveform (1,000 μ s) was also tested. All waveforms were delivered in biphasic and monophasic pulse types. Relative to the conventional 400 μ s waveform, response threshold intensities were lower with the 1,000 μ s waveform (-28 to -27%) and higher with high-frequency stimulation: 2 kHz (+26 to +43%), 5 kHz (+111 to +129%), and 10 kHz (+254 to +273%). Recruitment curve slopes were also steeper with the 1,000 μ s waveform (+33 to +46%) and generally less steep with high-frequency stimulation: 2 kHz (biphasic: -25%), 5 kHz (-50 to -46%), and 10 kHz (-75 to -64%). Paired-pulse depression was weak at intensities >100%-120% of threshold but increased markedly at higher intensities across all waveforms. The 10 kHz waveforms showed the weakest paired-pulse depression, consistent with a smaller sensory contribution than the conventional 400 μ s waveform. Onset latencies were comparable to peripheral conduction times at near-threshold intensities but became shorter at higher stimulation intensities, suggesting changes in the relative contributions of sensory and motor fiber activation. Overall, burst-modulated high-frequency waveforms required higher stimulation intensities than conventional waveforms to evoke spinally-evoked motor responses and provided no physiological evidence of an advantage over conventional waveforms.

items.title: What can behavior tell us about neural dynamics?
items.abstract: For decades, systems neuroscience treated behavior as an endpoint: a simplified output, such as a button press, lick, or saccade, used to isolate neural computations. Richer behavioral measurements have expanded this view by revealing neural dynamics hidden by simple outputs. Yet behavior is not a direct readout of brain activity, because similar behavioral outputs can arise from different neural mechanisms. Interpreting neural dynamics is therefore an inverse problem with no straightforward solution. Behavior can constrain this problem by exposing sensorimotor loops, narrowing plausible explanations for population activity, and formalizing neural-behavioral relationships in joint models. Together, these approaches position behavior as a principled constraint on interpreting neural dynamics and latent cognitive, affective, and computational states.

items.title: Multiple combinations of GPCR activation gate the induction of NMDAR-independent LTD in mouse visual cortex.
items.abstract: Activity-dependent synaptic weakening, including long-term depression (LTD), is a fundamental mechanism underlying experience-dependent circuit remodeling. At excitatory synapses, two mechanistically distinct forms of LTD have been identified: NMDAR-LTD, triggered by activation of NMDA receptors, and mGluR-LTD, mediated by group I metabotropic glutamate receptors. NMDAR-LTD is the best-characterized form and has been described in numerous brain regions. In contrast, in cortical synapses mGluR-LTD has been investigated primarily in the hippocampus, where it requires mGluR5 activation and its molecular mechanisms are well established. Although NMDAR-LTD is also well documented in the neocortex, mGluR-LTD remains comparatively poorly characterized, particularly in primary sensory cortices, despite growing evidence that mGluR signaling contributes to sensory deprivation-induced synaptic remodeling. We examined mGluR-LTD in slices of primary visual cortex of rats and mice of all sexes and found that layer II/III pyramidal neurons do express an NMDAR-independent LTD. Like in CA1, mGluR-LTD in V1 depends on mGluR5 activation and ongoing protein synthesis regulated by FMRP. Unlike CA1, however, where activation of mGluR5 alone is sufficient to induce mGluR-LTD, induction in V1 requires the co-activation of at least two neuromodulatory receptors, including mGluR5 together with muscarinic, noradrenergic, or serotonergic receptors. This more stringent gating mechanism may reflect the tighter constraints on synaptic plasticity in the neocortex, consistent with the view that the hippocampus and neocortex are specialized for rapid and gradual learning, respectively.Significance statement At excitatory synapses, two mechanistically distinct forms of long-term depression (LTD) have been identified: NMDAR-LTD and mGluR-LTD. While NMDAR-LTD is widespread, mGluR-LTD has been studied primarily in the hippocampus and remains poorly characterized in sensory cortices, despite evidence that mGluRs contribute to sensory deprivation-induced synaptic remodeling. This study shows that an NMDAR-independent form of LTD can be induced in visual cortical slices. Unlike hippocampus, where activation of mGluR5 alone is sufficient to induce mGluR-LTD, induction in visual cortex requires the co-activation of at least two neuromodulatory receptors, including mGluR5 together with muscarinic, noradrenergic, or serotonergic receptors. This stricter gating mechanism may reflect the tighter constraints on synaptic plasticity in the neocortex, consistent with its role in gradual, rather than rapid, learning.

items.title: Learning-dependent hippocampal-striatal reorganization during sequential decision-making in pigeons.
items.abstract: Adaptive sequential decision-making requires animals to learn how actions shape future states and rewards while adjusting behavioral strategies as experience accumulates. Although the hippocampus is implicated in state-structure representation and the striatum in value learning, how learning strategies evolve from exploratory sampling to efficient exploitation and how hippocampal-striatal interactions reorganize alongside this transition remain unclear. We trained six pigeons of undetermined sex to perform a probabilistic two-step decision task while simultaneously recording behavioral choices and hippocampal-striatal local field potentials. Strategy evolution was tracked using a dynamic reinforcement-learning framework in which model-based, model-free, and weighted model-based/model-free models were fitted across sliding windows. Hippocampal-striatal functional coordination was assessed using phase-locking analysis, and directed predictive influence was quantified using kernel Granger causality. The weighted model best explained choice dynamics, indicating a shift from model-based-like control during early acquisition toward model-free-like control during later stable performance. This behavioral shift was accompanied by two complementary neural changes: hippocampal-striatal phase coordination increased across learning, whereas hippocampus-to-striatum directed predictive influence decreased and covaried positively with model-based-like strategy weight. Direction-ratio analysis showed that hippocampus-to-striatum remained the predominant direction throughout learning, indicating reduced influence rather than directional reversal. After acquisition, hippocampus-to-striatum directed influence was not uniformly reduced but remained relatively preserved during rare, low-value, unrewarded, or less expected events. Together, these findings reveal a learning-dependent reorganization of hippocampal-striatal dynamics, in which increasing functional coordination is accompanied by reduced but condition-dependent hippocampal-to-striatal influence as behavior becomes more stable and efficient.Significance Statement Adaptive learning requires coordinated changes in behavioral strategy and neural interactions as animals progress from exploration to stable performance. Here, we show that pigeons gradually shifted from flexible, model-based-like control toward more stable, model-free-like behavior during sequential learning. In parallel, hippocampal-striatal interactions underwent a complementary reorganization: phase coordination progressively increased, whereas hippocampus-to-striatum directed predictive influence decreased with declining model-based-like control. Importantly, this directed influence remained relatively preserved during rare, low-value, or unrewarded events. These findings link behavioral strategy transition to the dynamic reorganization of hippocampal-striatal interactions, revealing how neural systems may simultaneously support efficient learned behavior while retaining sensitivity to behaviorally informative events.

items.title: Opioid-glutamate interactions modulate intrinsically rewarded communication in European starlings.
items.abstract: Affiliative, non-sexual vocal communication is essential for social learning and bonding, yet relatively little is known about its neural bases. Past research on songbirds demonstrates that song produced in affiliative, non-sexual flocks correlates positively with a bird's intrinsic reward state, and the link between song and reward is regulated by mu opioid receptors (MORs) in the medial preoptic area (MPOA). RNAseq studies also reveal a strong positive association between affiliative song and glutamatergic gene expression in MPOA, with NMDA receptor 1 (GRIN1) and glutamate receptor scaffolding protein (Shank2) correlating strongly with affiliative singing. In male European starlings we tested the hypothesis that MOR-glutamate interactions in the MPOA regulate affiliative communication. Peripheral administration of the MOR agonist fentanyl increased affiliative singing and calling behavior while reducing stress-related behavior, beak wiping. The effects on vocal but not stress-related behavior were prevented by administration of the NMDA receptor antagonist MK-801. c-Fos mapping revealed that fentanyl increased neural activity in caudal MPOA (cMPOA) and interconnected regions implicated in social behavior, song production, and reward, and that these effects were reversed by MK-801. To identify a local site of MOR-glutamate interaction, we used AAV shRNA to downregulate Shank2 in MPOA. This manipulation prevented fentanyl from stimulating affiliative singing behavior, also without affecting stress reduction, suggesting that MOR-glutamate interactions in the MPOA facilitate social communication but not associated stress reduction. Together these findings provide the first experimental evidence that MOR-glutamate interactions within the MPOA, particularly the cMPOA, contribute to affiliative, rewarding vocal communication.Significance Statement Affiliative, non-sexual vocal communication is fundamental to social cohesion and well-being, yet its neural mechanisms are poorly understood. This study identifies a critical role for interactions between mu opioid receptors and glutamatergic signaling in promoting non-sexual, rewarding vocal communication. In a songbird experimental system, we demonstrate that NMDA receptor activity and the postsynaptic glutamate receptor scaffolding protein Shank2 are required for opioid facilitation of affiliative song. Our findings further reveal the medial preoptic area, particularly its caudal subdivision, to be an important site of this opioid-glutamate interaction. Together, these results extend opioid-glutamate interaction frameworks beyond classic reward circuits and suggest the existence of a conserved neural mechanism supporting affiliative social behavior across vertebrates.

items.title: Hospital-wide massive transfusion over time: Indications, treatment strategies, and clinical outcomes.
items.abstract: Massive transfusion (MT) is a lifesaving intervention for severe hemorrhage. Contemporary data on indications, transfusion practices, and outcomes across a broad in-hospital population remain limited. This retrospective cohort study included adult patients receiving MT at Karolinska University Hospital between 2016 and 2021. MT was defined as transfusion of ≥10 red blood cell (RBC) units within 24 h. Data were obtained from the hospital transfusion registry and medical records. A total of 486 MT events were identified. Median age was 60 years (interquartile range [IQR] 46-70), and 65.6% of patients were male. The most common indications were trauma (15.6%), abdominal cancer surgery (15.0%), cardiothoracic surgery (14.0%), and vascular surgery (12.3%). The overall median RBC:plasma:platelet ratio was 5:5:1, consistent with balanced transfusion strategies. MT was more frequently associated with acute than elective procedures (67.2% vs. 32.8%, p < 0.001). Fibrinogen, tranexamic acid, and prothrombin complex concentrate were administered in 69.5%, 52.1%, and 13.6% of cases, respectively. Mortality was 10.3% at 24 h and 31.7% at 30 days. The annual number of MT events decreased significantly during the study period (p < 0.001), corresponding to an approximately 40% reduction between 2016 and 2021. MT was required across a wide range of surgical and medical specialties and remained associated with substantial mortality. Balanced transfusion strategies were well implemented, whereas the use of adjunct hemostatic therapies varied considerably. The marked reduction in MT events over time suggests improvements in hemorrhage management and bleeding control.

items.title: Quality and Quantity of Research Publications by Iranian Neurosurgeons: A Scopus-Based Bibliometric Analysis of the 21st Century.
items.abstract: Bibliometric analyses can clarify research productivity, collaboration, and evidence quality. Given expanding neuroscience research, improved bibliographic indexing, and the growth of neurosurgical practice in Iran, a comprehensive evaluation of Iranian neurosurgeons' publications is warranted to characterize long-term trends and guide future national research priorities. Iranian neurosurgeons were identified through a list obtained from the Iranian Medical Council Organization. These surgeons were verified, and their publications published through December 31, 2024, were identified through Scopus, followed by deduplication. Extracted variables included author characteristics, authorship roles, collaboration patterns, journal metrics, study design, citation counts, research topics, and levels of evidence (LOE). LOEs were classified from I (highest) to V (lowest) using an adapted Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine (OCEBM) 2009 framework, and temporal trends were analyzed across three time periods (2000-2010, 2011-2020, and 2021-2024). Overall, 4,338 unique publications were included. Publication output increased over time: 617 studies (2000-2010), 2,206 (2011-2020), and 1,515 (2021-2024). Tehran accounted for 58% of publications, followed by Fars, East Azerbaijan, and Razavi Khorasan. International co-authorship increased from 119 (19%) in 2000-2010 to 513 (34%) in 2021-2024 (p < 0.001). The median journal impact factor (IF) rose from 1.7 to 2.0. Most studies were level IV (40%) and level V (23%) of evidence. Among trauma-related studies, 45% were classified as Level I-II. Iranian neurosurgeons' contributions to academic publications increased during the 21st century, accompanied by growing international collaboration. High-level clinical evidence was limited, highlighting the need for strengthened research infrastructure and methodological support.

items.title: An unfair fight: multiorgan mechanisms that disarm host defenses and deplete the physiological reserve needed to withstand infection and sepsis after spinal cord injury.
items.abstract: Spinal cord injury (SCI) causes vulnerability to infection and sepsis that cannot be explained by impaired mobility and healthcare-related exposure alone. SCI is known to disrupt multiple organ systems, but how these disruptions collectively shift the balance between host protection and microbial challenge remains poorly defined. In this narrative review, we examine how systemic dysfunction caused by SCI impairs the capacity to prevent infection, contain established pathogens, and withstand escalating infectious stress. We organize clinical and experimental evidence around functions that together determine host protection: barrier protection, immune surveillance, pathogen clearance, and physiological reserve. The first three restrict microbial access, establishment, and burden, whereas physiological reserve determines the capacity of tissues and organs to maintain function as infectious stress escalates. We distinguish experimentally demonstrated mechanisms from clinical associations for infection vulnerability and examine how injury level and time shape these vulnerabilities. We trace how pneumonia, urinary tract infection, and pressure wound infection can progress to sepsis, and delineate the mechanisms that create increasingly unequal contests in which pathogens encounter a host with progressively weakened defenses, depleted physiological reserve, and an environment that favors pathogen establishment and persistence. This framework identifies testable gaps and a translational path toward earlier risk stratification, management of infection within the context of SCI, and potential strategies to preserve or restore host defense and resilience to infection, shifting the balance of this unequal contest back toward the host.

items.title: FGFR1-driven brachyury promotes endothelial-like differentiation of glioblastoma stem cells via SOX2/ZEB1/YAP1 signaling pathways.
items.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is characterized by intensive vascular proliferation that is essential for tumor growth. Recent studies indicate the existence of tumor-derived endothelial-like cells can arise from the differentiation of GBM stem cells (GSCs). The transcription factor brachyury plays a critical role in promoting stem cell identity and vasculogenesis during normal embryonic development. However, its involvement in endothelial-like differentiation of GSCs remains unknown. By integrating clinical bioinformatics from GBM databases with preclinical in vitro and in vivo models, including patient-derived GSC cell lines and xenografts, we found that brachyury is highly expressed in GBM tissues and correlates with angiogenesis genes. Our study demonstrated that brachyury is activated by fibroblast growth factor receptor 1 (FGFR1), which subsequently promotes GSC differentiation into endothelial-like cells via SOX2/ZEB1/YAP1 signaling. GSCs with high brachyury expression display great sensitivity to selective FGFR inhibitors in vascular tube formation assays. In vivo pharmacological targeting of FGFR1 with inhibitor E7090 or brachyury gene editing using Cas9/gRNA suppresses GBM neovascularization and tumor growth. Furthermore, gene signature analysis of GBM patients further demonstrated that a lower FGFR1/brachyury/SOX2/ZEB1/YAP1 signature score significantly correlates with favorable overall survival outcomes. These findings highlight the importance of FGFR1-driven brachyury activation in GSC-derived neovascularization and suggest that targeting the FGFR1-directed brachyury/SOX2/ZEB1/YAP1 signaling represents a promising therapeutic strategy for GBM.

items.title: Desync and connect: Noninvasive MEG evidence of long-range coupling between locally desynchronized regions.
items.abstract: A prevailing assumption in systems neuroscience is that long-range phase coupling between cortical regions requires locally synchronized oscillatory activity within each interacting area. Here we ask whether distal phase coupling can be detected from MEG data when both interacting regions undergo concurrent event-related desynchronization (ERD). Using controlled simulations with progressively disrupted local phase coherence, we first establish that the Context-Dependent PSIICOS (CD-PSIICOS) framework - a projection-based connectivity estimator that separates power-dominated spatial leakage from interaction-specific cross-spectral structure - can recover distal coupling under increasing local phase dispersion, whereas estimators based on the imaginary part of the cross-spectrum fail at near-zero lags. We then analyzed recordings of a center-out reaching dataset from nine participants. A group decomposition of the coupling time courses identifies four long-range networks in alpha (8-13 Hz) and two in beta (15-25 Hz), each with its own time window. For each network we follow the local connections between its own sources as the power-dominated subspace is projected out, separating leakage-driven from leakage-resistant local coupling. In the earliest alpha network the leakage-resistant pairs stay at or below their pre-stimulus level at every rank while the power of the same sources falls, so this interhemispheric interaction may have no stable local counterpart. In the beta networks such a counterpart does survive, but the coupling it carries is an order of magnitude weaker than the long-range coupling of the same sources. Only in the latest alpha window, by which time power has returned to baseline, do local and long-range coupling rise together. Factorising the coupling into the amplitude of the single-trial cross-terms and the consistency of their phases separates the same cases: in the networks without a local counterpart, phase consistency increases inside the window while the amplitude of the cross-terms declines, whereas in the network whose local coupling rises with it, the increase reflects a growth of the cross-terms themselves rather than any improvement in their phase agreement. Long-range phase coupling can therefore persist, and in places strengthen, between regions undergoing macroscopic ERD, and noninvasive MEG can resolve this dissociation when leakage-aware estimation is employed.

items.title: Clip-to-trial: EEG-based decoding network with long short-term self-attention for DRDS recognition.
items.abstract: Dynamic random-dot stereograms (DRDS) elicit stereoscopic perception associated with high-level binocular visual processing, which can be decoded from EEG signals. However, existing EEG-based approaches predominantly rely on clip-level learning, leading to feature-label misalignment and limited modeling of trial-level spatiotemporal dependencies. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a clip-to-trial long short-term self-attention network (C2T-LSTSA) for EEG-based DRDS recognition. The proposed method first extracts discriminative spatiotemporal features from EEG clips using a multi-scale local feature extraction module. A trial-level feature reconstruction module is then introduced to explicitly map clip-level representations into semantically consistent trial-level features. Furthermore, a long short-term self-attention module is employed to jointly model local temporal dependencies within each reconstructed trial representation and global dependencies among multiple reconstructed trial representations derived from the same original EEG trial. Extensive experiments on three EEG datasets collected from strabismus patients demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches under both subject-dependent and subject-independent evaluation protocols, indicating its effectiveness and robustness for objective assessment of stereoscopic visual function. The reference datasets are available at https://github.com/YANGeeg/TJU-SRD-datasets and the code is at https://github.com/wu860898-design/C2T-LSTSA.

items.title: Behavioral and neurobiological effects of vicarious social defeat stress in rodents: a scoping review.
items.abstract: Psychosocial stress is a risk factor for psychiatric disorders, and evidence indicates that witnessing adversity can be harmful. Vicarious social defeat stress (VSDS) models the indirect psychosocial suffering that arises when a rodent perceives the social defeat of a conspecific without being physically attacked. Despite the methodologically heterogeneous growth of this evidence, a map of its effects on observer animals was lacking. This scoping review aimed to map the behavioral effects and neurobiological alterations reported in rodents exposed to VSDS, and to characterize paradigm variants, exposure parameters and moderating variables (sex, age, strain). Its contribution is a detailed, observer-focused integration of behavioral domains, biological substrates and protocol characteristics across 60 studies. It was conducted according to the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and reported following the PRISMA extension for scoping reviews; the protocol was registered on the Open Science Framework, and sources were searched without language or date restrictions. The most frequently reported phenotypes were social avoidance, anxiety-like behavior and anhedonia, accompanied in subsets of studies by depression-like behavior, cognitive deficits, altered fear learning and escalated substance intake. Most studies reported neurobiological measures, with a predominance of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and adaptations across the mesocorticolimbic dopaminergic system, extended amygdala, hippocampal formation, medial prefrontal cortex and neuroimmune signatures. Direct witness-versus-defeated comparisons revealed qualitative convergence alongside dissociations, while females remained under-represented. VSDS yields consistently reported affective phenotypes and circuit-level adaptations, positioning it as a relevant model of indirect trauma whose advancement depends on methodological harmonization, sex-balanced designs and investigation of socially transmitted stress.

items.title: A superconserved orphan GPCR in brain function and disease: insights into GPR85.
items.abstract: G protein‑coupled receptor 85 (GPR85), also known as superconserved receptor expressed in brain 2 (SREB2), is a highly conserved orphan class A G protein-coupled receptors (GPCR) with preferential expression in the central nervous system (CNS). Since its identification, GPR85 has emerged as a critical regulator of neuronal development, synaptic function, and circuit excitability, with accumulating evidence implicating its involvement in cognitive and behavioral processes. Moreover, further studies have linked dysregulation of GPR85 to neuropsychiatric disorders, including schizophrenia and autism spectrum disorder (ASD), highlighting its potential relevance to human brain disease. In this review, we summarize current knowledge of GPR85 biology by integrating findings from animal models with emerging evidence from human studies as well as our analyses of publicly available human single-nucleus and spatial transcriptomic datasets to refine current understanding of GPR85 organization in the human brain. Together, these perspectives support a revised view of GPR85 as a context-dependent modulator of brain function operating across multiple cellular systems, highlighting the need to determine its roles in brain physiology, pathology, and therapeutic targeting.

items.title: Distinct drug and aversive cue-reactivity patterns are associated with opioid use disorder.
items.abstract: Although addiction models posit that drug and aversive cues contribute to relapse, few studies have investigated cue-elicited biomarkers of relapse in opioid use disorder (OUD). Individuals with OUD (n=64, 20F) and healthy controls (CTL; n=35, 19F) completed a cue-reactivity task during functional magnetic resonance imaging at baseline. Participants viewed Negative, Neutral, and Drug cues and provided ratings of valence, arousal, stress, and urge to use drugs. OUD participants were followed up for a three-month period to determine abstinence (n=29) versus relapse (n=35). Blood oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signals were extracted from striatum, insula, anterior cingulate cortex [ACC], amygdala, and hippocampus regions of interest (ROI). Linear mixed effects models were computed for ratings and ROI BOLD signals with group (OUD versus CTL; Abstinent versus Relapsed OUD subgroups) and condition as fixed factors. Whole-brain analyses were computed to complement ROI analyses, and both were corrected for multiple comparisons. Compared to CTL, OUD reported greater arousal, stress, and urge ratings to Drug cues but exhibited lower nucleus accumbens, insula, and ACC ROI BOLD signal to Negative cues. Whole-brain results replicated this pattern in OUD and also revealed blunted (a) inferior frontal and precentral gyri responses to Negative cues; and (b) orbitofrontal cortex responses to Drug cues. In contrast, OUD subgroups did not differ on subjective or brain responses. Disengagement from aversive stimuli via interoceptive and reward circuitry may be a vulnerability marker for OUD. Replication is warranted across additional aversive paradigms and OUD samples powered to evaluate longitudinal outcomes.

items.title: TrkB and NMDA receptor mRNA expression in phrenic motor neurons following cervical spinal hemisection.
items.abstract: Cervical spinal cord injury (SCI) can interrupt descending bulbospinal pathways that support breathing, increasing the risk of serious respiratory complications and death. The C2 spinal hemisection (C2SH) model reduces neural drive to the phrenic motor pool, impairing ventilatory-related diaphragm activity with incomplete spontaneous recovery. Signaling via the tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB) and glutamatergic transmission through N-methyl-d-aspartate receptors (NMDA-R) have been implicated in this recovery, but whether injury-related changes in TrkB and NMDA-R mRNA expression are uniform across phrenic motor neurons (PhMNs) remains unknown. We hypothesized that TrkB and NMDA-R mRNA transcript number or density would show size- and side-dependent regulation after C2SH. RNAscope was used to quantify the number and density of TrkB and NMDA-R mRNA transcripts in PhMNs ipsilateral and contralateral to C2SH in adult male rats. In mixed linear models with animal as a random effect, there was no effect of PhMN surface area, spinal cord side relative to C2SH or experimental group on TrkB or NMDA-R mRNA transcript number per PhMN. Interaction effects showed TrkB mRNA transcript number increased after C2SH, predominantly ipsilaterally and at larger PhMNs by 21 days post-C2SH (21DSH). Within individual PhMNs, concurrent increases in TrkB and NMDA-R mRNA transcript number were evident by 21DSH. Results were concordant for TrkB and NMDA-R mRNA density within motor neurons. These findings suggest size- and side-dependent changes in TrkB and NMDA-R mRNA regulation within the phrenic motor pool after C2SH, consistent with motor unit-specific plasticity that may contribute to spontaneous respiratory recovery after cervical SCI.

items.title: Age-dependent structural brain aging in medication-free major depressive disorder: A multi-site analysis from COORDINATE-MDD consortium.
items.abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is associated with altered brain structure and accelerated brain aging. However, previous studies have been limited by clinical samples with mixed medication status and multiple mood states, modest sample sizes, underrepresentation of older adults with MDD, and/or reliance on summary-level data. Harmonized T1-weighted MRI from MDD (n = 645), all medication-free and in a current depressive episode, and matched healthy controls (n = 645), segmented into 145 regional volumes, from 11 sites in COORDINATE-MDD consortium. Brain age gap (BAG) was estimated cross-sectionally using gradient boosting regression with nested cross-validation. Group differences in BAG (and age-corrected BAG [cBAG]) were examined across age strata. Regional contributions were evaluated using SHAP values. MDD was associated with significantly elevated cBAG compared with healthy controls (mean difference + 2.0 years [95% CI 1.251, 2.774], Cohen's d -0.289 [95% CI -0.399, -0.179]). Age-stratified analyses showed no differences before mid-30s, with progressively larger gaps thereafter, reaching +6.8 years in MDD aged 55 and older in unadjusted analyses (4.3 years after accounting for site). cBAG differed across neuroanatomical phenotypes previously identified using COORDINATE-MDD data. Key contributing regions included lateral and medial prefrontal regions, middle temporal gyrus, putamen, supplementary motor cortex, central operculum, and cerebellum. Structural brain aging in MDD is age-dependent and most pronounced in a neuroanatomical phenotype associated with poorer key clinical outcomes. The findings are consistent with, but do not establish, neuroprogression models of MDD and demonstrate that cBAG is not a uniform feature of MDD, being more strongly expressed in a specifically clinically vulnerable disease phenotype.

items.title: Immune-Microbiome Crosstalk in the Developmental Origins of Neurodevelopmental Disorders.
items.abstract: Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) arise from genetic and environmental factors converging across development, from embryogenesis through adulthood. Two systems central to brain development, the immune system and the microbiome, are incompletely formed at birth. Development of these immune and microbiome systems is shaped by factors transferred across prenatal and postnatal maternal-offspring interfaces including the placenta, birth canal, and breast. Despite literature linking each system independently to NDD risk, these fields have largely proceeded in parallel, rarely interrogating their interactions. This siloed approach constrains mechanistic understanding and progress. Here, we present evidence that the immune system and microbiome are interacting, not independent, influences on neurodevelopmental programming. Preclinical evidence from germ-free, antibiotic depletion, and maternal immune activation models demonstrates that perturbation of either system alters the other; human cohort evidence remains largely associational. Across each maternal-offspring interface, immune and microbial signals converge on the developing brain, acting on peripheral and neuroimmune populations. Microglia emerge as a recurring cellular mediator. Resolving mechanisms of NDD risk requires experimental designs that treat immune and microbial variables as interactive and that span prenatal through postnatal development. The field must move beyond disciplinary silos to integrate these systems across the full neurodevelopmental time course they jointly shape.

items.title: Post-transcriptional regulation of FGF signaling: insights from musculoskeletal system.
items.abstract: Fibroblast growth factor (FGF) signaling plays a pivotal role in the development, maintenance, and regeneration of musculoskeletal tissues. While its transcriptional regulation has been extensively characterized, accumulating evidence indicates that FGF activity is also modulated by a diverse array of post-transcriptional mechanisms. In this review, microRNAs, long non-coding RNAs, alternative splicing, and RNA modifications are examined as key regulators of FGF ligands and receptors across bone, cartilage, muscle, and tooth. RNA-binding proteins are also discussed as regulators of FGF transcript stability and translation. The effects of these RNA-based mechanisms on FGF ligand and receptor abundance, isoform production, and signaling responsiveness are compared, and a pathway-specific RNA regulome is proposed as an organizing framework to integrate these mechanisms across musculoskeletal tissues. This approach also distinguishes directly demonstrated RNA-FGF interactions from indirect associations with connected signaling pathways. The therapeutic implications of targeting post-transcriptional nodes, particularly through non-coding RNAs and epitranscriptomic marks, are discussed in the context of musculoskeletal disease and regeneration, highlighting promising avenues for future musculoskeletal interventions.

items.title: A systematic overview of the current strategies for managing cancer-related cognitive impairment in children and adolescent cancer survivors.
items.abstract: Childhood cancer survivors (CCSs) experience a premature onset of ageing-related morbidities, including cancer-related cognitive impairment (CRCI), attributable to epigenetic age acceleration (EAA). The National Cancer Institute (NCI) recommended non-pharmacological strategies (NPIs) as the optimal approach. To address current gaps in the literature, we conducted a systematic review of RCTs across six databases to provide a comprehensive overview of NPIs for managing CRCI in CCSs and adolescents, following the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions and the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analysis (PRISMA) statement. Thirteen publications and eleven RCTs were included, including two quasi-experimental and six pilot and feasibility studies. The sample included individuals aged 4 to 17 years with solid brain and haematological tumours. Strategies included academic skills interventions, cognitive-motor training with digital and analogue systems, computerised and non-computerised cognitive training, web-based physical activity, and physical activity with active video gaming or exergaming. The results suggest improvements in intellectual function and cognitive abilities following structured cognitive training programs. The integration of these interventions in a coordinated survivorship care plan across healthcare, educational, and family systems will support the cognitive development and adaptive outcomes to reduce learning and social disparities in children and adolescents with cancer. Further RCTs are needed to allow for rigorous quantitative data synthesis and to target specific age groups.

items.title: Neurotensin Signaling in Analgesia: Receptor Mechanisms, Targeted Drug Development, and Therapeutic Prospects for Pain and Comorbid Depression.
items.abstract: Opioids are effective for severe pain but are limited by adverse effects and the risk of opioid use disorder (OUD), while non-opioid analgesics may provide insufficient relief. Neurotensin (NT), an endogenous neuropeptide, has attracted interest as a potential analgesic, with encouraging findings mainly from preclinical studies. This review summarizes advances in NT-based analgesic development, focusing on the pain-modulatory mechanisms of NTSR1 and NTSR2, the two principal neurotensin G protein-coupled receptors recognized by IUPHAR/BPS, and receptor-directed drug-design strategies. Sortilin, historically termed NTSR3 in some literature, is discussed separately because it is structurally distinct from these GPCRs. We examine NT-derived ligands, opioid-NT bifunctional compounds such as BNT-12, and combination approaches involving NT and opioid therapies. Their potential benefits are considered alongside safety concerns and translational limitations, including opioid-related adverse effects and pruritus. Although preclinical studies suggest promising analgesic effects, the comparative safety advantages of these strategies remain unestablished. NT may also influence mood regulation, making it relevant to the frequent co-occurrence of chronic pain with depression and anxiety. Overall, receptor-selective, multitarget, and combination approaches based on NT may offer complementary strategies for treating pain and associated affective symptoms. Further research is needed to establish their efficacy, safety, and clinical applicability, including whether they can reduce adverse effects and abuse liability.

items.title: The Red Nucleus in Motor Control and Autism Spectrum Disorder.
items.abstract: Neuromotor differences of motor coordination, timing, postural regulation, and prospective motor control are common and emerge early in autism spectrum disorder (ASD). However, their underlying neural mechanisms remain incompletely understood, with existing research emphasising cortical and cerebellar systems. This review re-examines the red nucleus (RN), a midbrain structure embedded within cortical, cerebellar, and olivary motor pathways, as an underexplored component of distributed sensorimotor networks. We synthesise evidence from comparative neuroanatomy, animal experiments, human neuroimaging, movement disorders, and autism research, distinguishing direct RN findings from broader circuit-level inferences. Neuroimaging studies have reported RN-region susceptibility differences in autistic children, including an exploratory association with fine-motor development, but reproducible links to specific motor processes and RN-related causal mechanisms remain unestablished. We therefore propose a testable hypothesis that differences in RN structure, function, or connectivity may be associated with specific dimensions of motor function in autism. Error-related sensorimotor adaptation provides a primary experimental target, complemented by prospective motor control. Future investigations combining RN-sensitive neuroimaging, quantitative motor assessment, and transdiagnostic comparisons with developmental coordination disorder may determine whether RN-related measures provide explanatory information beyond sensorimotor systems. This framework positions the RN as a candidate component of autism-related motor networks.

items.title: Association between obsessive-compulsive symptoms, clozapine, and other antipsychotic treatment in psychotic disorders: a systematic review and meta-analysis of epidemiological findings.
items.abstract: Obsessive-compulsive symptoms (OCS) and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) are common in schizophrenia spectrum disorders (SCZ), yet their aetiology remains unclear. Antipsychotics, particularly clozapine (CLZ), have been implicated, but the strength and consistency of this association remain uncertain. A systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis was conducted to evaluate the incidence and prevalence of OCS and OCD in psychosis, comparing people treated with CLZ and other antipsychotics, including first and second generation. The search identified thirty two studies. The prevalence of OCS was similar between the CLZ-treated and the non-CLZ groups [41%, 95% CI: 28-54% vs. 30%, 95% CI: 22-38%; p=0.183]. In contrast, OCD prevalence was significantly higher in the CLZ group [25%, 95% CI: 18-33% vs. 12%, 95% CI: 7-18%; p=0.007]. De novo outcomes did not differ significantly between groups, de novo OCS was 26% [95% CI: 17-36%] with CLZ versus 14% [95% CI: 7-21%] with non-CLZ antipsychotics (p=0.239), and de novo OCD was 22% [95% CI: 9-36%] versus 19% [95% CI: 17-21%] (p=0.458). In the two studies that had measured the incidence of de novo OCS or OCD, the incidence rate was zero in all groups. These findings suggest a potential association between CLZ and increased rates of OCS and OCD in cross-sectional studies, though longitudinal evidence is lacking. Methodological limitations, including detection bias, confounding by indication and limited prospective data, highlight the need for further longitudinal and pharmacoepidemiologic research to clarify causal pathways.

items.title: Sex-dependent behavioral effects of chronic unpredictable stress in mice reveal methodological challenges in the assessment of stress-related phenotypes in females.
items.abstract: Chronic unpredictable stress (CUS) is widely used to model depression-like behaviors in rodents. However, its validation has been established in male animals, and its applicability to females remains poorly characterized. We evaluated the validity of a CUS protocol in male and female Balb/c mice using the sucrose preference test (SPT), forced swim test (FST), elevated plus maze (EPM), open field test (OFT), and integrated emotionality z-scores. Predictive validity was assessed using different imipramine treatment schedules. Additional experiments examined the influence of sucrose concentration and estrous cycle stage on basal sucrose preference in females. In male mice, 21 days of CUS reduced sucrose preference and emotionality z-scores. Chronic imipramine treatment initiated during the last 14 days of stress exposure prevented these behavioral alterations and reduced immobility time in the FST, whereas no significant effects were detected in the EPM. In female mice, CUS did not induce changes in sucrose preference or emotionality z-scores, although imipramine reduced immobility in the FST. Although CUS protocols are widely validated in male rodents, the protocol showed limited sensitivity in females. Basal sucrose preference was influenced by estrous cycle stage and sucrose concentration, with reduced preference during periovulatory and greater preference during post-ovulatory stages only when sucrose was 2%. These findings indicate that behavioral endpoints validated in male rodents may not show comparable sensitivity in females and highlight the importance of considering baseline behavioral characteristics, estrous cycle stage, and sucrose concentration when designing and interpreting chronic stress studies.

items.title: Multi-platform framework for mapping somatic retrotransposition in human tissues.
items.abstract: Mobile element insertions (MEIs) shape the human genome in both germline and somatic tissues. While inherited MEIs are well characterized, identifying somatic MEIs (sMEIs) in non-cancer tissues remains challenging due to their low allelic fraction and repetitive nature. Here, we present an integrative framework for sMEI mapping that leverages modern sequencing technologies and analytical innovations. We first benchmarked sMEI detection methods, demonstrating advantages of long-read and MEI-targeted sequencing for ultra-rare events, and established an effective cross-platform integrative approach using a mixture of well-established cell lines. Haplotype phasing and donor-specific genome assemblies further refined sMEI calls by distinguishing germline and false signals in in silico tumor-normal mixtures. We also developed a source-tracing approach based on sequence variation within MEIs, expanding the catalog of active source elements beyond traditional transduction-based inference. Applying this framework to benchmark donor tissues, we detected rare somatic L1 insertions in all four tissue types examined, revealing structural and source diversity. Our work provides a foundational framework and biological insight into somatic retrotransposition in the human body.

items.title: Microcephaly-causative ASPM mutations disrupt mitotic spindle orientation and timely specification of human outer radial glia cells.
items.abstract: Mutations in the gene abnormal spindle-like, microcephaly-associated (ASPM) are the most common cause of primary microcephaly (MCPH). The mechanisms underlying MCPH have remained unclear, as ASPM disruption leads to species-specific phenotypes. Using human cortical organoids, we observed premature mitotic spindle randomization in ASPM-mutant ventricular cortical progenitors, followed by their early delamination to the basal compartment. Similar delamination following mitotic spindle misorientation could be induced by overexpression of Inscuteable, further linking the two phenotypes. Delaminated progenitors resembled outer radial glial cells (oRGCs), which are selectively amplified in human corticogenesis, but they failed to adopt a bona fide oRGC identity, displaying downregulation of key oRGC genes required for their amplification and maintenance. Our findings link the evolutionarily conserved requirement of ASPM for proper mitotic spindle orientation to the species-specific timing of delamination and proper specification of human oRGC, shedding light on the origins of species-specific vulnerability to ASPM mutations.

items.title: Brain-wide activity imaging with electron microscopy reveals a distributed brain network for processing threatening somatosensory stimuli.
items.abstract: To understand how brains work, neural activity must be overlayed onto synaptic-resolution circuit architecture. Recent advances in light-sheet microscopy (LSM) enable whole-brain, cellular-resolution imaging of activity of all cell bodies; however, most neurons from such datasets cannot be identified. In most organisms, neurons are identifiable based on their projections (and not based on cell body position), which, when densely labeled, cannot be resolved using LSM. Here, we present a novel methodology to overcome this by combining whole-brain activity imaging with subsequent volume electron microscopy imaging of the same brain to visualize neuronal projections and identify neurons with interesting activity. We used this approach to identify brain neurons that process input from multisensory (nociceptive and mechanosensory) Basin interneurons that trigger vigorous escape in Drosophila larvae in response to threatening somatosensory stimuli. After whole-brain imaging of neuronal activity during Basin activation, we imaged the same brain with an enhanced focused ion-beam electron microscope (eFIB-SEM). We registered the functional and anatomical volumes and reconstructed (in the eFIB-SEM volume) the projections of neurons that responded to Basin activation to determine their developmental lineage and identity. This revealed a distributed network for processing threatening somatosensory stimuli that trigger vigorous escape spanning 25 distinct lineages and many distinct brain areas. Our workflow provides a powerful framework for mapping neuronal activity onto structure across an entire brain, yielding novel insights into the distributed central processing of somatosensory stimuli.

items.title: Tubulin autoregulation mediator TTC5 regulates neuronal morphology and migration.
items.abstract: Microtubule dynamics are essential for neuronal development, yet how neurons regulate tubulin levels remains poorly understood. Tetratricopeptide repeat domain 5 (TTC5) mediates tubulin autoregulation, the co-translational degradation of tubulin transcripts in response to excess soluble tubulin, and TTC5 mutations cause cerebral atrophy with speech and motor impairment. Here, we show that tubulin autoregulation is active in induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived cortical neurons and depends on TTC5. TTC5 loss, or structure-guided mutations that disable autoregulation suppress microtubule polymerization, axonal outgrowth, and arborization, while enhancing cellular motility. Motility changes extend to non-neuronal cells, where they alter focal adhesion dynamics and can be rescued by manipulating soluble tubulin levels. Furthermore, downregulation of TTC5 interactor and autoregulation mediator S-phase cyclin A-associated protein in the endoplasmic reticulum (SCAPER) also suppresses neurite outgrowth and enhances motility. In vivo, TTC5 loss in mouse cortical projection neurons disrupts axon and dendrite arborization and causes hypermigration, recapitulating the cellular phenotypes observed in vitro. Patient-derived TTC5 disease mutants phenocopy this motility dysregulation, directly linking loss of TTC5 function to neurological deficits seen in patients. Together, these findings establish TTC5 as an essential regulator of neuronal morphogenesis and connectivity, with direct implications for TTC5-associated neurodevelopmental disease.
