items.title: Improving Learner Performance Through Score Based Analysis on a Gamified AI Driven Cybersecurity Learning Platform
items.abstract: Abstract This study examines whether structured engagement with instructional content improves learner performance on Cyber Security Academy, an AI-driven, gamified cybersecurity learning platform. Activity logs covering 1,500 completed assessments from users in ten Anglophone and Francophone countries were analyzed by comparing learners who consulted the lessons and completed the full learning pathway (n = 900) with those who engaged only partially with the platform (n = 600). Group differences were tested with Welch's t-test, the Mann Whitney U test, one-way ANOVA, Spearman correlations, and Cohen's d as a measure of effect size. Learners who read the lessons before assessment obtained a mean score of 71.27 % versus 60.41 % for non-readers (Δ = +10.86 points; t(1192) = 12.21; p < 0.001; d = 0.650; 95 % CI [9.12, 12.60]), committed fewer errors (2.50 vs. 4.85; d = -1.069), and responded faster (9.85 vs. 12.69 minutes; d = -0.807), indicating greater fluency of cognitive processing. The effect decreased monotonically with age (d = 1.205 for learners aged 13 and under; d = 0.387 for those 22 and over) and with digital literacy (d = 1.434 for beginners; d = 0.524 for experts), while remaining positive in all ten countries. These findings indicate that structured, AI-personalized, and gamified learning environments substantially enhance cybersecurity learning outcomes, particularly for younger and less experienced users.

items.title: The environmental dependence of ecological interaction networks
items.abstract: Interactions between species are often assumed to occur whenever species pairs co-occur, allowing us to reconstruct local ecological networks from a deterministic 'metaweb'. Over the past few years, an increasing number of papers have called for a reassessment of this simplistic assumption. This new literature addresses how stochasticity in the occurrence of species and links, and environmental imprints on these, shape ecological interaction networks. In this review, we systematically demonstrate the imprints of stochasticity and environmental dependence on ecological interaction networks using both simulations and empirically-characterised networks. We find that both species and link occurrence are stochastic, with probabilities conditional on the environment. This insight improves our ability to model observed variation in network structures. We argue that future research should incorporate environmental impacts on both species and links, effectively abandoning the deterministic view on interactions and moving away from the metaweb approach.

items.title: Impacts of fire regime on small mammal communities in California
items.abstract: Across the world, climate change is contributing to altered fire regimes, including increases in the frequency, area burned, and severity of wildfires. As a result, our understanding of the effects of these changes on ecosystems, biodiversity, and wildlife remains incomplete. The Sierra Nevada region of California supports many important species and includes unique small mammal communities that represent a crucial component of healthy ecosystems. Recently, the Sierra Nevada has experienced increasing impacts of climate change, most notably demonstrated through extreme drought and alterations to the fire regime, such as increases in fire severity, intensity, frequency, and area burned. These factors contribute to changes in vegetation and habitat, to which small mammals are highly sensitive. However, the long-term influence of these changes is poorly understood. This study aims to understand the drivers of small mammal community composition, with a focus on fire regime. We make use of historical survey and resurvey data from the Sierra Nevada, which provide high-quality species occurrence records from several periods over the last century. We examine how small mammal richness and community turnover vary with different components of fire regime, climate, and habitat using single- and multiple-variable linear regression. We found that several fire regime variables explain variation in modern small mammal richness across the Sierra Nevada. Specifically, mean time since last fire had a significant positive relationship with small mammal richness, whereas number of fires, fire return interval, and the standard deviation of time since last fire had significant negative relationships with richness in the multivariate models, in combination with non-fire variables. Additionally, mean time since last fire, standard deviation of time since last fire, and number of fires in a sample area had significant positive relationships with small mammal community turnover. Overall, this work establishes that fire is an essential element that influences small mammal community structure in an era of global change and must be considered alongside climate and habitat. Worldwide, global climate change and anthropogenic influences impact natural fire regimes. We used multivariate linear models to test the impact of fire regime on small mammal communities (Rodentia, Eulipotyphla) in the California Sierra Nevada mountains. Small mammal richness was lower in areas with less time since last fire, longer fire return intervals, and a higher number of fires. Small mammal community turnover was higher in areas with more time since last fire and a higher number of fires.

items.title: Limited effect of basalt amendment and mycorrhizal inoculation on soil chemical properties and maize growth on a nutrient-rich soil
items.abstract: Abstract Enhanced weathering (EW) of silicate minerals has emerged as a promising carbon dioxide removal (CDR) strategy, with potential benefits for soil fertility and crop performance. However, the soil processes that determine these co-benefits remain poorly constrained. In particular, interactions between basalt amendments and soil biota such as arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) may influence nutrient mobilization and plant uptake, but these effects have rarely been quantified. In a 113-day mesocosm experiment with Zea mays using a Belgian, sandy loam soil, we investigated the effect of basalt and AMF inoculation on soil properties, nutrient and heavy metal availability, and crop yield and quality. We also assessed potential AMF-driven bio-weathering via cation mass balance and pore water dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC), pH, and alkalinity measurements. Basalt application, but not AMF, improved soil pH, cation exchange capacity, base saturation, and generally increased exchangeable Ca and Mg, whereas most other nutrients in the pore water remained unaffected. Crop yield and quality were largely unaltered by basalt or AMF, except for an increase in plant Mg with basalt application. Moreover, heavy metal availability and plant uptake were also generally unaffected, with the notable exception of soil pore water and corn Ni, which increased with basalt. These results suggest that risk for heavy metal contamination is not generic but may arise under specific environmental conditions. Finally, despite a synergistic effect of basalt and AMF on pore water DIC, we found no indication that AMF enhanced basalt weathering rates. Overall, AMF had limited influence on soil fertility indicators and crop performance. Basalt application improved key soil chemical indicators and increased the exchangeable fractions of Ca and Mg, demonstrating its role as a soil improver. Unlike several studies conducted in more acidic soils, these chemical enhancements did not increase maize growth here, indicating that the agronomic benefits of basalt are context-dependent.

items.title: Hierarchical mode of evolution in freshwater SAR11 driven by species dispersal and lake history
items.abstract: Abstract Microorganisms dominate aquatic ecosystems, yet the evolutionary forces shaping their biogeography remain poorly understood. Freshwater habitats, acting as “isolated islands", may generate distinct evolutionary patterns in contrast to globally connected marine systems. Here, we investigated the globally abundant freshwater SAR11 genus Fontibacterium using a comparative population genomics framework. We analysed genome-wide single nucleotide variants (SNVs) from three species with contrasting dispersal capacities: an African endemic ( F. africanum ), a temperate specialist ( F. temperatum ), and a cosmopolitan species ( F. commune ). All species exhibited significant lake-specific population structure, but the scale of differentiation was constrained by their dispersal potential, ranging from complete genetic isolation between ancient lakes in the endemic species to transcontinental cohesion in the cosmopolitan one. Notably, the cosmopolitan species showed near-complete genetic cohesion between antipodal populations (Japan and Brazil) suggesting stochastic long-distance dispersal without geographic barriers. Furthermore, population genetic signatures varied among lake systems, especially elevated nucleotide diversity and pN/pS ratios in ancient African lakes suggesting relaxed purifying selection; a pattern that may reflect their unique evolutionary history. These findings support a hierarchical model where a species' dispersal capacity sets the broad-scale potential for gene flow, while local lake history determines the fine-scale genetic structure of its populations.

items.title: Microbial carbon use efficiency emerges from interactions between soil structure and life-history strategies
items.abstract: Abstract. Microbial carbon use efficiency (CUE) is believed to be a key regulator of the accumulation of persistent soil organic carbon. Microbial processing of organic carbon in soil occurs in the pore network, the properties of which are known to affect microbial activity. However, the effects of interactions between pore architecture, and microbial life-history strategies on carbon dynamics, and house these interactions are modulated by moisture regime, remain poorly understood. Here, we use a spatially explicit model based on a cellular automaton, applied to realistic soil pore networks derived from X-ray tomographic images, to investigate how pore geometry and organic matter distribution shape microbial dynamics and CUE. The model explicitly represents r- and K-strategists that are either motile or immobile, and have different resource requirements for growth, maintenance and motility. The constraints imposed on substrate diffusion and the spatial domain in which motile bacteria can effectively disperse by the moisture regime are explicitly represented in the model, in order to capture how moisture regulate decomposer access to resources. The simulations show that pore architecture has a significant effect on microbial CUE. Micropores promoted high CUE and a dominance of K-strategists by limiting substrate diffusion, reducing pore connectivity, and constraining microbial access to spatially isolated resources. In contrast, macropores with high connectivity and greater substrate accessibility favor r-strategists, rapid biomass turnover and lower CUE. Motility emerges as advantageous in connected, carbon-rich macropores, but energetically unfavourable in confined or poorly connected micropores, where immobile strategies outperform motile ones. Overall, our results indicate that microbial CUE is not an intrinsic property of life-strategies alone, but emerges from the interaction between microbial life-strategies and pore-scale physical constraints. This study suggests that soil structure influences microbial strategies by limiting resource availability and dispersal.

items.title: Microplastics and forest fungi: a review and call for comprehensive research
items.abstract: Abstract Fungi are the main drivers of the global carbon and nutrient cycle and act as ecosystem engineers in forest ecosystems by regulating primary production and decomposition. Moreover, fungi are among the most diverse organisms in forest ecosystems and affect almost all forest microhabitats, from the canopy to the soil. In contrast to aquatic and agricultural ecosystems, forest ecosystems have received less attention in assessing the effects of microplastic pollution on biodiversity and ecosystem functioning. However, a recent study demonstrated that airborne microplastics are present even in remote forests, averaging 11.9 ± 7.1 particles m⁻³ of air. Thus, we summarize our current understanding of how microplastics enter forests and move within these ecosystems to assess potential risks to diverse fungal habitats. Next, we summarize the state of the art concerning how microplastics affect fungal individuals, fungal diversity, and related ecosystem processes. Our review revealed that forest management and recreational activities are the most important direct pathways, whereas atmospheric deposition is recognized as the main indirect pathway by which microplastics enter forest ecosystems. The movement and dynamics of microplastics within forest ecosystems result from complex abiotic and biotic mechanisms; however, these mechanisms remain poorly understood. Furthermore, while a few studies have investigated microplastic effects in forest ecosystems, their number is currently too small to support robust conclusions or any broader generalization regarding impacts on fungal diversity and related ecosystem processes. However, from other ecosystems, particularly agricultural soils, we have evidence that microplastic changes fungal diversity and influence key ecosystem processes, including primary production and decomposition, with the direction and magnitude of these effects depending on microplastic properties, concentration, and environmental conditions. From this, we hypothesize that microplastic contamination should be biologically relevant across fungal forest habitats with consequences for fungal diversity and the associated ecosystem processes. To address this challenge, we propose a conceptual framework based on ecological theory and provide testable hypotheses. Although taxon-specific mechanisms will require tailored sampling and analyses, our framework could serve as a general blueprint for assessing microplastic impacts across forest ecosystems and improving predictions of their effects on biodiversity, ecosystem functioning, and ecosystem services.

items.title: Exotic catenulid flatworms (Platyhelminthes, Catenulida) and where to find them in a temperate climate – a field study in a botanic garden
items.abstract: Abstract Catenulids are free-living flatworms, common in eutrophic freshwaters such as ponds, ditches, or peatbogs, with most of the diversity described from tropical regions to date. Although the majority of the species have been described from warmer climates, most molecular studies have been done on specimens from temperate zones in Europe. We addressed this gap by sampling for exotic species in localities available in a temperate climate. In this study, we investigated catenulid diversity in the greenhouses at the University of Warsaw Botanic Garden and recorded two species known only from tropical areas ( Stenostomum paraguayense and Suomina evelinae ) and one exotic species recorded previously from a greenhouse in Poland ( Stenostomum corderoi ). Additionally, in the latter species, we provide evidence for environmentally induced coloration of sensory pits, which has not been reported thus far. We placed the collected species on a phylogeny using barcoding of 18S, 28S, and COI genes and retrieved paraphyly of the family Catenulidae, with S. evelinae forming a sister group to the genus Paracatenula , and hence we propose a revision of its systematic position. In total, we recorded six species, including three with a wide cosmopolitan distribution (C. turgida , S. grande and S. tuberculosum ), and provided sequences for five of them, three of which had no previous molecular records (S. paraguayense, S. evelinae and S. corderoi) . Thus, we confirm that greenhouses represent an important source of exotic species for taxonomic work on microscopic invertebrates.

items.title: Metagenomic and metabolomic analysis of a bryozoan-associated microbial complex from the Hanjiang River, China
items.abstract: Abstract Background Bryozoans are ancient colonial animals that have existed for over 470 million years and are widely distributed across aquatic environments. Recently, many spherical colloids (average diameter≈1 meter in diameter), containing bryozoans and diverse microorganisms, were found in the Hanjiang river in China. In this study, we investigated these bryozoan-dominated microbial complexes using metagenomic sequencing, metabolomic profiling, and complementary approaches. Results The results revealed that the microbial structure dominated by bryozoans included eukaryotes such as fungi, microalgae, as well as prokaryotes such as bacteria, and acellular entities such as viruses. All members form a highly integrated consortium that collaboratively maintains community function and stability, which displayed the shape and structure of a regular microbial complex and increased in size. Additionally, the results suggested the predominately presence of Proteobacteria were particularly abundant and are known to produce bryozoans in response to bryozoan signals. Interesting, it was implied that a decrease or even a loss in virulence occurs when pathogenic microorganisms become members of the complex. This is the first study focusing on the composition and metabolites of the unusual microorganism complex. The results discovered the close and intriguing connections within the microbial communities dominated by the ancient organism bryozoan through multi-omics technologies. It showed that both eukaryotes and prokaryotes can coordinate, thereby forming a stable composite structure.

items.title: Sustaining the Third Pole (Himalayas): Artificial intelligence and blockchain for climate actions
items.abstract: The Himalayas, often known as the 'Third Pole' or 'Water Tower of Asia', are vital for the water security of millions residing in the Asian continent. The region is facing a number of ecological, environmental, and social challenges, such as climate change, biodiversity loss, pollution, and border disputes. Conventional strategies for addressing these challenges have mostly failed to yield satisfactory outcomes. The present study examines the challenges being faced by the Himalayan region. It also explores the potential of AI (Artificial Intelligence) and BT (Blockchain Technology) in solving these challenges by suggesting a conceptual framework for integrating AI and BT to deliver sustainable outcomes in the region. This framework is the multi-stage integration of AI-generated data and BT secure governance mechanism for transboundary climate action. AI offers advanced capabilities for data collection, climate modeling, disaster prediction, and monitoring of biodiversity and ecosystems in the Himalayas. BT can solve the issue of data transparency, security, and trust among the Himalayan nations. However, the implementation of these technologies is constrained due to limited infrastructure, high deployment costs, and cross-border data sharing issues. An inclusive approach leveraging on AI and BT, collaboration between Himalayan nations, support of developed nations, and climate concerns people will be crucial for promoting sustainable development in the Himalayan region.

items.title: Homogeneización estacional en las comunidades de aves del Área Metropolitana de Buenos Aires, Argentina, debido a la urbanización
items.abstract: 1. Las ciudades ubicadas en regiones templadas suelen mostrar una estabilización estacional de recursos para las aves. Esta estabilización ha sido asociada a una menor variación estacional en las comunidades de aves. Sin embargo, este tipo de análisis es escaso en la Región Pampeana.2. El objetivo de este estudio fue analizar la variación estacional de la riqueza y la composición de aves a lo largo del gradiente urbano-rural del Área Metropolitana de Buenos Aires, la segunda más grande de Sudamérica. Se realizaron conteos de aves en transectas durante las etapas reproductiva (primavera-verano) y no reproductiva (otoño-invierno) en cinco niveles de urbanización.3. La riqueza de aves mostró una relación negativa con la urbanización en la etapa reproductiva y fue máxima en niveles poco urbanizados durante la etapa no reproductiva. El cambio en la riqueza de especies entre estaciones fue máxima en el sector rural y no presentó cambios significativos en el sector poco urbanizado. El cambio de composición de especies entre etapas fue máximo en el sector rural y mínimo en el sector moderadamente urbanizado.4. Implicancias. Los resultados apoyan la idea de una homogeneización estacional de las comunidades de aves en áreas urbanas. Este trabajo mostró cambios estacionales en el sector más urbanizado, lo cual demuestra que el efecto homogeneizador de la urbanización sobre las comunidades de aves no es lineal.

items.title: PENERAPAN MODEL KOOPERATIF TIPE NUMBERED HEAD TOGETHER DALAM MENINGKATKAN HASIL BELAJAR PENDIDIKAN PANCASILA MURID KELAS IV
items.abstract: The learning outcomes of fourth-grade students in Pancasila Education at UPTD SD Negeri 074048 Luaha Bouso were still low because previous learning tended to be teacher-centered, resulting in limited student activity, collaboration, and participation. This study aimed to describe the implementation of the Numbered Head Together (NHT) cooperative learning model and to determine the improvement of students' learning outcomes in Pancasila Education after its implementation. The study employed Classroom Action Research using the Kemmis and McTaggart model and was conducted in two cycles. Each cycle consisted of planning, action, observation, and reflection, with two meetings in each cycle. The subjects were 19 fourth-grade students in the 2025/2026 academic year. Data were collected through observations of teacher and student activities, learning outcome tests, documentation, and field notes, and were analyzed descriptively using qualitative and quantitative approaches. The NHT implementation involved heterogeneous group formation, assigning numbers to group members, presenting questions or tasks, group discussion, random number calling, presentation of answers, and reinforcement. The findings showed that teacher activity increased from 58% in Cycle I Meeting I to 90% in Cycle II Meeting II, while student activity increased from 57.69% to 94.23%. Learning outcomes also improved, as indicated by an increase in the mean score from 62.68 in Cycle I to 80.63 in Cycle II and classical mastery from 47.37% to 84.21%. Therefore, the implementation of NHT improved student participation and learning outcomes in Pancasila Education.

items.title: Picloram-Induced Embryogenic Callus Formation and Proliferation from Nucellar Embryo of Mandarin ‘Berastagi’ (Citrus reticulata Blanco)
items.abstract: Mandarin ‘Berastagi’ (Citrus reticulata Blanco) is a key horticultural commodity in North Sumatra, Indonesia, with increasing demand for high quality, genetically uniform planting material. Biotechnological approaches, somatic embryogenesis, hold particularly significant potential enhancing propagation efficiency and crop quality. This study aimed to determine the optimal culture medium and picloram concentration for the induction and proliferation of embryogenic callus from nucellar explants of Mandarin ‘Berastagi’ in vitro. Two experiments were conducted: (1) induction of embryogenic callus from nucellar embryos isolated from young fruits (60–70 days after anthesis) cultured on different basal media supplemented with varying picloram concentrations, and (2) proliferation of embryogenic callus on media containing different carbohydrate concentrations. The Murashige and Wetmore (MW) medium supplemented with 1.5 mg/L picloram resulted in the highest callus induction rate (37.8%) and largest mean callus diameter (17.8 mm). For proliferation, MW medium containing 4% sucrose produced the best response, with an average callus diameter of 14 mm and 96% of explants developing globular stage somatic embryos. These results establish an efficient somatic embryogenesis protocol that can support large-scale propagation and future crop improvement programs in Mandarin ‘Berastagi’.

items.title: Helminth Fauna of the Caucasian Toad, Bufo verrucosissimus (Pallas, 1814) (Amphibia: Bufonidae), Collected from Türkiye
items.abstract: This study presents a helminthological investigation of 35 individuals (13♀♀ and 22♂♂) of the Caucasian toad, Bufo verrucosissimus (Pallas, 1814), collected from Artvin and Mersin provinces in Türkiye during 2024–2025. Six helminth species were identified: 1 species of Cestoda (Nematotaenia dispar (Goeze, 1782) Lühe, 1899), 4 species of Nematoda (Rhabdias bufonis (Schrank, 1788); Aplectana acuminata (Schrank, 1788) Railliet and Henry, 1916; Oxysomatium brevicaudatum (Zeder, 1800); Oswaldocruzia filiformis (Goeze, 1782)), and 1 species of Acanthocephala (Pseudoacanthocephalus caucasicus (Petrochenko, 1953)). This is the first helminthological study of B. verrucosissimus in Türkiye, and N. dispar and O. brevicaudatum represent new records for the host.

items.title: Can interspecific competition explain the absence of saline species in freshwaters? A test using water beetles
items.abstract: Abstract The habitats a species occupies are not determined solely by its environmental tolerance, because biotic interactions can further restrict its realised niche. This mismatch between fundamental and realised niches is well documented in saline-associated aquatic insects, many of which tolerate freshwater conditions in the laboratory yet are largely confined to saline waters in nature. We tested whether interspecific competition could contribute to the absence of the halophilic diving beetle Nebrioporus baeticus in freshwater. We compared its response to restricted food availability with that of the freshwater-associated N. clarkii under freshwater conditions, using single- and mixed-species treatments. Survival was monitored over a 30-day period, while feeding behaviour was assessed on days 1 and 7 based on feeding time and the number of contacts with the food resource. Contrary to our expectations, the halophilic beetle was not competitively disadvantaged by the freshwater congener. Interspecific coexistence instead had a transient negative effect on the feeding behaviour of the freshwater species, but not of the halophilic species. These findings suggest that competition alone cannot explain the absence of halophilic species from freshwater habitats, indicating that other factors are likely involved (e.g., predation pressure, parasitism, or other biotic interactions).

items.title: Thermal ecology drives alternate responses to rising temperatures in Caribbean anoles
items.abstract: Rapidly rising temperatures threaten populations of ectothermic animals worldwide, with the greatest impacts predicted in the tropics—hotspots for biodiversity. Ectotherms can respond to warming through two primary compensatory responses: behavioral thermoregulation, which buffers exposure to extreme temperatures; and heat tolerance increases via plasticity, adaptation, or both. The relative contribution of these responses is predicted to depend on ecological context, but whether these principles can anticipate organismal responses to contemporary warming remains largely untested. Here, using a decadal resurvey of anole lizards from Hispaniola, Jamaica, and Puerto Rico, we show that simple principles of thermal ecology can reliably anticipate organismal responses to rising temperatures. Species occupying thermally heterogeneous open/edge habitats, such as dry forests, behaviorally thermoregulate and have shown little to no increase in heat tolerance over the past decade. By contrast, species from thermally homogeneous closed-canopy environments are poor thermoregulators and have increased their heat tolerance by 2 °C, on average, over the same period. Seasonal comparisons, acclimation experiments, and laboratory-rearing experiments indicate that contemporary increases in heat tolerance likely reflect contributions from rapid evolutionary change and physiological plasticity. Thermal ecology, not phylogenetic or spatial proximity, is the key factor driving responses to rising temperatures. Our results consistently link organismal responses to habitat complexity and thermoregulatory behavior; we suggest that these factors are key to predicting how ectotherms respond to climate warming.

Bellingan || 102190 || HOLOTYPE | Albanycada bellinganorum | Villet & Price ”; AMGS. Paratypes (2 ♂♂), 1 ♂ “ RSA: Eastern Cape | Miller | Rietfontein Farm | S32°58'8.76" | E23°42'54.45" | 12. Dec. 2024 | T. A. Bellingan J. Zaayman | J. E. Bellingan A. J. Zaayman | J. E. Bellingan A. J. Bellingan || 102192 || PARATYPE | Albanycada bellinganorum | Villet & Price ”; AMGS. Additional material examined. 4 ♂♂; 1 ♀. The metadata on the labels of these specimens are not cited verbatim. South Africa – Eastern Cape • 1 ♂; nr Willowmore; 32.969°S, 23.715°E; 31 Jan. 2006; T. A. Bellingan leg.; MHV 0423; AMGS. • 2 ♂♂, 1 ♀; Rietfontein Farm; 32.969°S, 23.715°E; 19 Jan. 2008; B. W. Price & T. A. Bellingan leg.; MHV 1035; AMGS. – Western Cape • 1 ♂; Calitzdorp; 33.500°S, 21.750°E; 24 Dec. 1989; H. C. Ficq leg.; SANC. Morphological diagnosis. The external morphology and the male genitalia of A. bellinganorum Villet & Price, sp. nov. conform to the description of the genus (Figs 3 C, 3 D, 4). The primary feature distinguishing this species from A. albigera is the pigmentation pattern of its wings, especially the hind wing. Morphological description. Male fore wing length 23.4–24.3; fore wing width 9.4–10.1; body length 19.8–20.7; head width 8.0–8.3; mesonotum width 8.3–8.6. Female fore wing length 22.5; fore wing width 8.8; body length 18.3; head width 6.8; mesonotum width 8.1. Head with two black stripes running from eye to eye, one through the ocelli and the other across the bases of the antennae. Anteclypeus unmarked. Rostrum pale brown. Pronotum anterior margin blackened. Pronotal incisures variably black. Mesonotum the medial obconical spots black, the lateral obconical spots black with chestnut centres, a narrow median line brown, and a pair of spots just anterior to cruciform elevation black. Fore wing with grey feathering along the veins in the distal half, distinct blackening of the subapical crossveins, and two submarginal rows of dark grey spots that straddle the veins, the proximal spots being larger but not touching; the proximal half is opaque, marbled to a variable degree with grey, brown and white with an ill-defined, blackish disco-basal band, 3 rd and 4 th ulnar cells usually with a distinct whitish patch towards apex; venation pale brown; setae black. Hind wing burnt orange basally (fading to yellowish-ochre in dead specimens), area around distal veins and crossveins blackened, centres of apical cells hyaline; venation brown; crossveins not blackened; limbus crossed by evenly spaced black streaks hyaline; plaga greyish; jugum uniform. Legs brown; tibia often darker, with a dark brown patch near the proximal joint. Opercula dull brown. Abdominal tergites very dark brown; the posterior margins pale. Timbal cover brown. Tergite 8 bearing tomentum. Sternites unmarked. The sexes are similar in general appearance, colouration, body size and morphology, with the usual sexual dimorphisms of cicadas. Female opercula brown; tergite VII bearing tomentum; sternites unmarked; pygofer lacking ventral thorn, caudodorsal beak with apex sharply pointed; ovipositor sheaths reaching apex of caudodorsal beak; with 15 teeth. Molecular systematics and phylogenetic history. Sequences from four genes (genseq- 3 16S: FJ 168837; genseq- 3 COI: FJ 169041; genseq- 3 COII: GU 344010; and genseq- 3 EF- 1 α: GU 343829) are available for identifying this species (Price et al. 2019), which is estimated to have diverged from A. albigera about 5 Ma at the end of the Miocene (Price et al. 2019). Etymology. “Bellinganorum” is the Latin genitive neutral plural adjective indicating that this species is named in honour of the Bellingan family, who generously provided hospitality and assistance in obtaining specimens and sound recordings of A. bellinganorum Villet & Price, sp. nov. around their farm, Rietfontein. Distribution, ecology and biology. South Africa: apparently endemic to Arid Thicket and Mosaic Thicket with Fynbos variants of the Albany Thicket Biome of the westernmost Eastern Cape and eastern Western Cape, but the distribution is poorly sampled (Fig. 5). The biology of this species is known only from observations made in a patch of Arid Thicket vegetation on the farm Rietfontein, near Willowmore (Fig. 5), in the Albany Thicket Biome (Hoare et al. 2006; South African National Biodiversity Institute 2021). Adults are associated with Rhigozum obovatum Burch. (Granaatbos / Yellow Pomegranate), a relatively widespread bush. The type locality has a population of the endemic Aloe comptonii Reynolds, which may be a marker plant for this variant of Arid Thicket (van Wyk and Smith 2001; Klopper and Smith 2011). Apart from its plant associations, this species’ biology is probably similar to that of A. albigera. Adults are known to be active in January. Males do not form choruses. Like that of A. albigera, the calling song of A. bellinganorum Villet & Price, sp. nov. is a continuous, unmodulated whine that individual insects can sustain for long periods. It is pitched between 6.5–12.75 kHz, emphasized around 9.0 kHz, and with a pulse repetition rate of about 160 Hz (Fig. 8). The pulses are arranged in pairs in a manner similar to those in the calling songs of A. albigera and Kongota punctigera (Walker, 1850) (Villet 1989 figs 42–45). Recordings are available on the Bioacoustica website (https://bio.acousti.ca/sv/classification/albanycada-sp-01). Conservation. Area of Occupation (AOO) 8 km 2; Extent of Occurrence (EOO) 0 km 2 (only two sites); altitudinal range 255–935 m. The species inhabits one of the smallest biomes in South Africa; the biome is resistant to many natural perturbations but not resilient to degradation (South African National Biodiversity Institute 2021), and ~ 50 % of it is already transformed, although less so in the western parts (Carvalho et al. 2022). Although the known occurrences of A. bellinganorum are about 190 km apart, the intervening habitat is very elongated and very narrow (Fig. 5), so its true distribution merits investigation. The species’ IUCN status is Not Evaluated (NE); by criteria linked to its AOO and EOO and the characteristics of its habitat, it may well qualify as Critically Endangered (CR). Relevant conservation measures are lacking (Carvalho et al. 2022) and the species is not yet known from any formally conserved area.

items.title: Fire asymmetries across global borders reveal distinct ecological governance and cooperation priorities
items.abstract: Abstract International borders divide governance systems but often cut across continuous ecosystems, creating potential mismatches in fire management. We analyze 277 terrestrial international border pairs using a 21-year satellite fire record and integrate fire burden, relative cross-border asymmetry, ecological value, institutional challenge and cooperation challenge. Border fire burden broadly reproduces global fire geography, with the highest activity concentrated in major fire-prone regions, but our analysis shows that management implications differ markedly among borders. Among 128 active-fire pairs, fire burden and proportional asymmetry are weakly negatively associated and identify partly distinct priorities. Ecological value further reshapes priority geographies, while institutional and cooperation constraints define different governance contexts. Multivariate analysis separates these borders into operational profiles with contrasting management needs. Here, we show that transboundary fire priority cannot be inferred from fire activity alone but emerges from distinct combinations of fire, ecological and governance conditions, requiring border-specific approaches to monitoring, conservation and cooperation.

items.title: Marinas act as persistent introduction hubs driving the decadal accumulation of non-indigenous fouling species in an oceanic island system
items.abstract: Long–term monitoring of marine fouling assemblages and non‑indigenous species (NIS) has been historically scarce globally, particularly in island ecosystems, limiting the ability to distinguish transient detections from persistent populations. Using an 11–year monitoring dataset (2013–2025; 33 surveys, 131 sampling events) across four Madeira Archipelago marinas, we evaluated spatio-temporal patterns in biofouling assemblages. Across 71 recorded taxa, cumulative NIS richness increased steadily, ultimately accounting for nearly half (45–48%; 27–30 NIS per marina) of all recorded fouling species, reflecting major community transformation. Multivariate analyses identified marina identity as the primary driver structuring assemblages, maintaining distinct spatial signatures despite minimal thermal variation. Temporally, seasonal dynamics revealed a clear functional decoupling: mean observed richness per sampling event peaked during warmer periods, whereas cumulative multi-year species turnover was highest during cooler periods. This decoupling reflects seasonal thermal regimes, where summer warming creates windows that trigger reproductive pulses and space preemption by fast-growing colonial NIS, while cooler periods permit broader species turnover. Together, these findings confirm marinas as persistent introduction hubs, where repeated introductions, recruitment, and population persistence. Long–term, seasonally informed monitoring is therefore vital for early detection and marine biosecurity in island ecosystems.

items.title: Beyond the Green Image: A Visual-Documentary Framework for Evaluating Nature-Positive Evidence in Architecture
items.abstract: As architecture increasingly adopts biodiversity and nature-positive terminology, visually prominent greenness is often treated as evidence of ecological value. This chapter develops a visual-documentary framework that separates architectural visibility from ecological verifiability. Twelve international buildings comprising 16 ecological subsystems were examined through criterion-based purposive sampling. Visual Greenness Prominence was assessed independently from nine ecological criteria, while evidence level, source quality, baseline status and evidence architecture were coded separately. The analysis shows that high visual greenness is neither necessary nor sufficient for strong verified ecological response. The principal gap occurred between ecological provision and demonstrated outcome: habitat provision, heterogeneity and natural-process integration were common, but none of the subsystems demonstrated the full combination of broad quantified biodiversity improvement, a defensible baseline or counterfactual, and evidence sufficient to establish baseline- or counterfactual-relative positive biodiversity change. The framework therefore calibrates ecological claims to the quality and completeness of the evidence supporting them.

items.title: Reconstructing ancient ecosystems: guanaco and marine carrion as drivers of predator-prey networks in Southern South America
items.abstract: Understanding ancient trophic dynamics and human integration in terrestrial high-latitude ecosystems requires moving beyond traditional taxonomic lists to evaluate structural biological interactions. This study presents the first probabilistic, trait-based bipartite network reconstruction of ancient predator-prey assemblages in northern Tierra del Fuego, Southern South America, based on archeological records. By integrating a comprehensive zooarcheological dataset spanning 50 spatial-temporal contexts from the late Pleistocene through the late Holocene across steppe and forest habitats, we model trophic interactions including human subsistence strategies. In this region, dominated by grassy steppes and the forest-steppe ecotone, terrestrial hunter-gatherer societies were embedded in a complex predator-prey network in which the guanaco ( Lama guanicoe ) played a central role. However, the trophic structure of these interactions and how the introduction of humans as an unprecedented predator affected community-level properties is poorly understood. Our results reveal a significant chronological transformation in network architecture and diet composition. During the late Pleistocene, communities exhibited lower interaction diversity and high specialization centered around megaherbivores and multiple large predators. Following megafaunal extinction and island isolation during the mid-Holocene, the guanaco emerged as an enduring keystone herbivore and dietary anchor, while marine-derived carrion and littoral resources (mollusks and pinnipeds) provided critical energy subsidies. Humans acted as highly plastic generalist consumers, influencing network architecture across diverse habitats. In the steppe, foragers employed broad-spectrum strategies, whereas forest assemblages reflected specialized reliance on coastal resources. Ultimately, this community-level framework demonstrates that despite intense environmental shifts and insularization, the guanaco and marine necromass served as foundational trophic stabilizers, maintaining ecosystem and subsistence resilience over millennia.

items.title: From Jupyter Notebooks to DNA Encoding and Tensor Networks: A Mini-Review of Computational Bioinformatics Education and Insect Barcoding
items.abstract: Computational biology increasingly depends on algorithms, yet many life-science learners lack programming experience and practical strategies for transforming DNA strings into machine-readable data. This mini-review examines three connected themes: Python instruction through Jupyter notebooks, nucleotide representation using one-hot, binary, and integer encodings, and tensor-network classification of DNA barcodes. Synthesizing complementary publications spanning bioinformatics education, sequence modeling, DNA barcoding, and tensor methods, we explore the transition from instruction to model deployment. Jupyter notebooks integrate explanations, executable code, and visualization, supporting reproducible learning. Encoding determines information geometry, memory demands, and assumptions passed to classifiers. A published tensor-network model reported greater than 99% accuracy on a four-class Orthoptera dataset; this result remains dataset-specific and does not establish encoding superiority. We argue that strong computational foundations, paired with rigorous representation choices and external validation, can responsibly enable accurate machine learning for agriculture, ecology, and biodiversity monitoring in real-world settings.

items.title: Tracking deep-time environmental stability exposes a global conservation gap
items.abstract: Abstract Continents drift across latitudinal climate zones that are themselves shifting as Earth's climate evolves [1-5]. The relative speed of these two motions (tectonic versus climatic velocity) determines how much climate change a given landmass experiences over geological time: where plates and climate zones move in concert, local climates can remain stable for millions of years, allowing lineages to persist and diversify. However, whether this interplay has shaped deep-time environmental stability and, in turn, present-day biodiversity patterns remains untested. Here, using a Lagrangian framework to track land parcels through 60 million years of palaeogeographic, palaeoclimatic, and palaeoproductivity reconstructions, we show that in amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals, species richness increases with the time a parcel has spent within a stable environmental envelope. This accumulation shows no sign of saturation, instead accelerating across nearly all combinations of taxonomic group and environment. Integrating stability along tectonic trajectories identifies modern macroevolutionary refugia (>20 Myr of cumulative stability). Of these refugia, 77.9% lack legal protection---rising to 91.5% in Asia---and just 2.1% fall within strictly protected areas. Refugia are only modestly better protected than unstable land (22.1% versus 15.8%), with over three-quarters of this difference driven by the weakest protection tiers. Having assembled while their environments moved at centimetres to metres per year, these biotas face present-day climate velocities of hundreds of metres to kilometres per year [6, 7], a kinematic debt that protecting static coordinates alone cannot address.

items.title: Ecology and Sustainability in the 21st Century: An Interdisciplinary Integrative and Critical Review with a Focus on Portugal
items.abstract: Sustainability is an interdisciplinary scientific and institutional challenge that isolated improvements in technological efficiency, emissions reduction, or material substitution cannot adequately address. This study presents an interdisciplinary, integrative, and critical review of ecology and sustainability, complemented by documentary analysis and selected case studies. It examines ecological integrity, biodiversity, biophysical constraints, economic systems, environmental governance, and the distribution of environmental impacts across territories and generations, with particular attention to Portugal. The analysis highlights the limitations of treating efficiency, circularity, and innovation as sufficient evidence of environmental sustainability. Robust assessment requires explicit system boundaries, comparable functional units, consideration of indirect effects, and attention to the displacement of environmental costs. Selected SCI research cases illustrate the importance of evidence traceability and the limits of quantitative conclusions when underlying data cannot be adequately reconciled. The study distinguishes established scientific knowledge, documented SCI findings, and analytical interpretations. It does not constitute a systematic review or a scoping review conducted under PRISMA-ScR. Its conclusions are limited to the evidence examined. The paper contributes an interdisciplinary framework for understanding sustainability as preserving ecological functions alongside human well-being, social justice, and long-term institutional responsibility.

items.title: From fragmentation to conditional coordination: China Coast Guard environmental enforcement under ecological codification and the BBNJ Agreement
items.abstract: China’s consolidated maritime enforcement system connects dispersed domestic powers with new obligations under the Ecological and Environmental Code (EEC) and the Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ) Agreement. This study examines the relationship between China’s implementation responsibility and the legality of a specified China Coast Guard (CCG) measure. Five analytical inquiries distinguish institutional competence, applicable requirements, legal consequences, measure-specific authority, and international jurisdiction across three legal domains. They develop established legality review by pairing its measure-specific conclusion with a diagnosis of the implementation task that remains. Controlled variations show how the same rejection of boarding can correspond to referral, a necessary domestic implementing instrument, or procedural completion. Alternative routes are assessed against the applicable obligation’s addressee, required legal effect, timing, and mandatory procedures. For activities involving foreign-flagged vessels, Chinese incorporation identifies a personal nexus but must be connected to the corporation’s role in the particular activity. A proposed operational-control criterion examines executable decision powers over initiation, continuation, or environmentally material aspects of that activity. The framework distinguishes established, unresolved, absent and inapplicable requirements and links proposed implementation routes to administrative follow-up, operator responses and verification.

items.title: Inferring Long-Term Human Legacies in the Bornean Forests
items.abstract: The question of whether past human communities have left lasting ecological legacies in the forests they inhabited is a defining debate in tropical forest ecology. Borneo offers a unique context for examining this question, with an extensive archaeological record spanning at least 45,000 years and high-biodiversity forests. However, the ecological consequences of longterm human presence have remained largely unexamined. In this thesis, I use an interdisciplinary approach combining archaeology, remote sensing, environmental data, and functional and community ecology to produce the first integrated assessment of long-term human legacies in contemporary Bornean forests. I compiled the first island-wide synthesis of 73 archaeological sites across Borneo, characterising their climatic and environmental conditions against simulated random locations. Archaeological sites occur non-randomly under warmer, drier, low-elevation conditions near coasts and river networks, an environmental signature consistent with landscapes that concentrated resources and supported localised subsistence practices. Building on this foundation, I found that forests with long-term human activity exhibit a distinctive combination of conservative and acquisitive functional strategies, occupying an intermediate functional space between old-growth forests, regenerating forests, and agroforests, with lasting implications for how these ecosystems may respond to future environmental change. At the landscape scale, species diversity and basal area declined towards archaeological settlements, with the onset and duration of human occupation as significant predictors of diversity. Species composition near settlements remained floristically distinct, with an enrichment of ethnobotanically valued taxa and pioneer and mid-succesional species. Nearly 40% of all recorded taxa had documented ethnobotanical uses, identified independently of local knowledge, indicating that these forests preserve human legacies of past forest management that persist at least three millennia after abandonment. These findings reveal Bornean forests not as pristine but as landscapes shaped by the human communities that inhabited them, underscoring the need to integrate the deep history of human–forest interaction into the frameworks we use to identify, conserve and manage these irreplaceable ecosystems.

items.title: Sensory Ecology of Disturbance: Turbidity Mediates Estuarine Community Stability Following Extreme Events
items.abstract: Predators play a critical role in structuring communities, but their effects are mediated by environmental conditions that alter their foraging capability. In Texas oyster reef communities, visually foraging fish predators enhance biodiversity by suppressing mesopredators, but their forging effectiveness declines with increasing turbidity. We used widespread fish mortality caused by Winter Storm Uri (February 2021) to test how water clarity mediates oyster reef community response to disturbance. Fish abundance was higher in low turbidity, where foraging conditions were most favorable. Following the freeze, oyster community responses diverged; turbid reefs exhibited over double the annual variance in community composition relative to clear sites. We propose that sensory constraints on predation and lower fish abundance in turbid habitats amplified the effects of predator loss. In contrast, freeze effects were dampened in clear-water conditions that enhanced fish foraging and supported higher fish abundance. Our results demonstrate that sensory environments can influence the strength and stability of trophic interactions, with implications for predicting ecosystem responses to disturbance in increasingly turbid coastal systems.

items.title: A decade of open biodiversity data in the Azores: closing knowledge gaps and building a foundation for long-term monitoring
items.abstract: Ten years of dedicated biodiversity research and coordinated open-data publication have built an extensive, reusable knowledge base for the Azores. We synthesize this collective achievement through the AZORES BIOTA and BioMonI-Plot collections, evaluating its contribution to addressing the Wallacean and Prestonian shortfalls and identifying priorities for future research and monitoring. Focusing on the nine islands of this North Atlantic archipelago, we review publications issued between 2016 and May 2026, encompassing terrestrial and marine organisms across six kingdoms. We combine curated publication and dataset metadata with Darwin Core occurrenceID-linked species and subspecies records to assess spatial, taxonomic, temporal and methodological coverage, species accumulation by colonization status, and island species–area relationships. Across 91 publications, the collections document 931 animal, 1,185 plant and 742 fungal species and subspecies, alongside taxa from three additional kingdoms, and identify 598 additions to the Azorean Biodiversity Portal reference list. This sustained effort has substantially expanded accessible knowledge of species distributions, contributing to reducing the Wallacean shortfall. Arthropod abundance datasets and repeated standardized surveys also alleviate the Prestonian shortfall by enabling assessments of population and community change. Together, these resources establish valuable baselines for biodiversity assessment, invasion surveillance and conservation planning. The synthesis also reveals uneven coverage among islands, taxa and habitats, with spatial differences in research effort complicating interpretation of species–area relationships. The Azorean experience demonstrates the substantial scientific value of sustained regional expertise, collaboration and standardized open-data publication for understanding island biodiversity. By consolidating achievements and making remaining gaps explicit, this synthesis provides a foundation for targeted investment in underrepresented biota, spatially balanced surveys and sustained abundance monitoring, strengthening the evidence base for future biodiversity research and conservation.

items.title: Dark Energy Survey year 6 results: Cosmological constraints from galaxy clustering and weak lensing
items.abstract: We present cosmology results combining galaxy clustering and weak gravitational lensing measured in the full six years (Y6) of observations by the Dark Energy Survey (DES) covering $\sim$5000 deg$^2$. We perform a large-scale structure analysis using three two-point correlation functions (3$\times$2pt): (i) cosmic shear from 140 million source galaxy shapes, (ii) galaxy clustering of 9 million lens galaxy positions, and (iii) galaxy-galaxy lensing from their cross-correlation. We model the data in flat $Λ$CDM and $w$CDM cosmologies. The combined analysis yields $S_8\equiv σ_8 (Ω_{\rm m}/0.3)^{0.5} = 0.789^{+0.012}_{-0.012}$ and matter density $Ω_{\rm m} = 0.333^{+0.023}_{-0.028}$ in $Λ$CDM (68\% CL), where $σ_8$ is the clustering amplitude. These constraints show a (full-space) parameter difference of 1.8$σ$ from a combination of cosmic microwave background (CMB) primary anisotropy datasets from Planck 2018, ACT-DR6, and SPT-3G DR1. Projected only into $S_8$ the difference is $2.6σ$. In $w$CDM the Y6 3$\times$2pt results yield $S_8 = 0.782^{+0.021}_{-0.020}$, $Ω_{\rm m} = 0.325^{+0.032}_{-0.035}$, and dark energy equation-of-state parameter $w = -1.12^{+0.26}_{-0.20}$. For the first time, we combine all DES dark-energy probes: 3$\times$2pt, SNe Ia, BAO and Clusters. In $Λ$CDM this combination yields a $2.8σ$ parameter difference from the CMB. When combining DES 3$\times$2pt with other low-redshift datasets (DESI DR2 BAO, DES SNe Ia, SPT clusters), we find a 2.3$σ$ parameter difference with CMB. A joint fit of Y6 3$\times$2pt, CMB, and those low-redshift datasets produces the tightest $Λ$CDM constraints to date: $S_8 = 0.806^{+0.006}_{-0.007}$, $Ω_{\rm m} = 0.302^{+0.003}_{-0.003}$, $h = 0.683^{+0.003}_{-0.002}$, and $\sum m_ν< 0.14$ eV (95\% CL). In $w$CDM, this combination yields $w = -0.981^{+0.021}_{-0.022}$.

items.title: Disentangling anomalous Hall effect mechanisms and extra symmetry protection in altermagnetic systems
items.abstract: We investigate the evolution of Anomalous Hall Conductivity (AHC) in a coplanar and collinear antiferromagnetic system with varying spin canting angles. A tight-binding model based on three t2g-orbitals in a body-centered tetragonal lattice is constructed, where the inclusion of third-nearest neighbor hopping is demonstrated to be essential for capturing the characteristic energy band splitting of altermagnetic materials. By employing a symmetry analysis based on spin space groups and treating spin-orbit coupling (SOC) as a perturbation, we theoretically distinguish and numerically verify two origins of the transverse transport: the conventional anomalous Hall effect (AHE) induced by net magnetization and the Crystal Hall Effect (CHE) arising from specific crystal symmetries. Our results show that the conductivity components driven by these two mechanisms follow distinct trigonometric dependencies on the canting angle. Crucially, we identify a hidden C110 rotational symmetry that has been previously overlooked in static magnetic group analyses. By expanding the AHC in terms of spin orientation vectors, we demonstrate that this symmetry acts as a bridge connecting distinct magnetic configurations with different canting angles, thereby strictly protecting the equivalence of orthogonal conductivity components in the collinear system.

items.title: Euclid preparation. CXV. Galaxy power spectrum and bispectrum modelling
items.abstract: Higher-order correlation functions of the large-scale galaxy distribution offer access to information beyond that contained in standard two-point statistics, such as the power spectrum. In this work we assess the potential of the Euclid mission to provide such functions using synthetic catalogues of H,α galaxies based on the 54Ģpc Flagship 1 simulation, which is designed to reproduce the Euclid spectroscopic sample. We comprehensively validate the one-loop galaxy power spectrum and tree-level bispectrum predictions from perturbation theory in both real and redshift space. Assuming scale cuts consistent with our previous power spectrum study on the same catalogues, this modelling yielded unbiased cosmological constraints for the bispectrum up to ̊m max = 0.15̨Mpc in real space and 0.08 , (0.1)̨Mpc at the lowest (highest) redshift, corresponding to z=0.9 (z=1.8), for the monopole and quadrupole in redshift space using statistical uncertainties corresponding to the full simulation volume. With these scale cuts, adding bispectrum information to the power spectrum improves constraints on the amplitude of scalar perturbations and the matter density by up to 30%, increasing the overall figure of merit for key cosmological parameters by a factor of about 2.5. A simple rescaling of the statistical uncertainties to a Euclid -like volume indicates similar conclusions, highlighting the additional information gain from the bispectrum for the forthcoming data. Our analysis also provides the first detailed characterisation of the non-linear bias model of H,α emitters, showing that bias relations calibrated on low-resolution N-body simulations do not adequately describe the clustering of H,α galaxies at low redshift, whereas excursion-set and co-evolution relations for tidal biases remain accurate. Finally, we benchmarked six independent modelling codes, finding excellent agreement under matched assumptions, which testifies to the robustness of our results and provides a benchmark for the official analysis pipeline. items.title: Direction-selective intertwined charge, orbital, and lattice orders under uniaxial strain in the hole-doped manganite La 0.75 Ca 0.25 MnO 3
items.abstract: The complex interplay of charge, spin, orbital, and lattice degrees of freedom governs emergent phases in quantum materials, making strain a powerful control parameter. Recent advances in free-standing layer techniques have enabled extreme strains of nearly 8%, opening access to novel and often unexpected electronic and magnetic phases. Here, using a density functional theory approach, we investigate the effect of direction-selective uniaxial strain on the prototypical Jahn-Teller system La1-xCaxMnO3 (x = 0.25). We find that different strain directions stabilize qualitatively distinct structural, charge, and orbital responses, rather than merely different strengths of the same phase. In particular, extreme uniaxial strain selectively induces cooperative Jahn-Teller, breathing-like, and site-selective modulations, thereby enabling previously inaccessible intertwined orders in manganites. These results establish direction-selective uniaxial strain as a powerful and selective route for engineering emergent phases in quantum materials.

items.title: Open-source framework for GPU-accelerated numerical relativity
items.abstract: We present GRACE, a new GPU-accelerated numerical-relativity framework designed to run efficiently on heterogeneous high-performance computing platforms. Developed from scratch and built exclusively on open-source libraries, GRACE employs Kokkos for performance portability across CPU and GPU architectures and p4est for adaptive mesh refinement. The code evolves the equations of ideal GRMHD -- with divergence-free magnetic fields maintained by constrained transport -- self-consistently coupled to the Einstein equations in the Z4c formulation, on fixed or adaptively refined grids. We validate the implementation against a suite of standard tests, ranging from magnetized shock tubes and the magnetic rotor in flat spacetime, through (magnetized) Bondi accretion onto a Schwarzschild black hole and the ringdown of a perturbed spinning puncture, to neutron-star oscillation spectra in fixed and dynamical spacetimes and the merger of binary black holes. As more demanding applications, we evolve two binary neutron-star mergers -- an equal-mass, unmagnetized system with an ideal-gas equation of state and an unequal-mass, magnetized system with a finite-temperature tabulated equation of state -- finding the inspiral dynamics to agree well with the FIL code. We also report single-device throughput together with strong- and weak-scaling results on multiple GPU and CPU architectures. GRACE is publicly released together with GRACEpy, a basic post-processing and data-analysis environment.

items.title: New Concept of Space-time with Mathematical Measurements derived from the Holy Quran
items.abstract: Abstract T he main objective of this research is to present new concept of space-time through the expansion of the universe, with mathematical measurements (accumulated figures), based on a hypothesis derived from the Holy Quran, verse number 25 Alkahf Sura translated as “ They stayed in their Cave Three hundred years, and Add nine ” (ITANI). The story behind this holy verse came in verses number 9, 10, 11 and 12 in the same Sura about righteous youths escaped from their evil governor to a cave where they stayed there for a number of years indicated in this verse. We interpreted this verse in our previous paper on the construction of mathematical Hijri calendar as every 309 lunar years equal exactly 300 solar years, without any decimal point, and proved it in that paper, (Abuelyamen). In another research paper we used the same methodology to construct mathematical solar calendar. From the outcomes of the second paper we constructed the space-time measurements in this paper with the same methodology as for the two papers (Abuelyamen). The main findings of this research are the production of mathematical measurements for space-time, from the beginning of the least attainable scale of time to different stages of the expansion of the universe. Other three important findings are: first, identification of theoretical scale of time and length that is far smaller than Planck’s time and length, the famous known lowest wall, (wiki/Planck-time); second, development of some theories which would help in solving problems encountered with other physical theories specially the theory of everything; third, from the simulation we drew between our findings and other related verses in the Holly Quran, as well as scientific findings in this respect, we found that they are more or less consistent, a case which supports our findings.

items.title: GLOW. II. A Census of Oxygen in Low-mass Galaxies*
items.abstract: Abstract Oxygen is forged by stars and redistributed through galaxies by feedback-driven outflows, leaving a record of star formation and the baryon cycle imprinted on its present-day abundance and distribution. The Galaxies Losing Oxygen via Winds project quantifies the production, distribution, and retention of oxygen in 37 low-mass, low–metallicity, gas-rich galaxies in the nearby Universe ( D 0.5) and within 1 Mpc of a massive galaxy ( M * > 10 9 M ⊙ ), indicating the environment likely affects the amount of oxygen retained, recycled, or accreted to galaxies. Contrary to expectations, oxygen retention does not correlate with position on the mass–metallicity relation. Although ionized oxygen is detected in the CGM, it remains unclear whether most missing oxygen resides there or has been expelled entirely. Hydrodynamical simulations, despite successfully reproducing the mass–metallicity relation, predict much higher retention fractions than measured in low-mass galaxies. Simple modeling indicates that wind mass-loading and outflow metallicity govern oxygen retention, and that low-mass galaxies accrete less baryonic material relative to the cosmic baryon fraction.

items.title: The impact of magnitude uncertainties and K corrections on standard siren measurements of the Hubble constant
items.abstract: Gravitational-wave standard sirens provide an independent probe of the Hubble constant. Dark siren analyses that rely on galaxy catalogues are sensitive to catalogue-related uncertainties. While incompleteness, weighting schemes, and redshift errors have been studied extensively, the impact of magnitude uncertainties and K corrections has received little attention so far. We assess how magnitude errors and K corrections propagate into the Hubble constant inference, and compare their impact to that of realistic spectroscopic redshift errors to determine their relevance. We used a modified version of the Python package to construct line-of-sight redshift priors from a complete, volume-limited mock galaxy catalogue up to z<0.2. We simulated and analysed a sample of sim200 binary black hole events with luminosity weighting in the B and K bands and tested different uncertainty models for redshifts, magnitudes, and K corrections. gwcosmo The choice of luminosity-weighting scheme has a substantial impact on the inferred Hubble constant posterior, with the direct B- and K-band comparison producing differences comparable to the largest uncertainty-induced changes. Spectroscopic redshift errors produce the largest integrated changes in the Hubble constant posterior among the tested uncertainty treatments. Photometric magnitude uncertainties lead to substantially smaller, band-dependent deviations. In the K band, the tested K-correction treatments have only a minor impact in the present low-redshift mock analysis, with the empirical correction slightly reducing the integrated deviation relative to the no-correction case. Our results show that, for a complete, low-redshift mock catalogue, magnitude uncertainties and K-correction assumptions are subdominant compared to spectroscopic redshift errors, while the luminosity-weighting scheme represents an important modelling choice in catalogue-based dark siren inference. In realistic, flux-limited catalogues with larger localization areas and photometric or mixed redshift errors, the relative impact of magnitude uncertainties is expected to be even smaller, indicating that they need not be prioritized in near-future dark siren analyses.

items.title: Accretion Rates and Thermohaline Convection in Polluted White Dwarfs
items.abstract: Abstract The atmospheres of polluted white dwarfs contain information about the composition of disrupted planetary material. However, interpreting the observed abundances requires a quantitative description of the mixing processes that transport accreted material through their envelopes. In particular, the accretion of metal-rich debris drives thermohaline convection in the star’s radiative zone. Previous studies have modeled this form of turbulence as an enhanced diffusive process, often inferring mass accretion rates M ̇ acc that exceed X-ray constraints. Here we develop a time-dependent model that treats thermohaline mixing as a propagating front whose evolution is coupled self-consistently to the surface abundance of heavy elements. We perform hydrodynamical simulations which demonstrate that thermohaline mixing drives the composition gradient toward values slightly above marginal thermohaline stability. Using this condition, we derive analytic solutions for the mixed layer depth h and surface abundance X surf , finding that both scale as t 1/2 at early times, transitioning to h ∝ t 4/27 and X surf ∝ t 10/27 at later times. Without gravitational settling, the thermohaline front never reaches a steady state, while including settling leads to an equilibrium surface abundance X surf , eq ∝ M ̇ acc 30 / 43 . Applied to G 29–38, our model matches the observed heavy-element abundance for M ̇ acc ∼ 1 × 1 0 10 –2 × 10 10 g s −1 , comparable to previous findings using stellar evolution codes. These rates exceed the X-ray estimate by about an order of magnitude, which may point to a partially suppressed X-ray luminosity from the accretion boundary layer. We also present a practical prescription for inferring accretion rates directly from the observed surface abundance and stellar parameters for other polluted white dwarfs.

items.title: Charging of rotating black holes: Kinetic simulations of black hole magnetospheres
items.abstract: Whether a rotating black hole (BH) immersed in an external magnetic field charges up to the Wald value $Q_{\rm W}=2aMB$, where $M$ and $a$ are the BH mass and spin parameter, and $B$ is the strength of the external field, is a long-standing open question in BH electrodynamics, with consequences for charge separation, particle acceleration and the structure of BH magnetospheres. We address it with axisymmetric general-relativistic particle-in-cell simulations performed with GRZeltron, including self-consistent pair creation. For representative values of the BH spin, we evolve the same asymptotically uniform Wald field from two opposite initial horizon charges, $Q_{0}=0$ and $Q_{0}=Q_{\rm W}$, and track the accumulated charge through the BH horizon. We find that both branches relax within a few tens of gravitational times to the same saturated charge value. Thus, the equilibrium is a dynamical attractor of the kinetic magnetosphere rather than a memory of the initial data. The attractor lies well below $Q_{\rm W}$, at $ξ_{\rm eq}\equiv Q_{\rm eq}/Q_{\rm W}\approx 0.3$ for $a\lesssim0.7$, then falling almost to $ξ_{\rm eq}\approx0$ for large spins $a\approx1$. We derive an analytic expression for $ξ_{\rm eq}$ by requiring equal magnetic fluxes through the horizon associated with positive and negative charges, and find its spin dependence to be in agreement with the simulations. The charge state of an astrophysical BH is therefore driven by kinetic plasma processes, and the Wald charge is an upper bound, not a general equilibrium value. Since $ξ_{\rm eq}<1$, charging does not quench the horizon-infinity potential drop that powers energy-extraction processes such as the Blandford-Znajek mechanism.

items.title: Mode Switching in Two Blue Large-amplitude Pulsators Observed by OGLE, KMTNet, and DREAMS
items.abstract: Abstract Blue large-amplitude pulsators (BLAPs) are rare, hot, short-period pulsating stars whose rapid oscillations provide a unique probe of stellar interiors and atmospheres. In this paper, we study two short-period BLAPs in the Galactic bulge, Optical Gravitational Lensing Experiment (OGLE)-BLAP-142 ( P ≈ 6.6 minutes) and OGLE-BLAP-148 ( P ≈ 7.5 minutes), by combining light curves from the OGLE, KMTNet, and DREAMS surveys, spanning 17 yr with cadences ranging from minutes to hours to days. We perform generalized Lomb–Scargle periodogram analyses of their light curves and identify, for each BLAP, three closely spaced pulsation modes separated by ∼1%. The dominant mode can switch within timescales of order a year, accompanied by a likely blueward color shift (∼0.1–0.2 mag). The yearly period excursions of the resolved mode families imply apparent ∣ P ̇ / P ∣ values of order 10 −6 –10 −4 yr −1 , large enough to mimic or exceed smooth evolutionary period changes. One mode family in OGLE-BLAP-148 shows a coherent decade-long drift at the ∼10 −5 yr −1 level, but its failure to extrapolate to the earliest and latest epochs suggests a transient mode-family drift rather than secular evolution. Such close-spaced multiple pulsations and mode switching may be common among BLAPs with periods shorter than 10 minutes, and their physical origin remains unclear.

items.title: On the precise boundary of the Néel antiferromagnetic phase in the Shastry-Sutherland model
items.abstract: Abstract The ground state phase diagram of the Shastry-Sutherland model remains controversial. In particular, the nature of the transition between the plaquette valence bond solid (PVBS) phase and the Néel antiferromagnetic (AFM) phase is still under debate. While some studies suggest a direct transition between the two phases, others propose the existence of a narrow intermediate quantum spin liquid regime. To address this issue, we perform large-scale Density Matrix Renormalization Group calculations to determine the Néel AFM phase boundary in the Shastry-Sutherland model. By applying staggered boundary pinning fields and directly measuring the bulk staggered magnetization, and through systematic extrapolations with respect to truncation error as well as careful finite-size scaling, we find that the staggered magnetization remains finite across the controversial region 0.78 ≲ J 1 / J 2 ≤ 0.81, which was suggested to host a quantum spin liquid phase in some studies. Together with the previously established consensus placing the PVBS phase boundary at J 1 / J 2 ≈ 0.78, these results, within the resolution of the present calculations, provide evidence against the existence of an intermediate quantum spin liquid phase and support a direct PVBS-Néel AFM transition in the Shastry-Sutherland model.

items.title: Dual and lensed AGN at sub-arcsecond separations uncovered by ERIS
items.abstract: We present the first results of the ongoing INAF GTO programme focused on the search of sub--arcsecond dual active galactic nuclei (AGN), carried out with the near-infrared integral-field unit SPIFFIER of the Enhanced Resolution Imager and Spectrograph (ERIS) at the ESO Very Large Telescope, operating in adaptive-optics mode with a laser guide star. We report integral field spectroscopy with the low--resolution gratings (R ∼ 5000 - 5600) of 34 multiple AGN candidates selected from the Gaia Data Release 3 source catalogue via the Gaia Multipeak (GMP) method, which preferentially identifies luminous unobscured AGN at sub-arcsecond separations. The targets span the redshift range of 0.7 łesssim z łesssim 3.4 and exhibit projected angular separations between ∼0.2'' and ∼0.9'', corresponding to physical separations of ∼1.7--7.8 kpc. Of the 34 observed systems,13 (∼40%) are resolved into multiple AGN-like components; and 18 (∼53%) are classified as AGN plus foreground star superpositions, with one as a single AGN, and two as systems with an AGN primary and an unclassified secondary component. Among the multiple AGN systems, we confirm six dual AGN at projected separations of 0.26'' -- 0.80'' (2.2--6.7 kpc), in the redshift range of z = 0.68 -- 1.57, and with velocity offsets in the range of Δ v ∼ 290 -- 950 ̨ms. We also identify seven gravitationally lensed quasars, only one of which was previously known, including four doubly imaged and three quadruply imaged systems. These results substantially enlarge the census of spectroscopically confirmed compact multiple AGN systems at z > 0.5 and demonstrate the efficiency of ERIS--SPIFFIER for the systematic characterization of sub-arcsecond dual and lensed AGN candidates.

items.title: The Density Distribution of Dark Matter in the Milky Way Based on Stellar Velocities Measured by GAIA DR2
items.abstract: Since the early stages of the formation of the universe, dark matter has played a crucial role in mapping the large scale structures, being the frame of matter overdensities which grew up to form galactic and intergalactic structures. However, due to its mysterious nature and the property only interacting with gravitational fields, not much light is shed on the discovery and understanding of dark matter’s possible particle nature. This paper aims to interpret the density distribution of dark matter in different regions of the Milky Way(Bulge, Disk, Halo) from most recent models(NFW, Einasto, Isothermal, Burkert, Moore) and match it with the data of stellar rotational velocities measured by GAIA DR2 database. We do not directly derive velocities from raw GAIA DR2, but instead use compiled rotation curve data calibrated with GAIA measurements taken from Sofue et al. 2025[20]. We have also extrapolated parameters and normalization factors regarding each model, and evaluated with a more rudimentary method offered from Cirelli, M. et al. 2011[7]. Through our method, we provide a rudimentary overview on how the dark matter density profiles correlate with the newest DR2 data and evaluate their applicability. In turn, we hope the results offer insight on which model could be compatible concurrently in our galaxy.
