items.title: Time to AC-t: When AC-transmission changes capacity expansion planning
items.abstract: Capacity expansion models often dramatically simplify the physics of how power flows through a transmission network in order to preserve computational tractability. However, with the rapid growth of electrification, large loads, renewables, and storage, increased realism in planning future grids is imperative. We extend the open-source capacity expansion model GenX with AC optimal power flow physics, and analyze generation, storage, and transmission investment decisions for 20-zone, hourly models of Germany and Texas. We compare our results against those using two common approximations, the transport model and DC optimal power flow. We find that total costs and emissions largely agree across all formulations. However, we find substantial differences in outputs related to transmission, generation siting, storage, and reactive-power support between the approximate formulations and the true AC physics formulation. We identify where AC physics changes planning decisions and discuss how to potentially capture these effects without the full computational cost.

items.title: Precision Requirements for Robust Small Planet Classification
items.abstract: Classifying small exoplanets as rocky, volatile-rich, or iron-enriched is a prerequisite for efficient allocation of atmospheric characterization resources. The Nominally Rocky Planet Zone (NRPZ) provides a framework for this classification by comparing observed bulk densities against the expected density range for volatile-free rocky planets, calibrated from stellar abundance distributions. However, the efficacy of classifying a planet using the NRPZ is critically dependent on the precision of the underlying mass and radius measurements. Here, we perform an analytical propagation of observational uncertainties through the NRPZ classification framework for 37 candidate rocky exoplanets with radii below 2 Earth radii orbiting stars with visual magnitudes <11. Among the 37 planets, we find 12 already possess sufficiently precise mass and radius measurements to be confidently classified as Mini-Neptunes or Super-Mercuries. The remaining planets require approximately a ~60% reduction in the combined mass and radius uncertainties before they can be reliably classified. We find that 1-1,000 new observations are necessary to achieve these lower uncertainties, and these are likely lower limits. We argue that, while possible, this level of intense observation is likely not feasible for many of these planets and that mass-radius models alone are not likely to allow us to classify all but those planets with outlier densities. We therefore recommend a staged strategy in which improved mass and radius measurements are used to identify and prioritize ambiguous systems, followed (where feasible) by atmospheric observations with JWST or future facilities as a complementary test of whether selected planets retain substantial atmospheres.

items.title: Measuring the gas mass of the protoplanetary disk around HD 179218 with CO isotopologues
items.abstract: Carbon monoxide (CO) isotopologues are widely used to estimate protoplanetary disk gas masses, but their reliability is often compromised by CO freeze-out and subsequent chemical processing. The disk around the luminous Herbig star HD~179218 ($L_* \sim 100\,L_\odot$, $M_* \sim 3.0\,M_\odot$) offers a rare test case of CO-based mass measurements. Its CO snowline lies beyond the outer disk edge, and thus CO remains in the gas phase throughout. We present ALMA and NOEMA observations of six CO isotopologue lines ($^{13}$CO, C$^{18}$O, and C$^{17}$O, $J$=2--1 and 1--0). Fitting the spectral energy distribution yields $M_{dust} \approx 3 \times 10^{-5}\, M_\odot$. Modeling CO isotopologue emission with the thermochemical code DALI yields the gas-disk characteristic radius ($R_{c} \approx 90$~au) and the gas mass ($M_{gas} \approx 8 \times 10^{-3}\, M_\odot$). These results yield a gas-to-dust ratio of $\sim$270 for our fiducial dust opacity ($a_{\rm max} = 1$~mm), above the canonical interstellar value of $\sim$100. The thermal structure of our best-fitting model confirms that CO never freezes out in this disk, so the elevated ratio is not an artifact of CO depletion; together with the compact millimeter dust disk relative to the gas disk, it is consistent with substantial inward radial drift of millimeter dust. In addition, we find a gas cavity inside 50\,au that encloses the compact millimeter dust disk---the inverse of a typical transition disk---which we attribute to photoevaporative clearing of the inner gas after the pebbles drifted inward. HD~179218 thus provides a clean benchmark for studying the gas mass distribution and gas--dust interaction in protoplanetary disks, free from the CO-depletion biases that affect colder disks.

items.title: The Hot Neptune Initiative (HONEI): IV. TOI-4129 b, an Adolescent Neptune in the Ridge
items.abstract: Recent exoplanet demographics studies have uncovered the Neptune ridge: an overdensity of intermediate-size planets at orbital periods between 3--6~d. The origin of this pile-up remains unclear, but it could be a consequence of high-eccentricity migration (HEM). Here, we confirm TOI-4129\,b, a planet that may help to reveal the origin of the Neptune ridge. Using radial velocities from HARPS-N and transit photometry from TESS and four ground-based telescopes, we found that TOI-4129\,b has a relatively low density ($R_p = 5.7 \pm 0.2\, R_\oplus$, $M_p = 26\pm 6 \,M_\oplus$, $ρ_p = 0.8 \pm 0.2 ~\textrm{g}~\textrm{cm}^{-3}$) and orbits a $V = 12.9$ K dwarf star every 3.27~d, placing it at the inner edge of the Neptune ridge. We detect the stellar rotation period at 12.7~d in the photometry, implying a fairly young gyrochronal age of $1.20^{+0.16}_{-0.30}~$Gyr for the system. With a Transmission Spectroscopy Metric of $112\pm 30$, this adolescent Neptune is a good target for atmospheric observations with \textit{JWST} and \textit{Ariel}, and we also find that it is amenable to future constraints on the (three-dimensional) stellar obliquity. TOI-4129\,b will therefore be an important testing ground for the idea that planets in the Neptune ridge underwent HEM to arrive at their current locations.

items.title: Galactic-Scale Distribution of 10Be and Its Implications for the Early Solar System 10Be/9Be
items.abstract: Meteoritic inclusions indicate that the early Solar System contained a substantial abundance of the short-lived radionuclide 10Be. Whether it was inherited from the parent molecular cloud or requires local irradiation or late injection remains debated. Here we present the first three-dimensional simulations of a Milky Way-like disc that follow the multi-phase interstellar medium, cosmic rays (CRs), and the production and transport of 10Be by galactic CRs (GCRs) and in supernova remnants (SNRs). Nearly all 10Be is produced by GCR interactions; SNRs contribute at most about ten percent of the 10Be inherited by newly formed stars. The 10Be/9Be ratio traces the CR energy density, declining smoothly with galactocentric radius, and because stars form where supernovae inject CRs, their natal gas is CR-enriched roughly fivefold relative to the mean interstellar medium, which one-zone estimates miss. Accounting for a possibly higher Galactic star formation rate 4.6 Gyr ago, inheritance of GCR-produced 10Be can then explain the early Solar System's 10Be/9Be in our models, without late injection or local irradiation. Even when GCR-induced 10Be production in dense gas is reduced tenfold, the meteoritic value is reached in the innermost disc and missed by only a factor of a few elsewhere, so the main conclusion is robust to uncertain low-energy GCR penetration. The inferred birth radius of the Sun depends strongly on the CR diffusivity, ranging between 3 and 8 kpc, suggesting that improved modelling of low-energy CR transport could sharpen constraints on the birthplace of the Solar System.

items.title: The consciousness-first commitment of integrated information theory.
items.abstract: Integrated information theory (IIT) accounts for consciousness through its explanatory identity : an experience (the explanandum ) is identical to a causal structure (or Φ -structure, the explanans ). In other identities in science (e.g . 'water is H 2 O'), the power of the explanans (H 2 O) comes from the presumption that it somehow exists more fundamentally. Yet when our explanandum is experience itself, as in IIT, we must recalibrate the norms of explanation to the fact that experience exists immediately and irrefutably, while whatever we may posit about the world beyond experience is always an inference within experience.

items.title: Overcoming essentialism: evaluation of theories of consciousness by the lawful regularities they predict.
items.abstract: A common objection to consciousness research is that researchers cannot agree on what consciousness is. But how should a consensus on the nature of consciousness be reached? Does consciousness have essential features that one can be right or wrong about? Should we select theories of consciousness based on their descriptions of the essential features of experience alone? In this article, we will argue with the help of Popper that determining unquestionable essential features of consciousness is neither possible nor desirable. Instead, any account of what consciousness is, should be understood as a subjective selection of features and should not count as an insight. According to Popper, insights in science are achieved when novel regularities between observations are discovered that generalize to scientific laws. Furthermore, all results of research can be stated independently of the definitions that were used in their making. Therefore, no consensus on the nature of consciousness or on a theory of consciousness is needed for consciousness research to progress-in fact, a multitude of definitions and theories may be beneficial. Based on this, we argue that theories of consciousness be evaluated by their ability to propose concrete, testable laws rather than by their description of what consciousness is.

items.title: No Memory Is an Island: How Social Interactions Transform Autobiographical Memory.
items.abstract: Autobiographical memory is not merely a record of past events but a dynamic reconstruction shaped by context, emotion, and social interaction. In this hypothesis paper, we propose that empathic interactions can transform autobiographical memory, altering memory's content, emotional tone, and integration into the self. We begin by outlining the social foundations of autobiographical memory and the neural systems involved in its transformation, focusing on the hippocampus, prefrontal cortex, and amygdala. We then explore how empathic exchanges may lead to changes in memory specificity and coherence, emotional reappraisal, and self-concept, particularly within psychotherapy and close relationships. Central to our framework is the proposal that interbrain synchrony, neural coupling across individuals during interaction, facilitates the co-construction of meaning and shared understanding. Crucially, we argue that distinct forms of empathic interaction and patterns of interbrain synchrony support different mechanisms of memory change, including contextual binding, emotional regulation, narrative reframing, and self-relevant integration. We discuss how these mechanisms support memory updating through repeated interpersonal engagement. Finally, we offer testable predictions of our model and consider clinical and societal implications. Our framework bridges memory research and social neuroscience and offers a novel, integrative direction for understanding memory as a phenomenon co-constructed through interactions.

items.title: Microglia: Metabolic Adaptation in Neurodegeneration.
items.abstract: Microglia, the brain's primary innate immune cells, are metabolically dynamic cells whose functional states, from homeostatic surveillance to disease-associated phagocytosis, lipid droplet accumulation, and stress-induced neurotoxicity, are governed by distinct metabolic programs. Neurodegenerative stressors, including misfolded protein accumulation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and sustained inflammation, initially trigger adaptive metabolic reprogramming of glycolysis, the tricarboxylic acid cycle, and amino acid and lipid pathways. Under chronic stimuli, these same shifts become maladaptive, impairing microglial phagocytosis, promoting lipid accumulation, and driving the secretion of neurotoxic lipid species. A unifying theme emerging across metabolic pathways is that the intermediates produced under stress, lactate, succinate, ceramide, acetyl-CoA, and α-ketoglutarate, do not merely reflect cellular state but actively reshape it through epigenetic modification of histones and DNA. In this review, we examine how each major metabolic pathway responds to acute and chronic neurodegeneration-associated stress in microglia, highlight where epigenetic mechanisms convert transient metabolic shifts into durable changes in microglial identity, and identify genetic risk factors that encode metabolic vulnerability in neurodegenerative diseases, such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease.

items.title: The Experiences of Psychotherapy for People With Dementia: A Qualitative Interview Study With Family Members.
items.abstract: Psychotherapeutic interventions can support people with dementia. Family members often play a pivotal role in the therapeutic process but little is known about their experiences of therapy, how they perceive the impact on their relative, and how the experience affects them directly. This study aimed to explore the experiences of family members who engage in therapy, or support someone living with dementia to attend therapy. Individuals with dementia and their family members were recruited as participants through NHS Trusts, professional networks, social media and community and support groups based in England and Wales. Semi-structured qualitative individual or dyadic interviews were conducted with 17 participants, eight of whom were living with dementia and nine were family members. Framework analysis was used. Family members highlighted "the importance of feeling seen" as distinct individuals by clinicians when engaging with psychotherapy, and not just the carer of their partner. When working with "dementia as dynamic phenomenon", therapeutic approaches needed to balance being sufficiently structured and containing whilst allowing for adaptions to each individual changeable presentation. Participants highlighted how psychotherapy presented "expected and unexpected outcomes", challenges that arose when outcomes were not agreed upon, and how therapy functioned as a support structure in ways the participants did not foresee. Psychotherapeutic intervention provides meaningful support to the family members of individuals with dementia. Understanding the needs of family members, alongside the needs of the individual with dementia, and taking a systemic approach is conducive to better therapeutic outcomes. The changeable nature of dementia presentation means that a therapeutic approach should be flexible based on the needs of the family. Psychotherapeutic intervention with individuals with dementia can have a range of benefits for the individual and the wider family, when sufficient considerations are made to understand each person's needs.

items.title: Rapid sequence induction: a narrative review.
items.abstract: Introduction Pulmonary aspiration of gastric contents remains an important cause of anaesthetic morbidity and mortality, and is important medicolegally. Rapid sequence induction is a multi-element technique designed to mitigate risk in those patients at increased risk of pulmonary aspiration during induction of general anaesthesia. Methods We undertook a narrative review to summarise evidence and evidence gaps focusing on controversial aspects of rapid sequence induction. Results Despite widespread use of rapid sequence induction, many elements of the technique lack robust evidence and consensus. Nasogastric tubes can be used to reduce gastric content, but do not empty the stomach reliably. Correctly applied cricoid force obstructs the hypopharynx and has a limited impact on airway management, but incorrect application can cause clinically significant difficulties. Correct location of cricoid force may require ultrasound localisation of the cricoid cartilage. Applying the correct force, which varies with age and sex, is improved by education, practice and feedback. The use of videolaryngoscopy during rapid sequence induction is supported by evidence. The role of gastric ultrasound in determining anaesthetic technique is uncertain. Cardiovascular complications of rapid sequence induction are common, particularly in the patients who are critically ill, and modifications to the technique may reduce their frequency and severity. Effective use of airway rescue techniques may require removal of cricoid force. Discussion There is insufficient evidence for many of the elements of rapid sequence induction to determine whether they reduce patient harm or to state confidently that they do not. Controversies and evidence gaps should be acknowledged. Despite this, optimal use of rapid sequence induction requires a thorough knowledge of the subject, including areas of uncertainty to guide individualised risk assessment; clinical decision-making; and practical conduct of the technique.

items.title: No Additional Benefit of 185 Hz Versus 130 Hz at Equivalent Energy in Deep Brain Stimulation for Tremor: A Randomized Prospective Clinical Trial.
items.abstract: Background Deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the ventral intermediate nucleus and posterior subthalamic area (VIM/PSA) in Essential Tremor (ET) and the subthalamic nucleus (STN) in Parkinson's disease (PD) are established treatments for tremor. To achieve maximum tremor control, increasing stimulation frequency beyond 130 Hz is part of clinical practice, but lacks scientific evidence. Objective To compare tremor suppression under total electrical energy delivered (TEED)-equivalent stimulation at 130 versus 185 Hz in VIM/PSA-DBS for ET and STN-DBS for PD. Methods In this prospective, double-blind study, acute DBS effects were assessed in 18 people with ET (n = 29 hemispheres), and 25 people with PD (n = 30 hemispheres). Tremor-suppressive effects, evaluated by accelerometry, were compared with TEED-equivalent stimulation at 130 and 185 Hz using linear mixed-effects models, explorative pairwise comparisons, and equivalency testing. Results Linear mixed-effects models revealed no significant effect of stimulation frequency on tremor improvement in both cohorts. Pairwise comparisons showed no consistent differences in total tremor improvement with TEED-equivalent 130 Hz vs 185 Hz DBS. Post-hoc equivalence testing confirmed equivalence of stimulation frequencies under TEED-equivalent conditions within a ±20% margin of relative tremor improvement. Conclusion This study provides Level II evidence that a higher stimulation frequency of 185 Hz does not offer additional benefit in deep brain stimulation for tremor in VIM/PSA for Essential Tremor or in the STN for Parkinson's Disease in the acute setting and supports 130 Hz as the standard stimulation frequency for tremor suppression.

items.title: Fear generalization, cross-sensitization and behavioural responses to multiple dangers in a freshwater snail.
items.abstract: Behavioural responses to multiple stressors play a major role in survival and fitness. In this context, an important issue that has rarely been tested is fear generalization, where responses to disparate threats are correlated at the individual level. Furthermore, while sensitization to stressors is well studied, cross-sensitization, where exposure to one threat increases behavioural responsiveness to unrelated threats, is under-studied. We exposed juvenile Physid snails (Physa acuta) to one of two disparate threats throughout their developmental period: predator cues and ash, a wildfire-derived environmental stressor. We then assayed snails' responses, relative to control snails that had no experience with either threat, to three acute exposures of each stressor. We documented consistent individual differences in snails' avoidance of predation cues and of ash. Exposure to either stressor led to sensitization at short- and long-term timescales. Importantly, snails exhibited fear generalization; individuals that avoided predation cues more strongly also avoided ash more strongly. We also documented cross-sensitization; snails reared with ash showed heightened responses to predator cues while snails reared with predator cues showed heightened responses to ash. To our knowledge, this is the first study documenting behavioural cross-sensitization for threats as disparate as predation risk and fire residue in a non-human animal.

items.title: Dynamic ultrasound assessment of sciatic nerve excursion during neurodynamic mobilizations: a prospective observational study.
items.abstract: Purpose This study evaluates sciatic nerve excursion at the hamstring level during active and passive neurodynamic mobilization (NDM) of the tibial, superficial peroneal, deep peroneal, and sural nerves. The aim is to determine which NDM (active or passive) generates higher excursion. Methods This analytical observational study was carried out at the University Clinic of the University of Manresa over a period of 17 weeks. Participants were placed in a side-lying SLUMP position with 60° of hip flexion and full knee extension. Neurodynamic mobilizations were performed randomly either actively or passively. Simultaneously, sciatic nerve excursion was recorded using high-frequency ultrasound and subsequently quantified using MATLAB software (version 2019b) through a frame-by-frame cross-correlation analysis. A statistically significant difference was observed between the two conditions (p Conclusions The sciatic nerve can be mobilized through its four terminal branches using both active and passive neurodynamic techniques, all of which generate a proximal mechanical effect. Active self-mobilization, particularly through the tibial nerve, may represent an effective therapeutic intervention for patients with proximal sciatic nerve involvement, as it produces greater sciatic nerve excursion at the hamstring level.

items.title: The nanotubular network as a new dimension of intercellular communication in the nervous system.
items.abstract: Communication between cells in the nervous system has long been understood to occur through chemical and electrical synapses, and through the release of signalling molecules and extracellular vesicles across the extracellular space. Intercellular nanotubes (NTs) - thin, membranous tubular bridges that physically connect distant cells - represent a structurally distinct route of communication, enabling the direct, targeted transfer of cellular cargoes between selected cells. Once studied almost exclusively in culture, NTs have now been visualized in situ and in vivo throughout the nervous system, including dendritic NTs between neurons, NTs formed by microglia and astrocytes, interpericyte NTs in the retina and NTs between satellite glia and peripheral sensory neurons. Through these connections, cells exchange mitochondria, proteins and their aggregates, and calcium, supporting three emerging roles: homeostatic rescue of stressed cells, pathological propagation of toxic proteins in neurodegeneration and non-synaptic calcium signalling, respectively. NT networks are dynamic and stress-responsive, suggesting that they provide a plastic infrastructure for resource sharing among neurons and glia. Understanding their function will require establishing a standardized definition, achieving rigorous in situ validation and quantification, and developing specific molecular tools to manipulate NTs.

items.title: Amyloid beta governs mitochondrial lipid metabolism defects and neurodegenerative lysosomal stress.
items.abstract: Mechanisms linking amyloid peptides to mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired mitophagy in Alzheimer's disease (AD) remain poorly defined. Here, we report that, in healthy aging neurons, mitochondrial ceramide synthase 1 (CerS1) localization accompanies increased mitochondrial C18-ceramide and mitophagy in damaged mitochondria. In neuronal, mouse, and human AD tissues, amyloid precursor protein (APP) or Aβ40, but not Aβ42, shows increased proximity or co-association with TOM20/TOM40 alongside reduced mitochondrial CerS1/C18-ceramide accumulation and mitophagy. Mitochondria-excluded mutant APP does not reproduce these responses in neuronal cells. WT-APP expression is associated with reduced p17/PERMIT-ICT1 proximity, which does not establish direct APP-ICT1 binding or disruption of complex formation. Reduced mitophagy also accompanies lysosomal Aβ42 accumulation and secretion from neurons. Aged CerS1top/top mice, expressing catalytically inactive CerS1, exhibit mitochondrial dysfunction, behavioral deficits, and amyloid-positive plaque accumulation. Treatment with the peptide-targeted nanoparticle Pen-Cera-LCL768, which accumulates in the brain after intranasal administration, increases mitophagy-related readouts, reduces plaque burden, and improves behavioral performance in aged 3xTg and CerS1top/top mice. Mdivi-1 attenuates treatment effects in 3xTg mice, but its lack of specificity limits conclusions about mitophagy dependence.

items.title: Endogenous rhythms in deep-sea mussel cell culture and molecular clock characterization.
items.abstract: While biological rhythms are crucial to life, the deep sea has long been considered an arrhythmic exception. However, at hydrothermal vents - devoid of diel cues yet shaped by tides - the mussel Bathymodiolus azoricus shows both tidal and, unexpectedly, circadian rhythms at -1700 m. Whether endogenous clock(s) drive these cycles remained unanswered. Here, we report endogenous circadian rhythms in B. azoricus cell cultures under constant conditions: isolated cells display a circadian oscillation despite tidal-dominant rhythms in the natural environment. Reporter assays using genomic regions upstream of the mussel's per gene and containing E-box motifs suggest that a functional transcription-translation feedback loop (TTFL) contributes to circadian timing even in the deep sea. In mussels, BazPeriod lacks autonomous repressive activity but modulates BazCry2. As BazPeriod itself oscillates tidally, it may explain how a single endogenous clock yields both tidal and diel rhythms. The work also spotlights the highly time-sensitive biology of the vastly unexplored deep-sea environment.

items.title: Peripheral neuroimmune dialogues underlying pain states.
items.abstract: Pain is profoundly shaped by neuroimmune interactions within peripheral tissues. Nociceptors are specialized sensory neurons that express receptors for cytokines, lipid mediators, complement components, antibodies and microbial signals, enabling immune mediators to directly modulate neuronal excitability. In turn, nociceptors influence immune cell and stromal cell activity through the release of neuropeptides and cytokines. Some of these pathways are shared across multiple tissues in pathological pain states, whereas others reflect the distinct immune and stromal environments of the skin, joints, muscles, gut, peripheral nerves, sensory ganglia and meninges. Across these sites, immune-to-neuron signalling orchestrates the initiation and amplification of pain, while maladaptive feedback loops reinforce hypersensitivity. In concert, coordinated neuroimmune signalling also contributes to pain resolution by restoring homeostasis. Emerging human studies reveal convergent neuroimmune signatures across nociceptive, neuropathic and nociplastic pain conditions, underscoring their translational relevance. By integrating both shared mechanisms and tissue-specific mechanisms, this Review highlights how peripheral neuroimmune crosstalk shapes pain across diverse contexts. Furthermore, it outlines therapeutic opportunities to rebalance these pathways, offering prospects for durable and mechanism-based analgesia.

items.title: A multi-institutional investigation of psilocybin's effects on mouse behavior.
items.abstract: Studies reporting the effects of psychedelic drugs on mouse behavior are rapidly emerging. However, the reproducibility and reliability of these effects remain uncertain. Here we implemented a multi-institutional collaborative approach to assess which effects of psilocybin on mouse behavior are robust and replicable. Five independent laboratories performed the same experiments to test the acute and persistent effects of psilocybin (2 mg kg -1 , intraperitoneally) on various behaviors. Psilocybin acutely increased anxiety- and avoidance-related behaviors and decreased fear expression in a robust and replicable manner. Surprisingly, however, psilocybin did not have replicable effects 24 h after administration in terms of reducing anxiety- and depression-like behaviors or facilitating fear extinction learning. Additionally, we did not observe psilocybin-induced alterations in social preference or social reward learning. Our characterization of psilocybin's behavioral effects, using ~200 male and female mice per experiment across five laboratories, demonstrates several robust acute effects and suggests that some of psilocybin's reported persistent effects in mice may be modest and/or inconsistent.

items.title: Reframing perineural invasion in intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma as a spatial neuroimmune niche.
items.abstract: Perineural invasion (PNI) is an adverse histopathological feature in intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (iCCA), yet its biological meaning is often reduced to a binary pathology variable. This convention overlooks the spatial heterogeneity of the tumour-nerve interface, where nerve subtype, tumour-nerve geometry, stromal organization and immune-cell positioning may carry distinct clinical implications. Recent iCCA-specific evidence identifies, in selected PNI-positive tumours, TH-positive sympathetic fibres, increased norepinephrine, tumour-cell ADRB2-PI3K-AKT-NF-κB-MDK signalling and ferroptosis-associated dysfunction of CD56dimCD16+ natural killer cells. This is currently the strongest disease-specific neuroimmune axis, but it represents only one component of a broader niche that may include CD8+ T-cell exclusion or exhaustion, regulatory and helper T-cell states, macrophage/MDSC suppression, CAF/ECM barriers and TLS topology. In this Review, we distinguish direct iCCA or iCCA-PNI evidence from evidence from other CCA subtypes or general iCCA studies and from cross-cancer hypotheses. We propose a candidate, unvalidated spatial neuroimmune framework that integrates neural phenotyping, spatial immune mapping and imaging. The framework is intended to support four separate research uses-prognostic stratification, preoperative prediction of pathological PNI, pharmacodynamic monitoring and prospective treatment-benefit testing-and should not be treated as a validated clinical score or as a basis for unselected neural or immune therapy. This approach may move PNI reporting from a binary risk label toward a testable, spatially resolved model of iCCA heterogeneity.

items.title: Dynamic Resource Partitioning in a Marine Predator Community.
items.abstract: To avoid competition, species partition resource-use along various niche axes. However, variable resource availability, especially within dynamic environments, may influence this partitioning. Theory predicts that species will contract their ecological niche to limit competition during times of resource scarcity. We analysed blood δ 13 C and δ 15 N composition in four albatrosses, four penguin, two giant petrel and two fur seal species breeding on sub-Antarctic Marion Island, during two seasons (autumn and summer) over 3 years. Using the species' seasonal stable isotopic niche space as a proxy for trophic niche space, we investigated their trophic dynamics and maintenance of inter-specific resource partitioning. There were significant variations in the seasonal and inter-annual trophic niches of these predators. However, despite this high seasonal and annual variability, resource partitioning among the species was maintained over time. Between years, there was greater variability in the species' trophic niches in autumn than in summer. This might reflect species being better able to track productive dynamic oceanographic features during autumn, when most species are less spatially constrained by breeding commitments compared to during summer. Our results indicate that most of these marine predators have foraging behaviours that are either sufficiently flexible or general to cope with resources that are variable in space and time. Their foraging strategies minimise inter-specific overlap in food or foraging habitat preferences, potentially resulting from historic or present competition for resources.

items.title: Spotted Patterns of Glass Frogs Can Disguise Imperfections in Transparency to Improve Camouflage.
items.abstract: Transparency could be considered the idealized version of camouflage, capable of producing effective concealment across heterogeneous habitats. However, although examples of highly transparent species do exist, 'transparent' species are highly variable and are often either only partially transparent or better described as translucent. Exactly how these different forms of 'imperfect' transparency may act as camouflage remains largely unknown. The glass frogs (Centrolenidae) have long been thought of as a classic example of transparent camouflage due to their see-through ventral skin. Yet even in these seemingly exemplary cases, glass frogs are better described as translucent due to the presence of obligate opaque structures, such as the internal organs, within the body and opaque color patterns in their dorsal skin. These opaque patterns could be predicted to detract from transparency, with the potential to increase detectability and therefore predation risk. One potential explanation is that the addition of opaque patterning could help to conceal the internal organs from view while maintaining the cryptic effects of translucency. Here we tested whether the presence of opaque spots could reduce predation risk for translucent frogs by presenting model frogs, which differed in opacity and dorsal patterning, to wild birds and recording the rate at which these models were attacked. We found that the addition of opaque dorsal patterning reduced predation risk but there was no effect of translucency on survival. These data suggest that opaque patterning in glass frogs may help to conceal conspicuous internal structures but that partial translucency does not necessarily guarantee effective concealment. Future work is needed to explore the full range of dorsal patterning found in translucent glass frogs and to further examine how patterns comprised of both opaque and transparent elements may function as camouflage in a wider range of taxa.

items.title: Characteristics of Professionals Involved in Open Science in Ecology and Evolution.
items.abstract: Open science aims to improve research transparency, reuse and societal impact, yet its adoption and reach ultimately depend on people. Understanding how personal characteristics such as gender, work experience or professional role influence familiarity with, attitudes toward and engagement in open science is critical for the effective, widespread implementation of open science practices. We surveyed 342 individuals who produce, mobilise or use scientific knowledge in ecology and evolutionary biology. Their engagement was analysed using the open science change framework, which conceptualises open science as a progression from familiarity and perceptions to practices and support for societal goals, as outlined in the UNESCO Recommendations. Familiarity with open science emerged as a strongest and most consistent predictor of engagement: higher familiarity was associated with more positive attitudes, greater participation in open science practices and stronger agreement with UNESCO principles. Although these relationships are correlational and likely bidirectional, they highlight the central role of familiarity in open science engagement. Years of professional experience were associated with slightly less positive perceptions of open science, particularly among knowledge creators, while gender effects were weak across all stages of engagement. Stakeholder groups differed most in their familiarity with open science, while attitudes and support for broader goals were more similar once familiarity was considered. Together, these findings suggest that increasing familiarity with open science may be more effective than managing resistance or targeting specific demographic groups. Aligning incentives and practical support to increase familiarity offers actionable opportunities to strengthen open science engagement across the research ecosystem in ecology and evolutionary biology and enhance its societal impact.

items.title: Mapping Leopard Conservation Priorities in Southeast Asia.
items.abstract: The Indochinese leopard ( Panthera pardus delacouri ) is one of the most endangered leopard subspecies, restricted to < 4% of its historical range across Southeast Asia. With severe declines driven by poaching, habitat loss and fragmentation, and prey depletion, recovery requires urgent, spatially informed conservation action. This study presents the first connectivity analysis for the Indochinese leopard across its extant and former range, aiming to identify core habitats, priority connectivity areas and opportunities for population restoration. We used resistant kernel modelling through the CoLa Decision Support System to evaluate landscape connectivity across 14 forest complexes in the extant range and 11 potential reintroduction areas, considering scenarios of extant, reintroduction and combined range connectivity. Importance to connectivity was assessed based on Kernel Extent, Kernel Sum, movement density and protected area overlap. Our results confirmed the Dawna-Tenasserim landscape, spanning parts of Thailand and Myanmar, and Peninsular Malaysia as the most critical strongholds. In the former range, our analysis revealed potential for large-scale metapopulation structural connectivity across Cambodia and Lao PDR, despite recent extirpations. We stress that reintroduction opportunities will require actions such as reducing poaching, restoring prey and improving habitat management. In some complexes, intensive landscape restoration may be needed to reconnect major core areas with smaller reintroduction complexes that could be critical for meta-population connectivity. Despite increasing human pressure in the region, substantial habitat and connectivity potential remain. Our framework provides a spatial foundation to prioritise actions for preventing extinction of this subspecies and guiding large carnivore recovery across fragmented tropical landscapes.

items.title: More Than Color: Floral Color Polymorphism Is Associated With Scent Differentiation and Pollination Success in the Deceptive Orchid Anacamptis pyramidalis.
items.abstract: Floral color polymorphism is widespread among flowering plants, yet the mechanisms underlying its maintenance remain poorly understood, particularly in food-deceptive orchids where pollinator-mediated selection may differ from that operating in rewarding species. Here, we investigated the relationship among floral color polymorphism, ploidy variation, floral scent composition, and pollination in the Mediterranean deceptive orchid Anacamptis pyramidalis . Cytotypes were determined by flow cytometry, and floral volatile organic compounds (VOCs) were analyzed using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) in white- and pink-flowered individuals from multiple populations. VOC profiles were compared using multivariate and univariate statistical approaches. Pollination success was assessed in mixed-color diploid and tetraploid populations by quantifying the number of mature fruits produced per individual. Floral color morph was significantly associated with floral scent composition, accounting for approximately 6.5% of the total multivariate variation. Five VOCs differed significantly in relative abundance after correction for multiple comparisons, whereas total VOC emission did not differ significantly between morphs when cultivated in a common garden. No significant association between VOCs and cytotype was detected. White morphs consistently showed higher pollination success than pink morphs, producing significantly more fruits. By showing that floral color polymorphism is associated with both scent differentiation and differences in pollination success, our study highlights the importance of considering floral polymorphism as an integrated phenotype rather than a simple variation in flower pigmentation and helps explain its maintenance in the natural populations of this orchid.

items.title: Broadscale Distribution and Pronounced Mitochondrial Phylogeographic Structure in the Freshwater Minnow Opsariichthys bidens Across China's Major River Basins.
items.abstract: China's complex river basins constitute a critical biogeographic setting for investigating genetic differentiation and lineage divergence in freshwater fishes. Opsariichthys bidens is broadly distributed among multiple, hydrologically isolated river basins, rendering it a well-suited system for assessing mitochondrial phylogeographic structure across major river basins. Here, we used newly generated mitochondrial data to characterize broad-scale genetic variation in O. bidens across China's major river basins. We analyzed 379 cytochrome b ( cyt b ) sequences sampled from 13 geographically distinct populations, including seven populations from the Yangtze River and one population from each of six other major rivers, complemented by complete mitochondrial genomes from one individual from each population. Mitochondrial diversity was high at the species level (haplotype diversity, H d = 0.942; nucleotide diversity, π = 0.02526), but varied markedly among populations, with some populations showing haplotype fixation and others retaining divergent haplotypes. Genetic differentiation was pronounced, with 83.84% of variation attributable to differences among populations; 93.6% of pairwise F st values exceeded 0.25. Haplotype-network and phylogenetic analyses showed two deeply divergent mitochondrial lineages, broadly distributed in northern and southern China, respectively, with further substructure broadly associated with major river basins. Complete mitochondrial genomes exhibited high structural conservation across lineages, and the clearest lineage-associated annotation differences were observed in the termination codons of nd1 and cox3 . Overall, these results provide a broad-scale mitochondrial phylogeographic assessment of O. bidens and reveal a general association between river-basin geography and mitochondrial lineage structure across China.

items.title: Remote Sensing for Operational Surveillance of Mosquito-Borne Diseases.
items.abstract: Remote sensing observations have demonstrated increasing value in identifying human risk from mosquito-borne diseases because mosquito ecology is intrinsically tied to geophysical variables measurable by satellites. Satellite-based monitoring of environmental conditions at varying temporal and spatial scales has extended our capacity for mosquito surveillance and control for many mosquito-borne diseases, including malaria, dengue, Zika, West Nile fever, and Rift Valley fever. However, technical challenges and operational limitations continue to pose barriers for more routine integration of satellite data into management programs. To achieve this, we need to more explicitly connect these technologies to practical management scales, which are often disconnected from the spatial and temporal scales at which remote sensing data are readily accessible. Here, we comprehensively review advances in remote sensing and ecological research with a focus on their contributions to operational mosquito surveillance and control. We synthesize current research, derivative applications, and challenges associated with using remote sensing to understand mosquito-borne disease ecology and evaluate multi-scale satellite-based opportunities to translate technical advances to control and management actions. Finally, we develop actionable guidelines for an integrated strategy of cross-disciplinary collaboration in the public health community to expand adoption of remote sensing approaches for a variety of mosquito-borne infectious diseases.

items.title: Resource Availability Shaped the Female-Biased Floral Sex Allocation With Plant Size in Andromonoecious Capparis spinosa in Desert.
items.abstract: Although classic models of size-dependent sex allocation (SDS) generally predict that among animal-pollinated plants, female allocation increases with individual size, male-and female-biased allocation patterns have also been reported. We hypothesized that Capparis spinosa growing in resource-poor desert habitats would exhibit a female-biased sex allocation with increasing plant size, and that this pattern would be directly regulated by resource availability, because female function is generally more resource-demanding to verify this conjecture. We examined SDS patterns at the flowering stage in the andromonoecious desert plant C. spinosa and assessed the role of resource availability in shaping these patterns through resource supplementation and pruning treatments. The results indicated that male plants with a low biomass occurred at low frequencies (0.021-0.051) in seven of the nine assessed populations. Among andromonoecious individuals across the nine populations, with increasing plant size, we recorded increases in the numbers of male and hermaphroditic flowers, the proportion of hermaphroditic flowers, and values of Lloyd's phenotypic gender index. These findings indicate a strong female-biased sex allocation in C. spinosa plants of larger size. In addition, 2-year resource manipulation experiments revealed that both the supplementation of water and nutrients and pruning treatments significantly enhanced the proportion of hermaphroditic flowers, thereby indicating that floral sex allocation is directly regulated by resource availability. Our findings in this study highlight the role of resource availability in shaping size-dependent sex allocation patterns, particularly for plants in resource-poor desert habitats, and sheds light on the evolution of sexual systems in plants.

items.title: Thermoregulation in Heliconius butterflies is determined by habitat association and morphology but not phylogeny.
items.abstract: Temperature determines butterflies' physiological processes and performance. It varies strongly across time and space, with tropical butterflies experiencing temperatures close to their thermal limits. Climate change with more frequent heat waves may push species closer to these limits. Butterflies are known to thermoregulate, which is influenced by their morphology and behaviour. However, in tropical butterflies, little is known about how thermoregulatory abilities vary across habitats and if morphology or species relatedness are their drivers. We conducted a field and laboratory study on buffering ability-the ability to regulate body temperature with respect to air temperature-, take-off temperature and heating rate of mimetic Heliconius butterflies from different habitats. We tested whether butterfly thermoregulation varies across habitats and morphologies. We also tested whether closely related species exhibit more similar thermoregulatory abilities and explored the importance of behaviour. Mimetic Heliconius pairs are two species that have nearly identical wing coloration and are often in different phylogenetic clades. Studying these pairs allows us to quantify the contribution of morphology and phylogenetic relatedness to thermoregulation. Because mimetic species pairs are often restricted to specific habitats, thermoregulatory abilities can be compared across habitats. We found that butterflies from different habitats differed in their buffering ability, likely due to differences in morphology, such as wing colour. Take-off temperature was lowest in the only high-altitude species we studied, whereas species from lowland habitats did not differ. Live heating rate did not differ across habitats, yet it decreased with iridescence and forewing length. There was no phylogenetic signal in thermoregulatory abilities, indicating that more closely related species did not thermoregulate more similarly than expected by chance. Our results showed that the convergent wing patterns in Heliconius butterflies may contribute to thermoregulatory ability and that thermoregulation should be considered when investigating the habitat specificity of mimetic pairs. Furthermore, Heliconius thermoregulation is not constrained by shared ancestry, suggesting that the morphological traits observed in the different mimetic pairs may be advantageous in certain thermal environmental conditions. Overall, species differences in thermoregulatory abilities may shape how Heliconius distributions respond to climate change-driven temperature shifts.

items.title: Drivers of bird species turnover in the largest archipelago of China: Insights from zeta (ζ) diversity and multi-site generalized dissimilarity modelling (MS-GDM).
items.abstract: Species turnover, the spatial dissimilarity in species composition, is a central concept in island biogeography and community ecology. Traditional pairwise beta diversity metrics are limited to two-site comparisons and cannot fully resolve the mechanisms driving turnover across multiple communities. Zeta (ζ) diversity overcomes this limitation by quantifying multi-site species sharing and capturing how both rare and widespread species contribute to species turnover along a continuum. However, existing applications of zeta diversity to birds have focused mainly on continental, urban or land-use gradients, and have not examined island systems while simultaneously comparing phenological periods and migratory groups, nor have they separated richness differences from species replacement. As a typical land-bridge archipelago containing multiple bird groups, the Zhoushan Archipelago of China provides an ideal system for addressing these research gaps. We surveyed forest bird assemblages across 40 islands in this archipelago. We combined zeta diversity, multi-site generalized dissimilarity modelling (MS-GDM) and generalized additive models, using both Sørensen and Simpson normalizations to distinguish the contribution of richness differences from that of species replacement. We classified forest birds by season (breeding vs. wintering) and by migratory strategy (resident vs. migrant), yielding five ecological groups: all forest birds, breeding birds, wintering birds, residents and migrants. We then tested whether the relative importance of island characteristics varied among these five bird groups. Zeta decay followed a pure power-law form in all five bird groups, indicating a scale-invariant pattern of species loss across sites. Comparing MS-GDM results based on Sørensen-normalized and Simpson-normalized zeta diversity revealed a fundamental duality: island area primarily drove richness differences through selective species loss on small islands, whereas distance to the nearest mainland consistently governed true species replacement across all bird groups. Overall, our results demonstrate that deterministic assembly operates through two distinct pathways, that is area-driven environmental filtering and isolation-driven dispersal limitation, which jointly structure multi-site species turnover. The richness difference and replacement duality identified here can be generalizable to other land-bridge archipelagos and fragmented landscapes where area and isolation jointly shape community assembly, and provides a mechanistic framework for interpreting multi-site species turnover beyond simple richness gradients.

items.title: Herbivore thermoregulation, movement behaviour and survival during a severe drought in Namibia.
items.abstract: Climate change is expected to increase the frequency and severity of droughts in dryland ecosystems, yet the mechanisms determining whether large herbivores survive these events remain poorly understood. We investigated how an extreme drought influenced movement, water use, body temperature and survival of two water-dependent grazing herbivores, plains zebra (Equus quagga) and blue wildebeest (Connochaetes taurinus), in Etosha National Park, Namibia. GPS collars and abdominal temperature loggers were deployed on free-ranging animals during the most severe drought on record. We quantified changes in movement, drinking behaviour, thermoregulation and survival across seasons classified as cool drought, hot drought and rainy season recovery periods. Both species exhibited substantial behavioural plasticity as drought intensified, including shifts in diel activity, shorter median intervals between visits to perennial water sources and highly variable drinking schedules among individuals. Zebra increased daily travel during the hot drought, whereas wildebeest reduced daily travel and shifted activity toward cooler periods of the day, reflecting contrasting strategies for balancing resource acquisition with thermoregulation. Despite these behavioural adjustments, both species exhibited their greatest body temperature variability during both the cool and hot drought periods, indicating that these behavioural responses were insufficient to fully buffer the physiological consequences of the drought. Following rainfall, increased vegetation greenness was associated with higher minimum body temperatures and reduced daily temperature amplitudes, consistent with physiological recovery. Nevertheless, drought-related mortality reached 27% in zebra and 15% in wildebeest, differences that were not statistically significant. Although this drought was considerably more severe than those reported from other African protected areas, grazer mortality was comparable to or lower than that documented during less severe droughts, suggesting that behavioural flexibility together with the large, heterogeneous landscape of Etosha partially buffered drought impacts. Our findings demonstrate that behavioural responses can delay, but not fully prevent, the breakdown of physiological homeostasis during extreme drought. Integrating movement, physiology and survival provides a mechanistic framework for identifying populations approaching their resilience limits as climate change increases the frequency of extreme drought events.

items.title: Does the resource dispersion hypothesis predict grouping behaviour in a solitary megaherbivore?
items.abstract: The resource dispersion hypothesis (RDH) predicts that when resources are abundant and heterogeneously distributed, multiple individuals may satisfy their resource needs in a shared area without imposing large costs on one another. Under such conditions, groups can form even in the absence of other benefits, and other life history traits may not entirely explain group composition. For example, groups forming under conditions associated with the RDH may not display a biased sex ratio even if otherwise expected. Solitary herbivores, which are unlikely to gain benefits from grouping, may be strongly subject to the RDH, especially during growing seasons when there is an abundance of resources. However, to the best of our knowledge, no study has evaluated whether grouping behaviours in any solitary herbivore follows RDH predictions. To explore this, we used 48,678 sightings of black rhinos (Diceros bicornis) from 13 reserves in southern Africa to assess whether grouping behaviour in this solitary megaherbivore aligned with predictions of the RDH, or reflected predictions informed by the species ecology. We found that group formation and size largely followed RDH predictions where groups were more likely to form when resources were heterogenous and of high quality. Additionally, groups were larger during the growing season and when resources were heterogeneous. In contrast, as resource quality increased, group size decreased. Similarly, two of the four group composition results followed RDH predictions, where increasing group size was associated with decreasing within-group familiarity and an unbiased sex ratio in opposition to usual expectations. The other two followed species ecology predictions wherein increasing group size was associated with an increasing proportion of subadults and all large groups included at least one cow-calf pair. Ultimately, our results show that, in solitary herbivores, the RDH may be useful in predicting group formation and size and may explain instances when group composition diverges from species-specific expectations. Understanding grouping behaviour in endangered solitary species such as black rhino may improve management by allowing managers to identify conditions under which individuals are more tolerant of conspecifics.

items.title: The spatiotemporal effects of seasonal migration on passerine phylogenetic community structure.
items.abstract: Seasonal migration in birds involves a substantial spatial redistribution of avian biodiversity each year and drives seasonal changes in community composition. Migrants experience different combinations of species interactions over space and time, generating regular disassembly and reassembly of bird communities throughout their annual cycles. However, the effects of seasonal migration on phylogenetic community structure remain poorly understood. We assess spatiotemporal variation in phylogenetic community structure of North American passerines to test how seasonal migration restructures the evolutionary relatedness and dominant assembly mechanisms in bird communities throughout the annual cycle. Using distributional projections, we calculated metrics describing the phylogenetic dispersion of passerine communities each week of the year. We then tested the relationship between seasonal turnover in community phylogenetic dispersion and seasonal variation in species richness and proportion of migratory species. Seasonal migration, by changing spatial patterns of avian diversity, simultaneously drives a complex continental redistribution of phylogenetic community structure. We find evidence of taxonomic scale dependency to our results, wherein throughout North America, the seasonal influx of migrant passerines yields communities that are overall more phylogenetically clustered, yet also exhibit greater phylogenetic overdispersion at smaller taxonomic scales. Seasonal shifts in phylogenetic dispersion, though complex, track changes in diversity, manifesting as fluctuations in phylogenetic dispersion between northern and southern regions as seasonal migrants move between these regions. Our findings reveal a dynamic continental landscape of phylogenetic community structure directed by the movements of seasonal migrants.

items.title: The role of social sciences in addressing inequality related to Neglected Tropical Diseases (NTDs).
items.abstract: Neglected tropical diseases remain powerful markers of health inequity whose burdens are shaped not only by pathogens and treatment gaps, but also by stigma, marginalisation, gendered labour, poverty, weak infrastructure, fragile referral systems, limited awareness at the community level, and uneven policy implementation. The papers in this special collection show how people affected by mycetoma, podoconiosis, scabies, leprosy, Buruli ulcer, Chagas disease, and leishmaniasis navigate complex social worlds in which diagnosis, care seeking, therapeutic choice, participation in interventions, and public representation are all structured by inequity. Together, the contributions demonstrate the unique value of social science in illuminating lived experiences, contextualising health system performance, and reframing policy questions. The ethnographic, qualitative, participatory, and mixed-methods studies included in this collection bring to light the breadth and depth of experiences of those affected by NTDs, ranging from explorations of stigma, fear, trust, and resilience through to unseen dynamics impacting and influencing everyday life. The use of social sciences reveals that equitable responses to neglected tropical diseases must acknowledge the role of stigma, medical pluralism, gender, migration, ecology, institutions, and the contingent realities of policymaking, rather than relying on biomedical solutions alone. Neglected Tropical Diseases (NTDs) remain among the clearest expressions of global health inequity. They are pervasive among populations living with poverty, weak infrastructure, precarious livelihoods, poor housing, inadequate sanitation, and limited access to timely and respectful care. In as much as the burden of NTDs is not only biomedical, it also has social, moral, and political features. The papers in this special collection show that inequality is produced not simply by pathogens, but by stigma, marginalisation, gendered labour, delayed diagnosis, fragile referral systems, uneven implementation of interventions, and the persistent distance between policy ambitions and lived realities. This special collection brings together diverse and nuanced perspectives of NTD-related experiences across a range of conditions and settings. The papers move across mycetoma, podoconiosis, scabies, leprosy, Buruli ulcer, Chagas disease, and leishmaniasis, while also addressing broader questions of policy, advocacy, implementation, and health system transformation. Taken together, they make a compelling case that equity-oriented responses to NTDs must move beyond treatment alone and engage seriously with the social worlds in which illness is recognised, interpreted, hidden, negotiated, and managed. The contributions further extend these discussions of stigma, violence, and structural inequity. The studies demonstrate how people affected by skin NTDs experience intersecting forms of stigma, emotional, physical, financial, and gender-based violence across family, community, and health system settings. Similarly, authors have conceptualised scabies in refugee camps as a manifestation of structural violence, showing how overcrowding, displacement, social exclusion, and humanitarian neglect intensify suffering, stigma, and barriers to care. Together, the collection calls for a more socially informed and equity-oriented NTD agenda that places lived experience, structural conditions, and health-system transformation alongside biomedical intervention.

items.title: Isolation and characterization of diverse Veillonella phages reveal novel lineages and distinct host interactions
items.abstract: The human oral microbiome is diverse and home to many species of bacteria, archaea, microeukaryotes, fungi and viruses. Homeostasis in the oral microbiome is important for health and dysbiosis in these communities leads to periodontal and systemic diseases. Veillonella are gram-negative, anaerobic, lactate-fermenting early colonizers of the mouth and are abundant in healthy oral microbiomes. Although considered commensals, Veillonella serve as bridging species in dental biofilms, promoting later colonization by pathogens, with mounting evidence supporting their roles as accessory pathogens in dental caries and periodontal disease. Bacteriophages are key regulators of bacterial community composition and are important drivers of microbial diversity, evolution, and ecology of the oral environment. Despite the ecological importance of Veillonella in the oral microbiome, phages infecting Veillonella remain largely uncharacterized. Here, we report the isolation of ten phages infecting natural isolates of three Veillonella species, representing seven distinct phage genomes. These phages exhibit diverse morphologies, genome organizations, and host ranges, with infection restricted to strains within the species of isolation. Several phages establish stable lysogeny, confer resistance to superinfection, and differ substantially in spontaneous production of infectious phage progeny. Genetic analysis of resistant mutants implicates lipopolysaccharide O-antigen as the receptor for one phage. Although none of the isolated phages had close matches in existing oral virome catalogs, related sequences were detected in oral metagenomes from geographically diverse populations. Together, these findings establish an experimentally characterized collection of Veillonella phages and connect previously uncharacterized oral viral diversity to bacterial hosts and infection phenotypes.

items.title: The genetic basis of extra-lobed leaves in ivyleaf morning glory (Ipomoea hederacea)
items.abstract: Intraspecific leaf shape variation is common among angiosperms. Ivyleaf morning glory ( Ipomoea hederacea ) has become a useful system for studying the genetics and ecology of leaf shape variation as this species exhibits two leaf shapes: leaves with entire margins, and 3-lobed leaves. It is known that these phenotypes are controlled by a single locus, and differ in their ecophysiology, geographic distribution, ecology, and fitness. However, individuals producing leaves with 1-2 extra lobes have also been observed, but the genetic basis of these phenotypes have not been described. To investigate the genetic basis of extra-lobing, we compared phenotypic distributions of leaf shapes of an F2 generation to Mendelian ratios for a single locus trait, and conducted a bulked segregant analysis to uncover quantitative trait loci. Our results suggest that producing extra-lobed leaves has a complex genetic basis and that there are multiple QTLs underlying this phenotype containing potential candidate genes involved with auxin distribution and leaf development. Whether these extra-lobed phenotypes also differ in terms of their physiology and ecology remains unexplored.

items.title: Causes of bias in Delphi studies and consensus statements: a methodological review.
items.abstract: Introduction The Delphi methodology is a widely-used tool for achieving expert consensus in healthcare, particularly in areas where empirical evidence is limited or uncertain. Despite its structured design, the Delphi process remains vulnerable to implicit cognitive biases that may influence judgement and group decision-making. Such biases may inadvertently affect the quality of the consensus process, allow louder voices to influence outcomes, restrict inclusivity and undermine the validity, transparency and evidence-based nature of recommendations. Methods We conducted a methodological review synthesising literature from cognitive psychology, behavioural science and methodological research on consensus development and Delphi processes. Using a concept-mapping approach, established cognitive biases were mapped to different stages of the Delphi process, including study design; panel selection; survey development; iterative scoring; and consensus interpretation. Results Ten cognitive biases were organised into four domains reflecting different levels of influence within consensus development: steering-group and design-level biases, panel composition and contextual biases, social influence and conformity biases; and individual cognitive heuristic biases. A conceptual framework was developed to systematically identify these biases within Delphi-based consensus studies. Examples illustrating how these biases may arise in healthcare Delphi processes are presented, alongside potential mitigation strategies. Discussion Recognition and mitigation of cognitive biases are essential for strengthening the methodological rigour and credibility of Delphi studies. Strategies to reduce bias include diversifying expert panels; using neutral language in survey statements; maintaining anonymity during voting; involving methodological expertise in Delphi design; and ensuring transparent iterative feedback. The framework needs prospective validation before its widespread use and may assist journal editors and peer reviewers in critically appraising Delphi studies and improving reporting standards in consensus research.

items.title: The Polish version of the Survey of Autobiographical Memory (SAM): factor structure and psychometric evaluation.
items.abstract: The present study evaluated the psychometric properties of the Polish version of the Survey of Autobiographical Memory (SAM) as a self-report measure of perceived recollective capacity. We examined its reliability, tested several competing structural models, and assessed convergent validity with the Autobiographical Recollection Test (ART). Confirmatory factor analyses indicated that neither a one-factor nor an orthogonal four-factor model provided an adequate fit to the data. In contrast, the correlated four-factor solution - comprising Episodic, Semantic, Spatial, and Future components - offered the best representation of the data, replicating the original structure reported in prior validations. Correlations among subscales showed that the Episodic, Future, and Semantic dimensions shared substantial variance, whereas Spatial memory was relatively distinct. Convergent validity analyses revealed that the Episodic and Future subscales were most strongly associated with ART indices of vividness, coherence, imagery, and scene construction, consistent with theoretical models emphasising shared constructive processes in remembering and imagining. Overall, the Polish SAM demonstrated robust psychometric properties and strong theoretical coherence with contemporary accounts of autobiographical memory, providing a valid and reliable tool for assessing individual differences in the perceived richness and organisation of personal memories.

items.title: Knock, knock - who's there? Doorway event boundaries weaken but do not eliminate bindings in first-person perspective environments.
items.abstract: Current theories of action control assume that the binding and retrieval of features into and from common memory representations (i.e., event files) constitute core mechanisms supporting goal-directed behavior. Recent work found that individual responses within ongoing action sequences can be bound as higher-order representations that persist long enough to influence hierarchical event perception and action control (e.g., Moeller & Frings, 2021; Weissman, 2025). Initial evidence suggests that these binding processes may be disrupted when event boundaries are encountered, yet it remains unclear whether boundaries invariably interfere with binding to the extent that the influence of previous actions on current ones (i.e., binding effects) is no longer measurable. To address this issue, we investigated response-response bindings in a first-person virtual scenario involving perceptually similar events that were separated by a spatial boundary (a doorway between rooms). Responses executed within a single event produced stronger binding effects than responses that spanned the event boundary, indicating that boundary perception can attenuate, but does not fully abolish, binding processes. These results suggest that the cognitive system organizes continuous perceptual streams into discrete events in a manner that modulates ongoing action control. Crucially, by demonstrating that binding processes adapt to, rather than fail at, naturalistic event transitions, the present results highlight a key mechanism that supports reliable yet flexible action control in everyday behavior.

items.title: The good, the bad, and the cringy: Introducing the EmpaToM-pos and EmpaToM-embarrass as tools for assessing empathy and theory of mind in diverse emotional contexts.
items.abstract: Empathizing and mentalizing are crucial to social understanding, yet few instruments capture these processes across a broad emotional spectrum. The EmpaToM is a video-based paradigm that independently measures empathy and theory of mind (ToM) and can additionally incorporate a prosociality measure. As its current form is limited to negatively valenced emotional contexts, we introduce two expanded German versions: EmpaToM-pos, featuring positively valenced narrations, and EmpaToM-embarrass, featuring embarrassing narrations, alongside the original neutral and negative conditions. In two pilot studies (Ns = 28/27), we tested novel video stimuli and corresponding questions, revised them based on the data, and subsequently evaluated them in two higher-powered studies (Ns = 60/55). Results confirmed successful empathy induction in all emotional conditions: Participants reported feeling worse after negative, more joyful after positive, and more embarrassed after embarrassing narrations (compared to all other valence conditions, respectively). Emotional valence also influenced prosociality: Negative narrations prompted the highest willingness to invest, but positive and embarrassing narrations also elicited greater prosociality than the neutral condition. Both expanded versions supported reliable ToM assessment without ceiling effects and with similar performance levels in the ToM and control conditions. Analyses further revealed that, on an interindividual level, empathic resonance in both negative and positive contexts was positively correlated with the degree of prosociality, highlighting the interrelation between empathizing and social decision-making. By incorporating positive and embarrassing emotional contexts, the EmpaToM-pos and EmpaToM-embarrass broaden the range of assessable social-emotional experiences, offering new opportunities to investigate empathy, ToM, and prosociality in more ecologically valid and diverse settings.

items.title: From metaphorical to experienced time: Subjective experience of time's passage across self-time perspectives.
items.abstract: In language and metaphor, people think of their relationship to time in one of two ways: either as themselves moving in time, or as time moving past them. Take the following question: "If your Wednesday meeting is moved forward by two days, when is the new meeting?" There are two possible answers - depending on your metaphorical "self-time perspective." If you say "Friday," then the meeting is pushed ahead as you are moving in time (reflecting a "Mover" perspective). If you say "Monday," the meeting has moved forward as time moves towards you (reflecting a "Waiter" perspective). Might these differences in thinking about time be reflected in differences in perceived time? In a large-scale exploratory study, subjects reproduced the durations of blank intervals, either before or after an event, and were categorized based on their responses to the ambiguous question above. Those who reported a Waiter perspective tended to show less underestimation in their duration reproductions compared to those who reported a Mover perspective - though the interval position (i.e., before vs. after the event) and type of event (i.e., watching an event vs. performing an action) modulated these differences. These results suggest that whether a subject's temporal position is fixed (as in a Waiter perspective) or is constantly being updated (as in a Mover perspective) has consequences for their retrospective reproductions of how much time has passed. Navigating a dynamic world may thus shape (and be shaped by) our internal reference frames, not just of space, but also of time. STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE: We do not only experience time as going faster or slower depending on what we are doing (e.g., consider a day in a theme park vs. waiting at the dentist's), we also think about our relationship to time itself in sometimes surprisingly categorically opposing ways: with either time as a medium that we are moving through (i.e., a "Mover" perspective), versus time moving past us (i.e., a "Waiter" perspective). Here, using a simple method of having people reproduce durations of blank intervals, we find that these metaphorical self-time perspectives may correspond to actual differences in their subjective experience of time. OPEN PRACTICES STATEMENT: Materials and analysis code are available via the Open Science Framework at: https://osf.io/2m7cn .

items.title: How duration, difficulty, and boredom impact prospective and retrospective passage of time judgements and duration estimates.
items.abstract: Time perception research often involves asking people to estimate how long a task took to complete. Their estimate accuracy is then compared with the actual task's duration (an approach known as duration estimation). This method is commonly used for brief tasks and underpins several theories of psychological time. The present experiment aimed to explore additional ways of capturing the experience of time under varying conditions. An in-laboratory experiment was conducted in which 841 participants engaged in a visual and memory search task. Participants were assigned to either a prospective condition (told that they would estimate the task's duration) or a retrospective condition (were not told that they would estimate the duration). The difficulty and duration of the task were manipulated. Interestingly, task difficulty did not affect any measures of time perception. Moreover, these passage of time judgements did not correlate with duration estimates, suggesting that they may reflect different aspects of time perception. However, confidence ratings varied with estimation accuracy, suggesting that participants had insight into their time distortions. Additionally, engagement and boredom influenced how fast or slow time felt, but these affective states did not affect duration estimates. These findings reveal a disconnect between the subjective experience of time's passing and the accuracy of time estimation, highlighting the complexity of temporal experience. OPEN PRACTICES STATEMENT: This study was not preregistered. Derived subject-level data supporting the findings of this study are available online ( https://osf.io/bxy43/overview ).
