items.title: Differential Effect of Ivermectin on Intestinal Helminths in Multimmate Mouse (Mastomys natalensis).
items.abstract: Mastomys natalensis is a widespread rodent species in sub-Saharan Africa and is increasingly recognised as an important component of food systems in some communities. However, rodents may harbour gastrointestinal helminths with potential implications for animal health, food safety, and zoonotic disease transmission. Information on gastrointestinal helminth infections in M. natalensis and the response of these parasites to anthelmintic treatment is limited. This study investigated the prevalence and diversity of gastrointestinal helminths in M. natalensis and evaluated changes in helminth egg burden following treatment with Ivermectin. A total of 90 adult M. natalensis, comprising 43 males and 47 females, were captured, and their faecal samples were examined for gastrointestinal helminth eggs. Identified helminths were characterised and their prevalence was estimated with 95% confidence intervals. Following baseline assessment, the rodents were allocated to -treated and untreated control groups. Faecal egg counts, expressed as eggs per gram of faecal sample (EPG), were monitored every 14 days over an eight-week period. The change in egg burden was assessed using faecal egg count reduction (FECR). Five gastrointestinal helminth taxa were identified, of which Hymenolepis diminuta was the most prevalent (39%; 95% CI: 29.6-49.3%), followed by Physaloptera spp. (29%; 95% CI: 20.6-39.1%), Rodentolepis nana (12%; 95% CI: 6.8-20.3%), Strongyloides spp. (11%; 95% CI: 6.1-19.1%), and Trichuris spp. (9%; 95% CI: 4.6-16.7%). In the Ivermectin-treated rodents, mean EPG declined substantially across all five helminth taxa between baseline and weeks post-treatment. The highest egg reductions were observed for H. diminuta (96.4%) and Trichuris spp. (96.2%), followed by Strongyloides spp. (90.9%), Physaloptera spp. (85.5%), and R. nana (80.0%). The untreated control group showed comparatively little change in overall helminth egg burden. Sex-specific analyses showed substantial reductions in both males and females over the same period, except for, R. nana females, where egg counts showed an increase. These findings indicate the potential value of Ivermectin in reducing gastrointestinal helminth egg shedding by M. natalensis. Further studies with larger sample sizes, over a longer period, and appropriate experimental replication are warranted to validate treatment with the anthelminth and its implications for animal health, food safety, and potential zoonotic transmission.

items.title: Probiotic Intervention With Bacillus coagulans and Lactobacillus acidophilus in Small Animals Experimental Ulcerative Colitis: Insights From a Small Animal Model.
items.abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease is a significant health concern not only in humans but also in companion animals and livestock, where it manifests as chronic diarrhoea, abdominal pain, and mucosal injury. Probiotics have gained increasing attention as potential therapeutic agents due to their immunomodulatory effects and ability to restore intestinal homeostasis. This study investigated the therapeutic efficacy of Bacillus coagulans and Lactobacillus acidophilus in an acetic acid-induced ulcerative colitis model in Wistar rats. Forty male rats were randomly assigned to control, colitis, mesalazine, B. coagulans, and L. acidophilus treatment groups. Disease severity was evaluated by macroscopic and histopathological scoring, colon length and weight, pro-inflammatory cytokine levels (IL-1β, IL-17), and inflammasome-associated gene expression (NLRP3, Caspase-1, IL-18, TNF-α). The results showed that colitis induction significantly increased pro-inflammatory cytokine expression and histological damage compared with controls. Both probiotics markedly reduced inflammatory markers, improved colon morphology, and attenuated inflammasome activation. Their protective effects were comparable to mesalazine, the standard treatment. These findings suggest that B. coagulans and L. acidophilus can serve as effective adjunct therapies for ulcerative colitis in veterinary practice, with potential translational applications for companion animals and livestock.

items.title: A One Health Molecular Investigation and Exploratory Epidemiological Analysis of Cryptosporidium spp. in A Shared Human-Animal Ecosystem.
items.abstract: Introduction Cryptosporidium spp. are enteric protozoan parasites of public health importance, particularly in low-resource settings where humans, animals and environmental water sources frequently interact. This study investigated the prevalence, molecular diversity and environmental exposure-related variables in relation to Cryptosporidium infection in a rural community. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted using 180 faecal samples collected from humans, cattle, chickens, fish, cats, dogs, and ducks. Speciation and subtyping were determined through PCR amplification and sequencing of the 18S rRNA and gp60 genes. Epidemiological and environmental data were collected, and univariable analyses were conducted. An exploratory multivariable logistic regression model was subsequently performed for the human subset. Results The overall prevalence of Cryptosporidium infection was 9.40%, with the highest rates observed in humans (14.8%) and cattle (13.5%). Molecular characterisation identified C. hominis, C. parvum, C. bovis and C. felis. Among humans, C. hominis was the predominant, whereas C. parvum was also detected, including mixed infections. gp60 analysis identified multiple subtype families, including Ia, Ib, IIa, IIc and IId. Phylogenetic analysis demonstrated close genetic relationships between Bangladeshi isolates and previously reported reference strains from South Asia and the Middle East. Higher odds of Cryptosporidium infection were observed among individuals reporting river bathing and consumption of untreated water, whereas lower odds were observed among those reporting regular handwashing. No statistically significant associations were identified between evaluated environmental variables and infection among non-human hosts. Conclusion The study demonstrated the circulation of multiple Cryptosporidium species and subtype families within a shared human-animal ecosystem. The contaminated surface water and inadequate hygiene practices may represent important environmental exposure interfaces for Cryptosporidium infection in the study area. However, given the cross-sectional design and limited number of positive cases, the epidemiological findings should be interpreted as exploratory associations rather than definitive transmission pathways. Further longitudinal One Health investigations are needed.

items.title: No Trace of Blastocystis Parasite in Bats Caught in the Western and Southwestern Regions of Iran.
items.abstract: Background Blastocystis is a common parasite found in the human intestine, causing symptoms such as abdominal pain, bloating, and diarrhoea. Bats are potential hosts for this parasite, but little is known about their infection with Blastocystis. Objective Given the diversity of bat species in Iran, this study aimed to investigate Blastocystis infection in bats caught in the southwestern and western regions of the country. Methods Faecal samples were collected from 115 bats from five caves located in Fars, Kurdistan, and Kermanshah provinces. DNA was extracted, using the phenol-chloroform method, and PCR was performed to identify the Blastocystis 18S rRNA gene. Information on bat species was analysed descriptively. Results The four main bat species caught were Miniopterus pallidus (40%, n = 46), Myotis blythii (40%, n = 46), Rhinopoma microphyllum (12.18%, n = 14), and Rhinolophus euryale (7.82%, n = 9). However, none of the 115 stool samples examined showed evidence of Blastocystis infection by the molecular PCR method. Conclusion This study found no evidence of Blastocystis infection in the bat species examined. The unique lifestyle and diet of bats, such as living on cave walls and roofs, may explain this absence. Further studies are needed to clarify the role of bats in the epidemiology of Blastocystis in other regions of Iran.

items.title: Design of Lipopeptides and dsRNA-Lipopeptide Complexes for Sprayable RNAi-Based Plant Protection.
items.abstract: Broad-spectrum insecticides persist in the environment, affecting non-target organisms and selecting for resistant pest populations. In contrast, RNA interference (RNAi) achieves species-targeted pest control triggered by the delivery of exogenous double-stranded RNA (dsRNA), which is biodegradable and broken down into harmless components by nucleases. Sprayable applications require suitable formulation strategies for dsRNA protection during delivery. Here, we describe the preparation of dsRNA-lipopeptide complexes (LPCs) composed of non-toxic short-chain lipopeptide surfactants by microfluidic mixing, yielding positively charged dispersions of LPCs < 200 nm in diameter, which encapsulate and protect dsRNA from enzymatic degradation. Some lipopeptides were found to undergo thermo-reversible gelation, self-assembling to fibrillar nanostructures, but remained effective for dsRNA delivery to induce mortality in Colorado potato beetle larvae feeding on sprayed plants. Our results show that lipopeptide surfactants are suitable for the formulation of dsRNA to enable effective delivery to pest insects.

items.title: What health are we talking about? Biodiversity as the missing link between One Health and Planetary Health.
items.abstract: Health has become a central term in global sustainability policy, yet it is often used without sufficient conceptual precision. Public health, global health, One Health, EcoHealth, GeoHealth, and Planetary Health each emphasize different dimensions of the relationship between humans, animals, and the environment. In policy contexts, however, these distinctions are frequently blurred. We argue that biodiversity is often treated as an environmental co-benefit rather than as a foundational determinant of health. This weakens the implementation of One Health approaches because biodiversity underpins disease regulation, immune system development, food and water security, ecosystem functioning, resilience, and climate adaptation. At the same time, biodiversity provides a critical link between One Health and broader Planetary Health challenges, including global environmental change and the transgression of planetary boundaries. Future health and sustainability policies should move beyond generic references to health and explicitly recognize biodiversity as part of preventive health systems.

items.title: Recentering Resource-Based Livelihoods: Prosperity Beyond Extractivism and Pastoralism.
items.abstract: This research note, informed by qualitative fieldwork with resource harvesters in Nova Scotia, explores the effect of economic change and ecological crisis, the outcomes of rural development strategies, and demographic shifts that have shaped the province's rural areas in recent years. It argues that our present moment is ripe with opportunities for a renewed sociological attention on livelihoods in this region, which should take as its focus the relationship that people, communities, and government have with their physical environment. Rural places tend to be valued for their natural endowments, either industrially extracted or preserved and sold as a pastoral idyll. Nova Scotia's recent past has exacerbated this bifurcation. New work is needed to help find prosperous ground beyond both tendencies. This note attempts to spark that effort.

items.title: Nitrogen and Sulfur Assimilation in Fish Otoliths Evaluated by Stable Isotope Labeling and NanoSIMS Analysis.
items.abstract: Rationale Stable nitrogen (δ 15 N) and sulfur (δ 34 S) isotopes within the metabolically inert organic matrix of teleost otoliths provide high-fidelity archives for reconstructing animal life histories. However, low organic content limits the spatial resolution of conventional bulk isotopic analysis, leaving biomineralization kinetics and the temporal integration of these dietary signals poorly quantified. We utilized nanoscale secondary ion mass spectrometry (NanoSIMS) to overcome these limitations and determine intracrystalline isotopic dynamics. Methods Isotopic pulses were established by feeding juvenile Mozambique tilapia (Oreochromis mossambicus) 15 N-enriched algae and diets supplemented with L-methionine- 34 S, utilizing Alizarin Red S fluorescent marking for precise temporal referencing. High-resolution and in situ NanoSIMS analysis was applied to quantify the temporal distribution of the labeling signals within the otolith organic matrix. A first-order kinetic model was used to estimate isotopic dynamics half-lives (t 50% ). Results NanoSIMS analysis revealed rapid isotopic changes across both assimilation and depuration phases (t 50% = 0.5-13.9 days). Both δ 15 N and δ 34 S exhibited statistically indistinguishable kinetics, reflecting synchronized metabolic routing where dietary signals are deposited directly into the otolith without being buffered by internal tissue reserves. Crucially, the dietary matrix modulated assimilation; despite comparable dietary δ 34 S proportions, otolith sulfur incorporation and signal attenuation were significantly faster in fish fed algae-based diets than in those fed eel-meal-based diets. This demonstrates the preferential utilization of exogenous labeled methionine when the base diet is naturally deficient in this essential amino acid. Conclusions High-resolution NanoSIMS profiling demonstrates that the otolith organic matrix archives dietary signals governed by rapid assimilation pathways rather than strict thermodynamic equilibrium. This analytical approach establishes a crucial mechanistic basis and experimental framework for utilizing intracrystalline organic isotopes as precise indicators in trophic ecology.

items.title: Psychoeducational Challenges of Dyslexic Children During the COVID-19 Pandemic: A Systematic Review.
items.abstract: Dyslexic students faced psychological and educational challenges during the COVID-19 pandemic and online learning, including increased anxiety, low self-esteem, reduced reading interest, limited access to educational technologies, insufficient teacher support, and difficulties with reading fluency and concentration. Examining these challenges is crucial for implementing effective measures and enhancing post-pandemic learning. This study investigates the psycho-educational challenges of dyslexic children during the pandemic, highlighting the need for targeted interventions to support them in current and future contexts. This systematic review identified relevant articles through electronic searches of PubMed, Wiley, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and ScienceDirect, supplemented by the snowballing technique, which involved examining the bibliographies of retrieved references. The study identified two main categories of challenges for dyslexic children: psychological (mental health, emotional well-being, behavioural issues, parental stress) and educational (socioeconomic status, technology access, special educational needs, teacher support, remote learning difficulties) affecting children with learning disabilities. The research results show that dyslexic children faced various psychological and educational difficulties identified in this review during the COVID-19 pandemic. Therefore, targeted, evidence-based strategies-such as teacher training, family-school collaboration, adaptive learning technologies, and psychological support-are needed to mitigate these challenges in the post-pandemic period.

items.title: Leopard sterilisation in India: The ecological and ethical costs of anthropocentric wildlife management.
items.abstract: India's rising human-leopard conflict has prompted the government to adopt immune contraceptives to manage leopard populations. The decision has sparked debate among wildlife experts and conservation organisations, government officials, and local communities. Here, I discuss the ecological and ethical implications of this intervention and highlight alternative, coexistence-based approaches that recognise both humans and wildlife as stakeholders within shared socio-ecological systems.

items.title: Do Adverse Intrauterine Environments Affect Body Mass Index in Infants and Preschool Children?
items.abstract: Exposure to adverse intrauterine environments resulting from different maternal clinical conditions may alter childhood growth patterns. This study investigated the influence of such environments on body mass index-for-age (BMI-for-age) trajectories from birth to preschool age. A total of 342 mother-child dyads recruited from three hospitals in southern Brazil were allocated into five groups: diabetes mellitus (DM), systemic arterial hypertension (SAH), maternal smoking, small for gestational age (SGA, used here as a proxy for impaired fetal growth), and a control group. Children were assessed at seven time points from birth to preschool age using anthropometric measurements to calculate BMI-for-age z-scores. Generalized estimating equations (GEE) identified a significant interaction between group and time (p < 0.001). Among girls, at birth, the DM group presented higher BMI-for-age z-scores than the smoking group and reached elevated BMI-for-age z-scores at preschool age, differing from the control group. At 6 months of age, girls in the SGA group showed a marked increase in BMI-for-age. Among boys, the SGA group reached higher BMI-for-age values at preschool age than the DM and control groups. Differences were observed across time, group, and sex in the SGA and control groups (p < 0.001). These findings suggest that adverse intrauterine environments may influence BMI-for-age trajectories during early life, with greater variability and evidence of catch-up growth among children exposed to maternal DM and SGA. Results should be interpreted cautiously due to unequal subgroup sizes and substantial loss to follow-up at preschool age.

items.title: Capturing Thought Dynamics: Modeling the Structure of Spontaneous Associations.
items.abstract: Human thought unfolds in patterns that vary across individuals; some move fluidly across ideas, whereas others return to narrower or more repetitive paths. Here, we asked whether structural aspects of associative thinking-its breadth, trajectory, and temporal pace-can account for individual differences in repetitive thought styles such as rumination. Participants completed brief free-association tasks, and their responses were quantified using a model trained on large-scale free association data to derive individual structural profiles of associative flow. Across two independent samples, these profiles predicted self-reported measures of rumination and repetitive thinking, with nonlinear models accounting for meaningful inter-individual variation and showing generalization across tasks and datasets. These findings suggest that individual differences in repetitive thought are reflected not only in what people think about but also in how associations are organized and unfold over time. Structural modeling therefore provides a viable approach to characterizing spontaneous cognition through patterns of associative organization.

items.title: Ecological Momentary Assessments of Daily Pain Experiences in Bothersome and High-Impact Chronic Pain.
items.abstract: Background High-impact chronic pain (HICP), defined as persistent pain substantially limiting daily activities, affects millions of adults and poses a public health challenge. However, as prior knowledge comes largely from retrospective self-report measures, little is known about how HICP manifests in daily life. Methods This study used the comprehensive Ecological Momentary Assessment of pain (cEMAp) instrument to assess pain-related experiences four times daily over 7 days in individuals with chronic musculoskeletal pain. Using the Graded Chronic Pain Scale-Revised, we compared individuals with HICP (n = 66) with bothersome chronic pain (n = 41), a group with similar pain frequency but less interference with daily activities. Each prompt assessed pain intensity, interference, cognitions, behaviours, coping strategies, and pain characteristics over the preceding 2 h. Results Both groups reported similar pain intensity levels, but the HICP group reported more frequent interference with physical, mental, and social activities. No group differences emerged in daily mood or negative pain-related cognitions. Exploratory analyses suggested that many daily experiences were similar across groups, with differences observed in selected pain qualities, coping strategies, and pain behaviours. Analyses of response distributions showed some similarity across groups in many experiences. Conclusions The most consistent distinction between the groups was interference frequency, consistent with the operationalization of HICP as pain that disrupts daily functioning, while several other pain-related experiences were similar across groups. cEMAp data complement traditional retrospective assessment by providing a more detailed view of biopsychosocial aspects of chronic pain in everyday life. Significance statement Prior understanding of high-impact chronic pain (HICP) has largely relied on retrospective measures. Using the comprehensive Ecological Momentary Assessment of pain (cEMAp) instrument, we found that HICP was distinguished primarily by more frequent interference with daily activities rather than greater pain intensity. Our findings also reveal similarities and differences across other pain-related experiences, highlighting the value of multidimensional real-world assessment beyond pain intensity alone.

items.title: Strength-based organizational approaches facilitate workplace opportunities for people from lower socioeconomic status backgrounds.
items.abstract: The workplace stands as one of the most powerful drivers of societal (in)equality. For employees from lower socioeconomic status backgrounds, it can represent both a ticket toward upward mobility and a consequential source of stigma. Four studies build on emerging strength-based research to test whether workplaces can challenge this stigma by creating overarching cultures that recognize the beneficial skills employees gain from their otherwise marginalized identities. Study 1 provided foundational insights into these "strength-based organizational approaches" and their implications for key outcomes derived from the State Authenticity as Fit to Environment model. Employees from lower socioeconomic status backgrounds were especially unlikely to report that their workplaces valued their identities and associated skills, which partially explained subsequent disparities in employees' broad sense of comfort and efficacy at work. Studies 2a and 2b established these patterns experimentally by demonstrating that exposing participants to a workplace that does communicate a strength-based organizational approach facilitated these professionally productive outcomes while increasing participants' likelihood of disclosing their marginalized identities within a job application task. Study 3 extended these findings to consider how the approaches may also indirectly expand employees' equitable access to opportunity through reducing common biases among their supervisors. Randomly assigning workplace supervisors to briefly engage with a company that highlighted the value of employees' lower socioeconomic status backgrounds increased supervisors' positive evaluations and likelihood of promoting these employees by 38% relative to an active control condition. Collectively, these preregistered findings illuminate new opportunities to improve workplace functioning and pinpoint the organizational forces underlying person-context interactions. items.title: How we see relations: The case of containment and support.
items.abstract: To navigate and act in the environment, it is necessary to recognize objects and the relationships between them. Recognition of objects in visual scenes is rapid and automatic. Are relations between objects in a scene also extracted rapidly and automatically during perception? Here, we considered containment and support, two relations that are fundamental to our understanding of the physical world. Using frequency-tagging electroencephalography on human subjects, we measured stimulus-driven neural responses during rapid visual presentation of images (4 Hz), with a periodic oddball structure to isolate the selective response to object pairs presented side-by-side (e.g., a book and a table) versus two objects in support or containment relations (e.g., a book on a table). We found enhanced responses to objects in support/containment relations (vs. objects side-by-side) when a relation was instantiated by different exemplars of the same scene (e.g., a book on a table), but not by different scenes involving distinct object categories (e.g., a book on a table, a lamp on a stand, a laptop on a desk). These findings indicate that, during scene perception, relations are extracted in a format that generalizes within, but not across, types of visual scenes. We propose that, during perception, relations are not represented as discrete, abstract tokens ("in" or "on") but rather as objects' properties, such that changes in the objects entail changes in the relational representation. These results provide new insight into the perceptual foundations of relational processing underlying physical reasoning. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

items.title: Task-evoked pupillary responses reveal a role for attentional intensity in auditory discrimination.
items.abstract: Sensory discrimination has long been theorized to reflect a core cognitive function underlying intelligence. Building on this tradition, we examined whether task-evoked pupil responses, as an index of mental effort, relate to attention control (AC) and auditory discrimination ability. Using a large data set (N = 336), participants completed three adaptive auditory discrimination tasks (pitch, duration, loudness), a cognitive battery assessing AC, working memory capacity, and fluid intelligence, and pupillometry during task performance. Structural equation modeling confirmed that AC predicted auditory discrimination thresholds and fully mediated the relationship between task-evoked pupil dilation and performance. Trial-level multilevel models revealed that higher task difficulty and errors were associated with larger pupil dilations, especially in demanding tasks. Crucially, individuals with greater AC exhibited steeper increases in pupil dilation with rising task difficulty and were more resilient to performance declines. For high-AC individuals, large pupil responses predicted preserved accuracy; for low-AC individuals, they signaled compensatory effort with diminished success. These results suggest that AC governs both the extent and efficacy of mental effort, determining whether high arousal facilitates or fails to improve performance. This work refines classic resource models by demonstrating that cognitive effort, indexed via pupillometry, supports perception most effectively when guided by strong AC. Findings support a hierarchical model in which AC serves as the functional bridge between arousal, sensory discrimination, and higher order cognition. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

items.title: The orthographic mind: Orthographic imagery propensity correlates with semantic structure and sensory sensitivity.
items.abstract: Individuals differ in their habitual use of internal representational modes, including visual imagery, internal verbalization, and orthographic imagery (the mental simulation of written word forms). The present research examined whether such internal representational propensities relate to semantic organization and external information engagement. Across two studies (total N = 1,399), we assessed individuals' internal representational modes using the Internal Representations Questionnaire and examined their associations with semantic structure (nine-word semantic rating experiments; N = 1,109) and external information engagement (sensory-processing sensitivity and mobile app usage). Orthographic imagery showed robust associations with both semantic geometry and external information engagement patterns: Individuals with stronger orthographic imagery showed greater cross-category semantic association strength, lower semantic conformity, and lower sensory-processing sensitivity. Internal verbalization was positively associated with within-category semantic cohesion, while visual imagery showed no reliable associations with semantic geometry and limited associations with real-world media engagement. Effects were modest but consistent across experiments. These findings suggest that internal representational modes function as stable weighting biases, subtly modulating semantic geometry and sensory-processing profiles. Such propensities therefore correspond to structured variations in cognition, rather than merely phenomenological differences in inner experience. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

items.title: Children can suppress salient distractors.
items.abstract: From a very young age, our perceptual system is particularly sensitive to salient events. When such events are irrelevant, adults can prevent them from capturing attention by suppressing the salient features and by prioritizing task-relevant information. Previous research suggests that both distractor-suppression and target-prioritization mechanisms are not yet fully developed at ages 5-6. However, this work has not clearly disentangled the two mechanisms. Here, we specifically investigated whether children can suppress the salient feature of an irrelevant distractor. Two groups of children (aged 5-6 and 8-9) searched for a shape-defined target among heterogeneously shaped nontargets. All items had the same color throughout the experiment, but on two thirds of the trials, one item (the singleton distractor) had a unique color that changed at the beginning of each block. We expected this distractor to interfere with search performance during the first half of each block (i.e., when its color was novel). The critical question was whether this interference would be reduced during the second block half (i.e., with enough experience with the distractor's color). This finding would indicate that the children suppressed the salient distractor color. We found clear evidence for feature-based suppression, and this effect was similar for the two age groups. These findings indicate that feature-based suppression develops early and may already be established by ages 5-6. More broadly, they are consistent with accounts in which suppression emerges through implicit learning or habituation-like mechanisms that are operational early in development. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

items.title: Beliefs about the causal interdependence of virtues and vices.
items.abstract: How do people think different positive and negative moral traits (i.e., virtues and vices) affect one another? For example, do they think that improving one virtue (e.g., honesty) will facilitate improvements in another virtue (e.g., compassion)? Do people believe in "master virtues" that, when improved, have disproportionate positive impacts on other moral virtues? Here, we examine perceived causal interdependence among 15 moral virtues and 13 moral vices. Across four studies, participants indicated their beliefs about how increasing their virtues would impact their other virtues (Study 1; 275 Prolific participants), how increasing their vices would impact their other vices (Study 2; 423 undergraduate students), and how increases in virtues would affect vices (or vice versa; Studies 3 and 4; 337 undergraduate students and 298 Prolific participants). We find people generally believe in facilitation effects, where improving one trait improves other traits and worsening one trait worsens other traits. Specifically, people believe that increasing one virtue tends to increase other virtues (Study 1) and decrease other vices (Studies 3 and 4). Similarly, people believe that increasing one vice tends to increase other vices (Study 2) and decrease other virtues (Studies 3 and 4). Perceived trade-offs were rare and involved laziness and cowardice decreasing or being decreased by other vices. There was little evidence for beliefs in a "master virtue." However, we find some evidence that people think cruelty and greed are disproportionately impactful "master vices." These results enhance our understanding of lay moral concepts by painting a comprehensive picture of people's beliefs about the causal interdependence among moral virtues and vices. items.title: Investigating how reward retroactively improves memory for associations and items: A registered report.
items.abstract: Given we cannot remember all our experiences, it seems intuitive that we should prioritize events of consequence, like those that lead to a reward. However, rewards have had inconsistent effects on people's memory for preceding neutral experiences in experiments, raising questions as to whether our minds are equipped to remember adaptively. Here, we used online testing in a registered report to investigate whether rewards tend to retroactively enhance certain types of memories. Consistent with prior research and theories involving how dopamine modulates the hippocampus, we hypothesized that reward would retroactively enhance memory in a delay-dependent manner, emerging only after a period of consolidation. Crucially, we further predicted that this long-delay modulation of memory would be stronger for associative memory than for item recognition-a factor not previously considered despite its clear theoretical grounding. Our planned confirmatory analyses did not reveal any evidence for retroactive effects of reward on either associative or item memory. However, in exploratory analyses examining only individuals who were behaviorally sensitive to the reward manipulation, as measured by an independent task, we found evidence that reward retroactively enhanced associative-but not item-memory in a delay-dependent manner. This work sheds light on important open questions about the mechanisms by which reward retroactively enhances memory, elucidating the conditions under which this key aspect of adaptive memory emerges. items.title: Correction to "Systematically reducing schematic information during encoding differentially impacts true and false memory at retrieval in younger and older adults" by Becker et al. (2026).
items.abstract: Reports an error in "Systematically reducing schematic information during encoding differentially impacts true and false memory at retrieval in younger and older adults" by Alexa Becker, Rebecca L. Wagner and Nancy A. Dennis ( Psychology and Aging , Advanced Online Publication, Jul 23, 2026, np; see record 2028-01807-001). Jordan Chamberlain was missing from the author list in the submitted manuscript. The authorship has been corrected with the agreement of all authors. All versions of this article have been corrected. (The following abstract of the original article appeared in record 2028-01807-001.) Schemas are abstract representations that aid memory performance by providing a structured context through which memories can be both encoded and retrieved. Older adults have been shown to particularly benefit from schema support as a memory aid. Yet, while helpful to true memory for schematic information, reliance on schemas has also been shown to lead to high rates of false memories for novel yet schematically related information, as well as diminished memory for information that falls outside of an active schema. The current research sought to examine how systematically manipulating naturalistic contextualization as well as the density of schematic information present during encoding may alter subsequent true and false memory for both schematic and nonschematic information. To examine this, we systematically altered the ratio of schematic-to-nonschematic information present during encoding across four conditions in a sample of healthy younger and older adults. Overall, both younger and older adults responded more accurately to schematic compared to nonschematic targets, replicating past work highlighting the benefit of schemas to memory performance. Results also showed that systematically reducing the amount of schematic information present at encoding improved memory discriminability. Specifically, as there was less schematic information present at encoding, false alarms to schematic lures decreased, and hits to nonschematic targets increased. Additionally, when items were decontextualized from a naturalistic scene, false alarms to nonschematic lures decreased. Hits to schematic targets were equitable across conditions. Taken together, the results demonstrate that while schemas maintain a strong influence on memory performance across the lifespan, this effect can be manipulated with reduced schematic information. Such findings reveal the extent to which the pervasive influence of schemas on memory can be swayed by manipulating the amount of schematic information present during encoding and provide critical knowledge for the optimal usage of schemas as a memory support across the lifespan. items.title: Different object features shape mnemonic discrimination in younger and older adults.
items.abstract: The ability to discriminate experiences in memory is an important indicator of cognitive health in older age and a sensitive marker of hippocampal integrity. Measures of mnemonic discrimination, such as the mnemonic similarity task, have the potential to become early diagnostic tools of Alzheimer's dementia. It is thus important to understand how hippocampus-dependent memory functions interact with nonmnemonic processes to determine mnemonic discrimination performance. In this study, we investigate which features contribute to mnemonic discrimination in younger and older age. First, we found in a sample of younger (n = 93, 20-30 years) and older adults (n = 103, 65-82 years) that age impacted performance on the mnemonic similarity task above and beyond the effect of perceptual discrimination of novel 2D configurative objects. Next, in two experiments, we acquired similarity and feature difference ratings for the mnemonic similarity task lures from younger (n = 25 and n = 47, 19-37 years) and older (n = 25 and n = 47, 65-79 years) adults. Using random forest regression and representational similarity analysis, we found that the two groups exhibited unique similarity rating patterns. Finally, enriching our memory data with the feature information, we showed, on the trial level, that mnemonic decisions of older and younger adults are affected by distinct object features. Altogether, these results provide evidence that older adults perceive the differences in lure images distinctively and they may rely on different levels of representations for mnemonic discrimination. items.title: Age-related changes in memory for gist and details: New perspectives on the representational quality of episodic memory.
items.abstract: Substantial heterogeneity in adult age-related declines in episodic memory within and across tasks and individuals has prompted extensive theoretical debate about the source of these variations. Today, many theories assume that age-related changes in the representational fidelity of memory and the degree to which a test demands the retrieval of specific details of past experiences underlie much of this variability. This special issue of Psychology and Aging presents 19 contributions from researchers from around the world that together aim to enrich our understanding of the representational basis of age-related memory change. These contributions explore several interrelated themes related to measuring, predicting, and, at times, counteracting age-related declines in memory specificity while extending representational accounts to new tasks, more naturalistic contexts, and populations spanning the adult lifespan as well as individuals with neurocognitive impairment. The breadth of coverage spans multiple research domains with rich histories in the field of cognitive aging, including recognition memory, autobiographical memory, event memory, decision making, comprehension, and computational modeling. Collectively, the diversity of questions posed by the articles and the varied methods they advance to addressing them highlight the value of integrating findings across different research traditions to develop a more unified framework for studying age-related changes in memory specificity. items.title: Developmental engaged methods of observation (DEMO): A proposal for science and society.
items.abstract: Observational research that involves observers from the communities and contexts researchers aim to study can make research more valid while representing community views and interests. Developmental science is a key area where community-engaged approaches can make valuable contributions, especially considering the challenges inherent in observing children and families. This conceptual article proposes an approach for effectively gathering observational data while enhancing equity in science: Developmental Engaged Methods of Observation. This approach brings together insights from developmental science, participatory science research (which involves training community members to serve as data collectors who observe the world around them), and participatory action research (which centers the voices of the communities that are being studied). This article illustrates what the approach can look like by discussing several case studies from contemporary developmental research in families, schools, and everyday settings on topics like human development, academic integrity, and science identity. The Developmental Engaged Methods of Observation approach forwards new ways of thinking about developmental observation research that can bolster diversity in science, create new insight into developmental processes and mechanisms across contexts, and create opportunities for trust and partnership with stakeholders across a range of communities. items.title: Feasibility and equity in the assessment of parent-child interactions: Lessons from three approaches.
items.abstract: Observations of parent-child interactions provide critical insights that directly inform developmental theory and treatment initiatives. Equitable and feasible assessment is necessary to fully understand the spectrum of relevant parent and child behaviors accounting for cultural, ethnic, racial, and linguistic diversity. Parent-child observational research has primarily relied on structured, in-person recordings later coded by research assistants. This approach introduces logistical barriers for families coming into the laboratory, significant time and labor cost for coding, and potential limitations in ecological validity. With the advent and application of new, agile approaches for parent-child behavioral observation and coding, it is critical to evaluate which methods may improve feasibility, accessibility of participation, diverse representation, and ecological validity. This article examines the strengths and limitations of three innovative observational methodologies to assess parent-child interactions among ethnically, linguistically, and geographically diverse families: (a) structured male-caregiver-child interactions via videoconferencing with live coding (N = 114), (b) recording speech in naturalistic parent-child interactions via smartphone application with AI-supported coding (N = 27), and (c) naturalistic interactions in the home via wearable video-recording device (N = 27). A detailed discussion is provided focused on the (a) feasibility, utility, and cost of these methods, (b) clinical implications, (c) ability to overcome logistical barriers and promote equitable access to diverse families, (d) and ethical implications of standard, AI-supported, and live coding methods. Implications of this work contribute to understanding how to improve equity in the assessment of parent-child interactions, as well as increase the feasibility of behavioral observation for researchers. items.title: Applying observational methods to antiracist research with White families.
items.abstract: In an effort to disrupt ongoing racial injustice, many areas of psychology are increasingly interrogating Whiteness-defined as a system of cultural practices, laws, and institutions that confer privilege and resources to White individuals. Features of Whiteness, including avoidance, defensiveness, and self-presentation bias, present unique methodological challenges that render observational methods indispensable for antiracist research with White participants and families. This article outlines innovative approaches to manage the influence of Whiteness and racism on research teams and observational methodologies, tailor methods to both parents' and children's developmental levels, and incorporate technology to expand observations beyond the lab. In particular, we focus on the use of observational methods to study White racial socialization, a key mechanism through which racism or antiracism is conveyed across generations. Our recommendations are illustrated through practical and empirical lessons from a case study of The CARPE DIEM Study, which evaluates a novel antiracist parenting intervention for White mothers of White children. items.title: Methodological innovations for advancing equitable observations of human behavior and social interactions in psychological science.
items.abstract: The purpose of this special issue was to bring together articles discussing pragmatic, new, equitably informed methodologies for the use of behavioral observation in psychology. This introduction highlights main themes that emerged across the published articles, such as the importance of theory and innovative methods in observational research, the use of artificial intelligence in observational coding and data collection, and methods that advance equitable observation principles. Articles highlight strategies and tips for the use of observational methods that are more pragmatic, less costly, and less time intensive. Additionally, articles discuss the use of observational methods across settings (e.g., home, school, and therapeutic), modalities (e.g., wearables, virtual), and analytic methods (e.g., machine learning). We conclude the introduction with ethical considerations that emerged across the special issue, as well as the need for the use of pragmatic observational methods in large, epidemiological studies. items.title: Investigating Interoceptive Beliefs in Individuals With Endometriosis.
items.abstract: Background Research has indicated that individuals experiencing chronic pain differ in their ability to sense and interpret signals arising from inside the body, termed interoception. It is unclear whether differences in interoception exist for those with endometriosis, a common condition where pain is a major symptom. Methods This study aimed to investigate whether interoceptive beliefs are altered in individuals with a diagnosis of endometriosis compared to those without, and whether pain experienced by those with endometriosis predicted interoceptive beliefs. Interoceptive beliefs were assessed in 247 participants with endometriosis and 98 participants without the condition. Those with endometriosis also reported their experience of dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, dyschezia, and chronic pelvic pain. Results Individuals with endometriosis reported that they noticed more internal signals but had reduced trust in these signals and were more worried by them. They also reported that they try to distract themselves from internal sensations more than those without endometriosis. Increased pain intensity predicted higher scores in one facet of interoceptive beliefs, such that higher levels of pain were associated with higher awareness of internal sensations in individuals with endometriosis. Conclusions These results indicate that those with endometriosis differ in their interoceptive beliefs and that these differences may be influenced by their pain experience. Given these findings largely align with changes observed in other conditions marked by pain, it is possible that interoceptive changes may represent a transdiagnostic characteristic across individuals experiencing pain. Significance This study addresses previously conflicted findings in the literature, providing a clearer picture of the changes in interoceptive beliefs present in people with endometriosis. Developing a stronger understanding of interoceptive functioning in this unique population may lead to opportunities to develop stronger interventions targeting bodily sensations in pain management in those with the condition.

items.title: Time Flows With the Changing of Events.
items.abstract: In recent years, investigations into the psychological experience of time have rapidly accelerated. The experience of time could depend on a ticking internal clock or rely on contextual changes within and between events. Cognitive theories of memory propose that the presence of event boundaries, as defined by unexpected changes, is crucial for the segmentation of sequenced content and ultimately, the formation of long-term memories. Interestingly, the experience of change also influences the temporal distances between memories. Concurrent lines of research have developed similar theories on the experience of time, with salient contextual changes distorting temporal experience. Herein, we propose a unification of theories from the fields of time and memory. Events are creatively constructed and encoded into long-term memory if sufficient changes occur. The subjective experience of time is also determined by an accumulation of changes creating temporal distances between memories. The encoding of memories provides temporal tags at multiple nested timescales, with no need to synchronize with the relative number of seconds that have passed, and duration estimates require a reconstruction of information between anchor points. Time does not exist without change, and experiencing change is fundamental for the formation of lasting memories.

items.title: GABAergic Network Dysregulation in Alcohol Use Disorder: Receptor-Transporter Interactions Driving the Transition From Goal-Directed to Compulsive Behaviour.
items.abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is characterized by a shift from controlled, goal-directed drinking to compulsive, habitual alcohol (a.k.a. ethanol) seeking, even in the face of negative outcomes. This transition is closely associated with alterations in cortico-striatal circuitry and dysregulated GABAergic signalling, both of which drive the progression from flexible control to compulsive behaviour. Acute alcohol exposure enhances GABAergic inhibition, primarily by increasing presynaptic GABA release. Chronic exposure leads to compensatory neuroadaptations, such as subunit reorganization, receptor internalization and diminished GABA receptor sensitivity. While these neuroadaptations alter receptor-mediated GABAergic signalling during dependence and withdrawal, they also alter dopaminergic regulation and further reinforce alcohol-seeking behaviour. Beyond receptor-level adaptations, impaired GABA clearance, especially through the astrocytic transporter GAT3, plays a crucial role in regulating extracellular GABA concentrations and tonic inhibition. This effect is particularly evident within the dorsal striatum, where elevated tonic GABA shifts control from flexible, goal-directed action towards rigid, habitual responding by altering the balance between the dorsomedial and dorsolateral subregions. Consistent with these mechanistic insights, animal and human studies demonstrate that reduced GAT3 expression is associated with compulsive alcohol use and impaired reward-related behaviour, reinforcing impaired GABA clearance as a central mechanism in this behavioural shift. Taken together, these lines of evidence validate a central therapeutic model, namely, that targeting altered tonic inhibition and impaired GABA clearance in AUD could address the inhibitory dysfunction that sustains the disorder. Overall, this work supports a unifying model in which receptor adaptations and disrupted GABA removal maintain altered inhibitory tone, driving maladaptive circuit function and contributing to the persistence of AUD.

items.title: The impact of patient weight status on healthcare students' attitudes: Two experimental studies in midwifery and dental students.
items.abstract: Background Weight stigma refers to prejudice and discrimination based on body weight. Healthcare professionals often hold negative attitudes towards patients with overweight, which can negatively affect patient care and health outcomes. However, weight stigma is yet to be explored in midwifery and dental students. Methods Two online experimental studies using hypothetical patient vignettes were conducted in midwifery (n = 281; Study 1) and dental and non-dental students (n = 528; Study 2). Participants were randomly assigned to view a healthy-weight, overweight or obese patient vignette and then reported their attitudes, predicted time, advice they would provide and beliefs about obesity. Data were analysed using ANOVA and logistic regression. Results In Study 1, midwifery students held significantly more stigmatizing attitudes towards patients who were overweight than healthy-weight patients; however, there was no significant difference in attitudes towards patients with obesity. Predicted time spent with patients did not significantly differ as a function of patient weight status. In Study 2, dental and non-dental students reported more stigmatizing attitudes towards overweight and obese patients compared to healthy-weight patients. Predicted time spent with patients did not differ significantly. Dental and non-dental students were more likely to offer lifestyle-related advice to overweight and obese patients. There was no significant relationship between beliefs about obesity and attitudes towards treating patients. Conclusions Weight stigma is evident among healthcare students and can affect healthcare advice. Increased awareness of potential biases in midwives and dental students is needed and should form formal training to improve equitable healthcare delivery.

items.title: Virtual Social Interaction and Psychological Capital in Chemotherapy Patients: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
items.abstract: Background Cancer-related psychological distress remains underaddressed globally. Virtual interventions offer promising alternatives but lack evidence for enhancing Psychological Capital (PsyCap) in chemotherapy patients. Objective This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy of a virtual social interaction intervention on PsyCap in patients undergoing chemotherapy. Methods This single-blind randomized controlled trial (RCT) enrolled 76 chemotherapy patients hospitalized in the oncology ward of Imam Sajjad Hospital, Ramsar, Mazandaran, Iran. Participants were selected via convenience sampling and then allocated to intervention or control groups using an odd-even (alternating) assignment method. The intervention group participated in 6 weeks of virtual social interactions, consisting of asynchronous materials (recorded audio, short videos, images, PDF, and PowerPoint files) uploaded weekly to Iranian messaging platforms (Eitaa), as well as live synchronous group sessions conducted on the Skyroom platform with a minimum of 10 participants per session. The control group received standard care. The PsyCap was measured using Luthans' Psychological Capital Questionnaire at both baseline and post-intervention. The Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA) models (A/B) were adjusted for baseline scores and age. Results The intervention group showed improvements across all outcomes, with the total PsyCap score increasing by 23.6 points. Components significantly increased: self-efficacy by 5.8 points, resilience by 5.8, hope by 5.5, and optimism by 6.5 (p 1). Conclusions Virtual social interactions significantly enhance PsyCap in chemotherapy patients. However, to confidently generalize these findings and make recommendations, similar studies need to be conducted and replicated in larger, multicenter trials.

items.title: Family Engagement and Shared Decision-Making in Adult Intensive Care Nursing: A Bibliometric Review and Thematic Analysis.
items.abstract: Background Family members contribute information, emotional support, bedside care and surrogate decision-making in adult intensive care, yet the nursing literature on family engagement remains conceptually and geographically fragmented. Aims To map the development, intellectual structure, collaboration patterns and thematic evolution of research on family engagement and shared decision-making in adult intensive care nursing. Study design This study was a bibliometric review with complementary thematic content analysis. Following the framework of Donthu et al., Scopus was searched on 16 July 2026 from inception, with bibliometric coverage restricted to complete calendar years through 31 December 2025. Scopus was used because it provides the cited-reference data required for co-citation and bibliographic-coupling analyses. Eligible records were journal articles and reviews concerning adult intensive care that examined family engagement or shared decision-making and included an identifiable nursing component. Performance analysis, co-authorship analysis, reference co-citation, bibliographic coupling, and keyword co-occurrence analysis were conducted using Python and VOSviewer, while cluster content was interpreted using inductive qualitative content analysis. Reporting followed the BIBLIO guideline. Results The review included 278 publications (1993-2025) from 117 journals and 47 countries. Annual output increased from two publications in 1993 to 32 publications in 2025; 141 publications (50.7%) were published during 2020-2025. Nursing journals produced most publications, whereas two multidisciplinary critical care journals produced 23 publications (8.3%) but 3090 of 11 220 citations (27.5%). The United States led with 104 publications; 23.9% were internationally co-authored. Co-citation analysis identified four intellectual foundations and bibliographic coupling five research fronts, led by family participation and nurse-family engagement. Thirty-nine author keywords formed six themes spanning end-of-life communication and ethics, family-centred nursing engagement and surrogate participation, family support and visitation, family presence in high-acuity care, caregiver experience and bereavement. Keyword trends moved from family needs and withholding treatment towards active engagement, implementation barriers and family nursing. Conclusion The field has progressed towards partnership but continues to under-specify nurses' roles, use inconsistent terminology and draw disproportionately on high-income Western settings. Relevance to clinical practice Critical care services should formalise nurses' responsibilities in family assessment, communication, advocacy and decision support while developing culturally responsive and implementable engagement models.

items.title: Associations Between Parity and Parasympathetic Regulation in Response to Infant Crying.
items.abstract: Research suggests that women's parasympathetic response to infant crying reflects regulation of arousal and is associated with caregiving behaviors. In particular, respiratory sinus arrhythmia (RSA) withdrawal in response to infant cry stimuli has been associated with maternal sensitivity. However, the ways in which multiple reproductive and caregiving experiences (in terms of giving birth and raising a child) can modulate women's RSA in response to infant crying are still unknown. Our aim was to test whether women's RSA in response to infant crying is associated with parity. Participants included 184 women (62 nulliparous women; 86 primiparous women; 36 multiparous women). RSA was measured while women were watching a neutral video, followed by videos of crying infants. Analyses revealed that perception of infant crying was associated with a significant RSA withdrawal, compared to the baseline condition, in both multiparous and nulliparous women. A statistically significant RSA withdrawal was absent among primiparous women, possibly reflecting a more sustained physiological arousal to infant crying. We discuss the potential challenges in physiological regulation, indexed by RSA withdrawal, among primiparous women in response to infant crying. More sustained arousal may support an increased focus on infant signals but also predispose new mothers to perceive greater stress.

items.title: Incidence of Intensive Care Unit Delirium After Heart Surgery: A Feasibility Study of a Forest Environment Intervention.
items.abstract: Background Postoperative delirium is a serious complication in intensive care units (ICUs), particularly following cardiac surgery. It is associated with circadian rhythm disruption, sleep disturbances and adverse outcomes. ICU environments often lack natural time cues, which may exacerbate circadian misalignment and increase delirium risk. Aim The primary aim of the study was the evaluation of the implementation of two chronotherapeutic ICU interventions regarding recruitment, implementability and safety. Its secondary aim was to descriptively assess postoperative delirium across intervention groups. Study design This randomized feasibility study was conducted in a tertiary cardiac surgery ICU in Austria. Adult patients undergoing elective cardiac surgery were allocated to one of three groups: (1) forest environment, (2) light exposure or (3) standard ICU care. Interventions were applied for 12 h daily. Delirium was assessed at three postoperative time points using the confusion assessment method for the ICU (CAM-ICU) and intensive care delirium screening checklist (ICDSC). Results This study was conducted between March 2020 and 2025. Seventy-seven patients were enrolled, and 64 remained in the final analytical cohort. Interventions were delivered within routine care. Patients and ICU staff did not report intervention-related concerns. Implementation challenges included ICU restructuring, patient transfers due to COVID-19 and deviations from randomized allocation because of operational constraints. No intervention-related adverse events occurred. Delirium assessments were limited at several time points because of sedation, early ICU discharge or transfer. Across all groups, postoperative delirium was detected in 5 of 130 CAM-ICU completed assessments (3.8%) and 8 of 115 ICDSC completed assessments (6.9%), precluding inferential group comparisons. Conclusions Chronotherapeutic environmental interventions were feasible and safe in ICU care. Feasibility results highlighted challenges related to ICU logistics, sedation-related assessment limitations and pandemic-related disruptions. The unexpectedly low delirium incidence limited conclusions regarding intervention efficacy. Future trials should include larger high-risk populations and prospectively defined feasibility outcomes. Relevance to clinical practice Optimized ICU environments, including noise reduction and light management, may support delirium prevention. Chronotherapeutic environmental interventions are feasible additions to routine ICU care.

items.title: Pre-Drinking and Its Relationship to Sexual Diversity and Sexual Harassment in Nightlife Settings.
items.abstract: Introduction Sexual harassment is experienced by 50% of nightlife patrons and disproportionately more by LGBTQIA+ (i.e., lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, intersex, asexual) patrons. The present study did not find that sexually diverse individuals engaged in more pre-drinking behaviours than heterosexual individuals, nor that LGBTQIA+ individuals report greater rates of sexual harassment than individuals identifying as heterosexual. However, women reported a larger number of sexual harassment experiences. Using these findings to inform interventions to reduce sexual harassment is indicated.

items.title: A pilot study of electromagnetic therapy versus biofeedback-based pelvic floor muscle training for pelvic organ prolapse: A mixed-methods approach.
items.abstract: Objectives This pilot study aimed to: (1) evaluate the effects of high-intensity focused electromagnetic (HIFEM) therapy on pelvic organ prolapse (POP) symptoms and pelvic floor function; (2) compare outcomes across HIFEM, pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT) with biofeedback and/or electrostimulation, and usual care; and (3) explore participant acceptability of the interventions. Materials and methods A mixed-methods pilot study was conducted in women aged >20 years with stage I-III POP. Participants were randomized to HIFEM, PFMT, or usual care. The HIFEM group underwent twice-weekly 28-min sessions for eight weeks using a non-invasive electromagnetic chair. PFMT consisted of supervised sessions incorporating biofeedback and/or electrostimulation. Usual care included lifestyle advice. Outcomes were assessed using validated questionnaires for POP symptoms and pelvic floor distress, digital palpation, and transperineal ultrasound. Results Twenty-eight women completed the study (HIFEM, n = 10; PFMT, n = 9; usual care, n = 9). Compared with usual care, HIFEM significantly improved pelvic floor muscle endurance (p = 0.001), whereas PFMT significantly improved muscle strength (p = 0.034), endurance (p = 0.023), and rapid contractions (p = 0.019). Only HIFEM demonstrated significant improvements in POP symptom severity (p = 0.015) and pelvic floor distress (p = 0.041). No serious adverse events were reported. Participant satisfaction was highest in the HIFEM group (100%). Qualitative analysis supported intervention acceptability, with participants reporting increased pelvic floor awareness, improved symptom control, and enhanced psychological well-being. Conclusions Both HIFEM and PFMT with biofeedback appear to be safe, acceptable, and effective non-surgical treatment options for women with POP. Although no significant differences were observed between the two interventions, these findings should be interpreted with caution because of the small sample size. Larger studies are needed to confirm comparative efficacy and inform clinical implementation. Clinical trial registration number NCT06532292. items.title: Voluntary exercise mitigates the effects of peri-adolescent social isolation on emotion recognition and the oxytocinergic system in male mice.
items.abstract: Social isolation, particularly during adolescence, is known to affect cognitive, emotional, and social behaviors as well as brain modulatory systems such as the hypothalamic oxytocinergic system. Interestingly, recent evidence indicates that exercise can exert beneficial effects on behaviors through the activation of the oxytocinergic system. Weaned male mice were either singly- or group-housed and were exposed to either an igloo or a running wheel until the end of the experiment. After 12 weeks in these experimental conditions, they were subjected to various behavioral tests to assess different dimensions of social behaviors (sociability, social recognition and emotion discrimination), anxiety levels, and spatial memory. The impact of peri-adolescent social isolation and of voluntary running activity on the oxytocinergic system was also evaluated. We found that peri-adolescent social isolation enhanced social investigation (social rebound) and impaired emotion discrimination in male mice, without affecting social novelty recognition, spatial memory or anxiety-like behavior. Social isolation also decreased the number of oxytocinergic neurons in the hypothalamic paraventricular nucleus, but not in the supraoptic nucleus, and did not affect circulating OXT levels. Voluntary exercise protected against social isolation-induced deficits in affective state discrimination and enhanced OXT plasma levels without altering the number of oxytocinergic neurons. Our results indicate that peri-adolescent isolation particularly alters socio-affective discrimination and the oxytocinergic system, that are mitigated by voluntary exercise. This suggests that exercise could alleviate emotion discrimination deficits induced by isolation, possibly through the improvement of oxytocinergic signaling.

items.title: ANCHOR: Communication Partner Training for Maintaining Friendships After Aphasia.
items.abstract: Background Aphasia significantly disrupts social relationships, with friendship loss occurring early after stroke and continuing into chronic stages. Despite friendships being prioritised by people with aphasia and families, they rarely receive explicit focus in rehabilitation. Communication partner training is an intervention with potential to keep friendship bonds strong after aphasia. Aims This paper describes the development of ANCHOR (Aphasia: Nurturing Connection, Honoring Ongoing Relationships), a communication partner training intervention protoype designed specifically for people with aphasia and their pre-existing friends-and the foundational elements of ANCHOR and how they informed its design and components, and then situates ANCHOR within the broader communication partner training literature with attention to partner type, candidacy and real-world delivery in service settings. Main contribution ANCHOR represents the first communication partner training intervention explicitly targeting friendship maintenance after aphasia. Development was grounded in a systematic research progression including lived experience research, relational competence theory and the behaviour change wheel, and a planned cycle of refinement across a two-year development period. Key distinguishing features include a hybrid delivery model that combines self-paced digital modules with in-person coaching sessions, universal 'talking tools' accessible to friends with minimal aphasia knowledge, first-year post-stroke timing to prevent relationship deterioration, and explicit attention to implementation barriers. Conclusions By grounding communication partner training design in lived experience, relationship theory and implementation science, ANCHOR is designed as a comprehensive, implementable approach to sustaining friendships after aphasia, thereby addressing a critical gap in post-stroke rehabilitation with potential to reduce social isolation and support mental health. ANCHOR is an intervention prototype and its core functions, forms and implementation supports will be refined as feasibility and trial data accrue. What this paper adds What is already known on this subject Aphasia greatly impacts the ability for people to maintain a strong social network. People with aphasia often lose most of their pre-stroke friends early in the recovery journey. Friends of people with aphasia need access to interventions that can help them understand aphasia and its impact on communication. What this study adds to the existing knowledge We developed a communication partner training program called ANCHOR based upon lived experience research involving people with aphasia and their friends and theories and relationship maintenance and behaviour change. ANCHOR is different than other communication partner training programs which target family members or healthcare providers in that it is limited to three face-to-face sessions, includes a self-guided digital component, and focuses on a standard package of communication strategies. What are the potential clinical implications of the study? ANCHOR continues to be refined and evaluated. It is our hope that ANCHOR will be a clinically feasible and person-centered communication partner training program that is effective in improving communication and relationships for people with aphasia and their friends.

items.title: Not All Thwarting Is Equal: Distinct Temporal Patterns Linking Teachers' Psychological Needs to Turnover Intention.
items.abstract: Background Teacher turnover intention has become a critical global concern, compromising teachers' psychological well-being, school workforce stability, and student learning outcomes. While psychological need thwarting (PNT) is recognized as a key antecedent of turnover intention, existing research has predominantly treated PNT as a unidimensional construct and overlooked the possibility that turnover intention may reciprocally shape teachers' subsequent need experiences. Integrating self-determination theory and conservation of resources theory, this study employed a two-wave cross-lagged panel model to examine bidirectional associations between the three PNT dimensions and turnover intention among Chinese teachers. Methods Data were collected from 1,061 teachers at Time 1 and 812 at Time 2 under a design permitting voluntary, wave-specific participation, with 332 teachers participating in both waves (M age = 41.19 years, SD = 9.13; 69.6% female); cross-lagged models controlling for gender and age were estimated using full information maximum likelihood, drawing on all available observations from 1,541 unique participants, with school ownership and school type incorporated into the missing-data model. Results An asymmetric temporal pattern emerged: among the three dimensions, only autonomy thwarting predicted subsequent turnover intention (B = 0.09, 95% CI [0.01, 0.17], β = 0.12, p = 0.023), whereas turnover intention predicted later competence thwarting (B = 0.22, 95% CI [0.02, 0.41], β = 0.11, p = 0.031) and relatedness thwarting (B = 0.19, 95% CI [0.01, 0.37], β = 0.13, p = 0.048) but not autonomy thwarting (B = 0.08, 95% CI [-0.07, 0.24], β = 0.06, p = 0.276). Although these cross-lagged effects were small in magnitude, they demonstrated distinct directional patterns across the three needs. Conclusion These findings suggest that turnover intention may function not only as an outcome of adverse need experiences but also as an antecedent of subsequent need states. This asymmetric pattern points to potentially relevant intervention targets: autonomy support for teachers who have not yet developed turnover intention, and competence and relatedness support for those already considering leaving.

items.title: The Impact of Cladribine Tablets on Cognition Over One Year in Patients With Multiple Sclerosis: A Preliminary Study.
items.abstract: Introduction Cognitive impairment is common in multiple sclerosis (MS), affecting >40% of patients. Cladribine tablets are a high-efficacy MS disease-modifying therapy to prevent relapses and limit disease progression. Our previous study showed cortical gray matter lesion stability over one year after the start of cladribine, though its effect on cognition is not well known. This study aimed to investigate the one-year impact of cladribine tablets on cognition in multiple sclerosis. Methods Fourteen MS subjects [age (mean ± SD) 50.2 ± 10.8, 7.14% men, 57.1% relapsing-remitting MS (n = 8), 42.9% secondary progressive (n = 6), expanded disability status scale 4.1 ± 2.1] were administered the Brief Repeatable Battery of Neuropsychological Tests (BRB-N) and the Stroop Color and Word Test (Stroop) at an average of 1.5 months from cladribine start. The BRB-N measures information processing speed (Symbol Digit Modalities Test, Paced Auditory Serial Addition Test [PASAT]), verbal memory (Selective Reminding Test [SRT]), visual-spatial memory (10/36 Spatial Recall Test), and verbal fluency (Word List Generation). Stroop assesses processing speed and executive function. When available, alternate versions of the individual cognitive tests were used at follow-up to reduce practice effects. Paired t-tests compared within-subject baseline and follow-up data. Results After one year, no worsening was noted on any cognitive test. Furthermore, both PASAT 3-second total correct and SRT total delayed recall trended toward improved scores on-study, with an average 3.4 (p = 0.07) and 1.1 (p = 0.05) point increase, respectively. Conclusion In this preliminary study, no clear decline in cognitive performance was detectable over one year in patients newly started on cladribine tablets.

items.title: Inpatient Dementia Mental Health Care in the UK: A National Mapping Survey of Ward Provision and Family Carer Involvement.
items.abstract: Objectives Inpatient mental health wards provide specialist care for people with dementia experiencing acute behavioural disturbance. The scale and configuration of this provision, and how these services involve family carers, have not previously been described at a national level. This study aimed to map ward provision across the UK and characterise existing policies and practices related to carer involvement. Methods A national cross-sectional online mapping survey was conducted across mental health wards providing care for people with dementia in the UK. Wards were identified through a structured multi-source search strategy. The survey captured ward characteristics, patient profile, staffing and approaches to carer involvement. Quantitative data were analysed descriptively; Fisher's exact test was used to examine associations between categorical variables. Results 209 wards comprising over 3100 beds across 80 provider organisations were identified. 63 wards (30.1%) participated, reporting 801 patients. Most patients were detained under mental health or capacity legislation (87.8%) and few were expected to return home (14.8%). While all wards reported involving carers in clinical decision-making, 44.4% indicated carers did not routinely attend MDT meetings and 30.2% did not routinely share care plans. Staff training in carer engagement was a consistent marker of greater carer involvement across multiple measures. Conclusions This survey provides the first national picture of inpatient dementia mental health care in the UK, revealing a service under considerable pressure and a consistent gap between the basic infrastructure for carer involvement and its meaningful integration into clinical practice. Staff training in carer engagement was strongly associated with greater carer involvement, pointing to an actionable route to improvement.
