items.title: Early-Life Polyethylene Microplastic Exposure Exacerbates ADHD-Like Behaviors in Mice via PI3K/AKT1/Nrf2 Signaling: Evidence From the Pilot Cohort and Multi-Omics Analyses.
items.abstract: Microplastic pollution may influence neurodevelopment, yet its relationship with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) remains unclear. We integrated a pediatric cohort, multi-omics analyses, network toxicology, and animal experiments to investigate polyethylene (PE) microplastic exposure in ADHD vulnerability. Among 90 children, PE was the predominant polymer detected in blood and was more abundant in children with ADHD. Higher PE burden was associated with greater symptom severity, increased IL-6, and reduced antioxidant capacity. Multi-omics and network analyses converged on PI3K/AKT1/Nrf2 signaling. In a perinatal nicotine mouse model, developmental PE co-exposure exacerbated ADHD-like behaviors, dopaminergic dysfunction, and oxidative injury. Melatonin partially alleviated these abnormalities by restoring PI3K/AKT1/GSK3β and Nrf2 signaling, whereas AAV-mediated PI3K knockdown weakened its protective effects. Collectively, the human findings identify circulating PE burden as an environmental correlate of ADHD-related neurodevelopmental vulnerability, while the animal experiments provide evidence that developmental PE co-exposure can aggravate ADHD-like abnormalities in a susceptible background.

items.title: Risky Alcohol Use in Individuals With Anxiety Disorders: Relationships and Predictors Based on Early Maladaptive Schemas and Attachment Styles.
items.abstract: Background and aim This study aims to evaluate the differences between the groups with and without risky alcohol use (RAU) in terms of sociodemographic characteristics, anxiety level, adult attachment styles (AASs) and early maladaptive schemas (EMSs) in individuals diagnosed with anxiety disorders (ADs). Furthermore, we aim to investigate whether RAU in individuals with ADs can be predicted by EMS or AAS. Methods In this prospective study, a total of 128 individuals diagnosed with ADs were divided into two groups based on the Michigan Alcoholism Screening Test (MAST) cut-off score (≥ 5). Scores from the Adult Attachment Style Scale, Young Schema Questionnaire and Beck Anxiety Inventory (BAI), as well as demographic and clinical variables, were analysed. Results The RAU group showed higher rates of suicide history and higher scores on the abandonment and unrelenting standards (US) schemas. Higher scores on abandonment and US schemas were associated with a greater likelihood of RAU. MAST scores positively correlated with emotional deprivation, failure to achieve, pessimism, social isolation, AS, dependence, abandonment, vulnerability schema scores and BAI scores in individuals with RAU. Hierarchical regression showed that attachment and schema subscales accounted for 42% of the variance in MAST scores. The higher scores on emotional inhibition, defectiveness, vulnerability schemas and anxious attachment style significantly predicted MAST scores. Conclusion These findings support the theoretical basis for attachment-based and schema therapy-based interventions, highlighting the importance of assessing especially abandonment, US, defectiveness, vulnerability schemas and anxious attachment style.

items.title: Navigating social space: transgender inclusion in Guwahati city, Assam, India.
items.abstract: This qualitative study examined the lived experiences of people with transgender identities in the urban social spaces of Guwahati, India, through an intersectional lens. The study was informed by data drawn from three key informant interviews with gender rights activists, one focus group discussion with kinnar community members, and eight in-depth interviews with persons identifying as trans women, trans men, gender fluid or non-binary. The social spaces of Guwahati, considered in this study, were categorised into public spaces and education and workplaces. Using Braun and Clarke's six-phase thematic analysis , the study provided insights into the experiences of people with transgender identities in the city's different social spaces. The findings reveal their experiences are not uniform but are impacted by the intersection between an individual's gender identity and social location, including their socio-economic status and educational attainment. The work contributes to an understanding of the complex relationship between transgender and social spaces in regional cities such as Guwahati, underscoring the importance of adopting an intersectional approach when working to create inclusive and equitable environments for gender minorities in the Global South.

items.title: Membrane-Targeted Nanoparticles for Neuronal Photomodulation.
items.abstract: Selective targeting of nanoparticles to the neuronal interface is central for the tailored development of precision neurotechnologies. Here, we report the targeting of gold bipyramids, as a model nanomaterial, on the membrane of primary neurons using a bioorthogonal approach. In a two-step process, linker molecules anchor to receptors that expose trans-cyclooctene, which forms a covalent bond with the tetrazine functional group on nanoparticles, leading to the retention of hundreds of nanoparticles per cell. Selective labeling of neuronal membranes with plasmonic nanoparticles via a bioorthogonal strategy enabled inhibition of neuronal activity through photothermal effects under NIR laser irradiation in synchronized cell cultures. The linker and/or nanoparticles alone have a negligible effect on neuromodulation. Nanoparticle retention at the membrane is rapid, requiring only one hour of total incubation, with no cytotoxic effect. These results expand the repertoire of light-activated nanomaterials for non-invasive neuromodulation.

items.title: Maximising Cancer Prevention and Early Detection in the Australian Cancer Plan: Where Are We Now and What Should Come Next?
items.abstract: Cancer accounts for three in 10 deaths in Australia, yet many cases are preventable or can be detected at an early stage. Maximising cancer prevention and early detection is one of the six strategic objectives of the 10-year Australian Cancer Plan. This perspective article reviews the current progress and challenges of reducing the cancer burden, along with future opportunities. It explores how to address modifiable risk factors, particularly tobacco smoking, alcohol use and sun exposure and the advances in screening programs for bowel, breast, cervical and lung cancers. It highlights the potential for risk-stratified and genomics-informed screening, emphasising the need to support participation through equitable and culturally safe approaches.

items.title: Cortical long-range dynamics track excitation-inhibition balance across cognitive states and organizational principles
items.abstract: A fundamental question in systems neuroscience is how the brain's excitation-inhibition (E/I) balance shapes the temporal structure of neural activity and whether we can non-invasively recover this relationship from neural scaling properties. We show that MRS-derived E/I balance is expressed in long-range temporal dynamics and constrained by cytoarchitecture. The laminar organisation of inhibitory circuits, spanning agranular to granular cortex, determines how faithfully regional dynamics reflect E/I balance. This neurochemical signature is state-dependent: its relationship with cortical dynamics reverses during task engagement, consistent with traversal of dynamical regimes around a critical point. It extends beyond fMRI to arousal-linked dynamics, indexed by pupil diameter and microsaccades, indicating a global mode of cortical state rather than a regionally isolated property. The imprint of E/I balance on long-range dynamics follows the sensory-association axis at rest, and is reconfigured during task engagement. These findings establish E/I balance as a neurochemical quantity with structured, scalable signatures across the temporal and spatial organization of the human cortex.

items.title: "We Desperately Need More Training": A Qualitative Exploration of Emergency Department Nurses’ Experiences with and Training Needs for End-Of-Life Communication
items.abstract: Abstract Background Approximately 75% of decedents aged ≥ 65 years visited the emergency department in their last six months of life, underscoring the emergency department as a pivotal setting for end-of-life communication. Nurses play a significant role in palliative care, however, little research has been performed on their end-of-life communication experiences and training needs. Methods A qualitative descriptive study reported with reference to the COREQ checklist was conducted. A total of 12 ED nurses from a tertiary hospital in Shenzhen, Guangdong Province, China, were recruited through a purposive sampling method. Semi-structured interviews were conducted from April to June 2026, audio-recorded, and transcribed verbatim. Data were analysed using qualitative content analysis with an inductive coding approach. Results Four overarching themes were identified, including: (1) Complex emotional experiences (Powerless and conflicted; Compassionate and sorrowful; Fear of communication missteps; Compassion fatigue; Sense of mission and achievement) ; (2) Multidimensional barriers (Environment-related; Patient-related; Family-related; Nurse-related barrier ) ; (3) Core knowledge and skills needs (Disease-related knowledge; Psychology-related knowledge; Breaking-bad-news skill; Empathy and emotion regulation skill) ; and (4) Expectations for future training (Specialized teaching content; Practical teaching method; Accessible teaching format) . Conclusions Participants perceived a need for practical and ED-specific EOL communication training. Future programs should adopt blended, simulation-based, and context-specific pedagogical frameworks to address the identified gaps.

items.title: A Safe–Connect–Evolve positive psychology-informed support pathway for a university student with prior bullying victimization: a qualitative single-case study in China
items.abstract: Abstract Background Bullying victimization can have psychological and social consequences that persist beyond the original school context and into university. This study examined the longer-term support process of a university student with prior bullying victimization and developed a staged, practice-oriented support framework. Methods This retrospective qualitative single-case study focused on Student Z at University A in China. Existing case materials generated during routine student support between 2024 and 2026 included case conversations and collateral information, observational and support records, psychological assessment summaries, counseling records, and multisystem coordination records. A case-oriented, process-focused analysis examined presenting difficulties, support systems, support activities, and changes over time. Results Student Z’s difficulties after university entry were associated with delayed recognition of earlier bullying, limited emotional support, and fragmented professional support. The case record showed a gradual progression from establishing psychological safety and trust, to rebuilding family, peer, academic, and professional support, and subsequently to greater agency and campus participation. Psychological screening scores for interpersonal sensitivity, depression, anxiety, and hostility were lower at later assessment points than in October 2024 and remained within the reference range in March 2026. Retrospective synthesis of the case yielded a three-stage Safe–Connect–Evolve pathway. Conclusions The Safe–Connect–Evolve pathway provides a case-derived, practice-oriented framework for organizing support for university students with prior bullying victimization. It should not be regarded as a validated intervention protocol. Further multi-case research using prospectively defined qualitative procedures, standardized outcome measures, and longer-term follow-up is needed to examine its transferability.

items.title: How Does Mazu Festival Affect the Well-being of Elderly Tourists?An Empirical Study from the Perspective of Restorative Experience
items.abstract: Abstract Restorative environment research has predominantly focused on natural settings, with limited attention to short-duration, high-density folk festivals and elderly populations. Drawing upon the stimulus–organism–response (S-O-R) framework, this study integrates attention restoration theory and place attachment theory to construct a serial mediation model of “Perceived Restorative Environment through Place attachment and psychological recovery to Hedonic Well-being.” Using the Mazu Festival on Meizhou Island as the case site, a questionnaire survey was conducted among 552 elderly tourists aged 55 and above, and partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) was employed to test the hypotheses. The results indicate that Perceived Restorative Environment enhances Hedonic Well-being through dual mechanisms—a direct emotional gain pathway and a sequential cognitive–affective pathway via Place attachment and psychological recovery. Legibility exhibits robust explanatory power in the festival context. Short-term festival participation primarily yields attentional recovery, while deep psychological restoration is constrained by limited stay duration. At the theoretical level, this study proposes the “Dual-Pathway Model of Festival Restorative Experience,” extending the applicability of restorative environment theory from natural landscapes to cultural festival settings, and reveals how temporal constraints and cognitive aging shape the restoration pathways, thereby offering a new theoretical framework for understanding elderly well-being generation in culturally intensive tourism contexts. At the practical level, the findings provide concrete pathways for the age-friendly design of folk festival spaces and offer empirical support for transforming folk cultural tourism resources into public mental health intervention tools for the elderly, contributing to the improvement of active aging social service systems.

items.title: The impact of periodontitis in cardiac autonomic dysfunction by hrv analysis.
items.abstract: Introduction: Periodontitis is a chronic inflammatory disease damaging the supportive structure of teeth. It has systemic impacts including cardiac autonomic dysfunction. Heart Rate Variability (HRV) measures an objective analysis of the extent of autonomic regulation and where decreased parasympathetic activity coupled with increased sympathetic predominance was determined to correlate well with risk in cardiovascular events. This research ascertains periodontitis and its correlation to autonomic dysfunction by HRV analysis. Methodology: In total, 54 periodontitis patients were involved in the study, categorized under four groups, namely Gingivitis (n=14), Mild Periodontitis (n=13), Moderate Periodontitis (n=13), and Severe Periodontitis (n=14). Kubios HRV software version 3.5 was used for the analysis of time-domain and frequency-domain parameters of lead II ECG for HRV analysis. The indices of SNS and PNS were calculated for the assessment of autonomic balance. The correlation between the HRV parameters with the severity of periodontal disease was performed statistically. Results: The SNS index was higher in the periodontitis groups than in the gingivitis group (Gingivitis: 1.09 ± 0.60; Mild: 4.25 ± 2.4; Moderate: 3.82 ± 2.2; Severe: 4.45 ± 1.5; p < 0.001), although the pattern was not strictly progressive. Conclusion: Differences in autonomic regulation, including higher SNS index and lower PNS index values, were associated with periodontal disease categories. These findings should be interpreted cautiously because the study lacked a healthy control group and was cross-sectional.

items.title: Mapping Anaesthetic Syringe Labelling Practices, Perceived Standards Alignment and Educational Needs Among Anaesthesia Trainees and Technicians in India: A National Online Cross-Sectional Survey.
items.abstract: Background: Unlabelled or incompletely labelled anaesthetic syringes create preventable wrong-drug risk. This study evaluated syringe labelling practices, perceived standards alignment and educational needs among anaesthesia trainees and technicians in India. Methods: A national online cross-sectional survey was conducted across India from February to May 2025 using non-probability recruitment through professional networks and academic forums. Because recruitment did not use a closed centre-specific sampling frame, the number invited, exact number of contributing centres and conventional response rate were not available. An expert-reviewed and pilot-tested 21-item questionnaire assessed labelling frequency, timing, label completeness, exposure to unlabelled syringes, response behaviour, training, barriers and improvement priorities. Formal quantitative psychometric indices were not estimated. Data were summarized descriptively, and an exploratory Chi-square test assessed the unadjusted association between formal training and consistent labelling. Results: Of 421 complete responses, 344 (81.7%) respondents handled anaesthetic syringes daily. Consistent labelling was reported by 391 (92.9%), but pre-labelling of empty syringes was reported by 71 (16.9%). Expiry date documentation was never performed by 179 (42.5%), and only 111 (26.4%) included expiry details as a label component. Exposure to unlabelled or improperly labelled syringes occurred frequently or occasionally in 177 (42.1%). Although 278 (66.0%) discarded such syringes, the remainder used verification, self-labelling or confirmation-based workarounds. Formal training was reported by 361 (85.8%); an exploratory unadjusted analysis indicated an association with consistent labelling (P=0.039). Participant-level demographic and institutional covariates were unavailable for adjusted analysis. Only 137 (32.5%) perceived their practice as fully aligned with recommended standards. Conclusions: High self-reported labelling frequency coexisted with clinically important gaps in timing, completeness and disposal-related safety behaviour. The findings identify potentially important targets for structured training, readily available standardized labels, protocol reinforcement, audit-feedback cycles and safer workflow design. Because the study was cross-sectional and self-reported, the observed training association should not be interpreted as causal.

items.title: Navigating Reading Challenges: Phenomenological Study of Teachers Supporting Struggling Readers in Philippine Context
items.abstract: Struggling readers are a persistent concern in Philippine elementary education, yet research has largely examined student reading outcomes rather than the professional, emotional, and instructional experiences of the teachers who support these learners in resource-constrained, multilingual classrooms. This study investigated the lived experiences of elementary English teachers in identifying and supporting struggling readers, and how they adapt their pedagogy and negotiate contextual barriers. Transcendental phenomenological design was employed. Fifteen proficient public elementary English teachers in Baguio City, Philippines, were selected through criterion purposive sampling and interviewed using semi-structured, face-to-face interviews. Transcripts were analyzed using Braun and Clarke’s six-phase thematic analysis, and trustworthiness was supported through member checking. Four themes emerged: (a) diagnostic triage through standardized literacy assessments, (b) pedagogical flexibility and differentiated scaffolded instruction, (c) ecosystemic collaboration via remedial and peer networks, and (d) socio-contextual barriers, including parental illiteracy and resource constraints. The findings suggest that Vygotskian scaffolding must be extended to account for ecological and linguistic barriers in post-colonial multilingual classrooms, because its effectiveness is bounded by the educational and socioeconomic capital of the home. Implications for teacher professional development, curriculum localization, language-in-education policy, and parental partnership are discussed.

items.title: Urban and peri-urban agriculture in the Global South: Nexus and policies to reduce territorial inequalities and improve social welfare
items.abstract: In the Global South, rapid urbanization intensifies pressures on natural resources, food security, and social equity, progressively displacing agriculture toward vulnerable peri-urban areas. Urban and peri-urban agriculture (UPA) has emerged as a strategic approach not only for food production but also for strengthening social cohesion, climate resilience, and territorial integration. Despite growing relevance, the literature lacks systematic understanding of how Nexus frameworks are operationalized in UPA research and how they inform inclusive policy design. This study aims to systematically review UPA-Nexus research to identify emerging trends, regional patterns, governance arrangements, and policy pathways for reducing territorial inequalities in the Global South. Following the PRISMA protocol, a systematic literature review was conducted in the Scopus database (2017–2024) using Boolean operators related to UPA and Nexus frameworks. Of 92 identified documents, 49 met inclusion criteria (peer-reviewed, open-access, English-language, explicit UPA-Nexus focus). Data were systematically extracted on Nexus categories, territorial scope, governance arrangements, implementation scale, and reported outcomes. An inductive thematic analysis identified patterns and gaps across the reviewed literature. The review reveals three major contributions. First, we identify 17 distinct Nexus categories—demonstrating substantial conceptual diversification beyond the traditional Water-Energy-Food (WEF) Nexus, with emerging frameworks incorporating health, waste, climate, and social dimensions. Second, comparative analysis shows a marked regional divergence: Global North research emphasizes technological efficiency, optimization, and participatory innovation, while Global South literature addresses structural constraints, subsistence strategies, and institutional fragmentation, with studies concentrated in Africa, Asia, and Iran. Third, the analysis identifies critical governance gaps: despite policy recognition, implementation remains fragmented, with regulatory instruments ranking most effective yet predominantly locally focused, limiting territorial integration. UPA-Nexus approaches can reduce territorial inequalities when supported by enabling institutional frameworks, participatory governance, and context-sensitive policies. The review advances a conceptual framework integrating Nexus configurations, territorial dynamics, and institutional arrangements to inform integrated policy design. Findings highlight the need for strengthened institutional coordination, secure land tenure, and inclusive governance mechanisms to realize UPA's potential for advancing the SDGs in the Global South.

The newly collected georeferenced vouchers provide an important contemporary reference for future taxonomic, ecological and conservation assessments of L. stracheyi .

items.title: Beta diversity analysis reveals high turnover in benthic assemblages between tropical coral and subtropical rocky reefs
items.abstract: Abstract Understanding species distributions and biodiversity patterns is an old challenge in ecology and biogeography. This approach is especially important because of the current increase in anthropogenic pressure on coastal ecosystems. The Brazilian coastline is a mosaic of complex marine habitats, including extensive rocky shores and the largest coral reef formation in the Atlantic. By decomposing beta diversity into nestedness and turnover components, we investigated how benthic assemblages are structured and how species composition changes along the transitional zone between rocky and coral reefs. To assess the spatial components of alpha diversity, we also analyzed how species richness varies between neighboring habitats. The pairwise comparison of beta diversity revealed the highest turnover rates between the southern and northern assemblages, suggesting differentiation between the two bioprovinces. Southern provinces were characterized by suspension feeders, whereas northern provinces were dominated by stony corals along a north‒south diversity gradient. Redundancy analysis indicated that temperature was the most important environmental driver shaping benthic composition and distribution. Based on these results, we recognize different diversity patterns among two provinces and detect different levels of vulnerability should a stochastic event occur. Considering that human interference tends to increase in this area, the use of beta diversity partitioning can be a useful analytical tool to recognize communities with different levels of priority for monitoring and establishing conservation efforts.

items.title: An outlook on varied ecological engineering solutions for landslide prevention
items.abstract: This review assesses ecological engineering solutions for landslide prevention and slope stabilization by synthesizing evidence identified through scientific databases. The review encompasses the idea of applying vegetation-based techniques, including live stakes, brush layering, revegetation, grasses, herbaceous plants, bamboo plantations, and lithophytic life forms, together with conventional and structural measures such as natural geotextiles, live wooden crib walls, wattle fences, live silt fences, and live gully breaks. The reviewed evidence highlights the importance of species with strong root systems, which can influence the effectiveness of bioengineering interventions. Species such as Vetiver, Bermuda Grass, Ryegrass, Alder, selected Ficus species, and bamboo show deep-rooted control over soil reinforcement, erosion, and slope stabilization, while lithophytic life forms and pioneer colonizers may support the restoration of exposed rocky and landslide-affected surfaces. The review also examines the contribution of artificial intelligence, remote sensing, unmanned aerial vehicles, LiDAR, interferometric synthetic aperture radar, and machine learning models in landslide susceptibility assessment, monitoring, and advance warning. Overall, the findings revealed that integrated ecological engineering and data-driven monitoring may complement conventional stabilization measures, reduce landslide risk, restore degraded slopes, and inform sustainable land-management planning.

items.title: The Effect of High-Performance Work Systems on Financial Management Behavior of Healthcare Professionals
items.abstract: This study was conducted to examine the effects of high-performance work systems on the financial management behaviors of healthcare professionals. The relationship between employees’ perceptions of high-performance work system practices and their individual financial decision-making processes was evaluated. The research population consisted of healthcare and administrative personnel working at Mersin University Faculty of Medicine Hospital. The sample size was determined as 325 individuals, and survey data were collected from 330 participants and analyzed. Descriptive statistics were used for data analysis, model significance was tested with ANOVA, and multicollinearity was evaluated through VIF values. Reverse-coded items in the dataset were corrected, and analyses were performed using a free statistical software. The findings indicated that the perception of employment security played a significant role in determining financial management behaviors. Employment security had a positive and significant effect on cash and credit management, while it showed a negative and significant effect on savings/investment and insurance management. Perceived compensation showed a positive and significant relationship with insurance management behavior. The effects of other variables were not found to be statistically significant. The study demonstrated that human resource strategies influence both organizational and individual financial decision-making. This finding contributes to the understanding of financial behaviors in healthcare institutions. Future studies are recommended to examine similar variables in different sectors.

items.title: Incorporating reef condition into conservation planning to meet place‐based biodiversity outcomes under the Global Biodiversity Framework
items.abstract: Abstract To achieve Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) Target 3, the selection of protected areas must consider the condition of ecosystems at sites in addition to the GBF 30% area target. Implementing this consideration for coral reef ecosystems is challenging because data describing condition are patchy and limited. Thus, there is uncertainty in how effective coral reef condition data are for informing conservation priorities. To address this uncertainty, we evaluated whether including ecosystem condition data changed conservation priorities when the objective was to protect reefs and implement Target 3. We tested multiple static and modeled temporal coral reef condition datasets for the Great Barrier Reef and found that including reef condition significantly altered spatial planning priorities ( p < 0.001), with effects varying according to the condition indicator used. Almost half of the reefs prioritized for protection when condition metrics were included became low priority when they were excluded. Ignoring information about condition missed conservation targets for ∼22% of reef habitats once condition measures were included, highlighting how presence‐only approaches can overestimate conservation benefits by treating lower‐condition reefs as equal contributors to biodiversity protection. These differences in priority areas highlight the need to develop and use effective condition metrics for designing marine protected area systems for coral reefs globally. Making such data available and usable for managers and practitioners is a priority for coral reef conservation.

items.title: Modeling Visual Cortex with Layerwise Multiscale Manifold Capacity Maximization
items.abstract: Task-optimized deep neural networks have risen to prominence as the most predictive phenomenological models of responses in primate visual cortex, but leave much to be desired from the perspective of biological plausibility. One such limitation is the reliance on precise credit assignment through global backpropagation of error signals. Recent work has shown that this weakness can be circumvented by requiring each subsequent stage to solve a distinct and increasingly complex task, allowing for layerwise local learning signals. We propose a novel strategy for crafting such intermediate losses that uses an efficient coding framework formulated in terms of manifold capacity, and which can be computed using a sequence of {canonical cortical computations}. In particular, we leverage the relationship between the multiscale nature of visual signals and the dilation of receptive field sizes in cascaded visual representations to modulate complexity, allowing for the reapplication of these common loss computations at each stage of the hierarchy. We evaluate our approach on its ability to predict neural datasets spanning three areas of the ventral stream hierarchy in macaques, as well as human psychophysical data on an object classification task. We find that our unsupervised layerwise model matches or exceeds the performance of competitive architecture-matched baselines on all evaluations considered.

items.title: Statistical mechanics of spontaneous behavior
items.abstract: Why do a few behaviors fill most of an animal's time? The usual answer is that these behaviors are started more often, because learning and reinforcement favor them. Here we show that how long a behavior lasts can, by itself, explain much of what is observed. We consider a system that runs until it meets a constraint, such as a wall, and then resets. The fraction of time it spends in each behavior then follows the Boltzmann law, and the partition function is the mean time between resets. The four laws of thermodynamics follow as theorems from four postulates, and critical points that act as bottlenecks become the most occupied states. In 47 multi-day recordings of fruit flies, the dominant behavior accounts for only $13\%$ of bout starts yet fills $49\%$ of the time, and its typical duration identifies the individual fly. These results lay the groundwork for a statistical mechanics of behavior.

items.title: Do agents need to sleep?
items.abstract: LLM-based agents, which increasingly operate persistently across sessions and accumulate memory through interaction, already exhibit the familiar symptoms of unchecked plasticity: semantic drift, degraded retrieval precision, propagation of stored errors, and saturation of memory capacity. Drawing on the selectionist "ringing, resonance and renormalization" (RRR) account of sleep, we propose that each of its three phases maps onto an operation feasible in digital memory architectures. Engineers building stateful agents, meanwhile, are independently rediscovering the problems sleep evolved to solve: what to forget, and when to do the forgetting. From this we derive the falsifiable prediction that selectionist consolidation will outperform instructionist alternatives as memory stores grow large. The core claim concerns the nature of continuous learning itself: plasticity has a price, and for any system that learns continuously under finite capacity while coupled to its environment, that price is sleep.

items.title: A Planar Switching Neuron Shares Logarithmic First-Spike Latency with Its Three-Dimensional Parent But Not Its Onset Mechanism
items.abstract: Can a reduced neuron model reproduce first-spike latency scaling while changing how a stimulus initiates sustained firing? We compare a piecewise-linear planar Neurosimilator with its three-dimensional parent. Both exhibit logarithmic latency dependence over the investigated input intervals, with different fitted coefficients. The mechanisms differ. In the parent, sustained spiking and a stable resting focus coexist in a spiking--rest bistability regime. An abrupt step accesses spiking, while slow stimulation can retain rest at the same final input. Its step-induced firing threshold is therefore an operational basin-access threshold below the saddle-node limit point, not a loss of equilibrium stability. In the planar model, the resting equilibrium instead reaches a switching boundary while its subthreshold eigenvalues remain negative. We derive the planar latency law from this boundary approach. The model generates repetitive excursions without an imposed reset and admits exact trajectories within six switching regions. Similar measured latency scaling thus coexists with different mechanisms of access to firing. Validating a reduced model's mechanism of excitability requires examination of stimulus protocol and attractor access alongside equilibrium structure and spike timing.

items.title: Solving the Mystery of the Electron Radiation Belt at Uranus: Leveraging Knowledge of Earth's Radiation Belts in a Re-Examination of Voyager 2 Observations
items.abstract: Voyager 2 provided the only direct measurement of the radiation environment at Uranus and established the well-accepted characterization of a system with a weaker ion radiation belt and surprisingly intense electron radiation belt. Recent re-analysis of the flyby, however, suggests that these observations were not taken during normal solar wind conditions, and instead occurred while a large solar wind transient, a corotating interaction region, was passing over the system. With this context, this study compares the Voyager 2 observations to a similar event observed at Earth. This comparative approach, along with an expanded contextual interpretation of the Voyager 2 flyby, suggests that solar wind-magnetospheric interactions at Uranus may have driven enhanced lower band chorus wave emissions capable of accelerating electrons to relativistic energies. This motivates new, more expansive questions to be explored at Uranus and highlights the need for a Uranus orbiter mission.

items.title: Current Sheets and Magnetic Reconnection statistics by Solar Orbiter at few to tens of Ion Inertial Lengths II: Conditions for Reconnection, and Current Sheet Planarity
items.abstract: We present a statistical study of magnetic reconnection and current sheet (CS) properties at scales from the ion inertial length ($δ_i$), up to 86.4 $δ_i$. We analyze 103 hours of high-cadence (4 samples/s) in-situ Solar Orbiter ion data, collected from July 2020 to September 2022, which correspond mainly to slow and Alfvénic solar wind. We applied an automatic detection algorithm to find CSs of thicknesses near and above the ion inertial length ($δ_i$), and classify them as Alfvénic or reconnecting. The orientation of the CSs is consistent with an isotropic distribution of the discontinuities. The median ratio of reconnection jet velocity to theoretical outflow velocity is 0.71. We find that the diamagnetic drift reconnection suppression mechanism has no impact on the cataloged CSs, due to the symmetry of their upstream conditions. We find that a flow shear in the reconnection direction suppresses magnetic reconnection, and it is consistently greater for Alfvénic than for reconnecting CSs. Flow shear in the guide-field direction is too small to suppress magnetic reconnection in ion scale solar wind CSs.

items.title: When Does Triadic Balance Reduce to Pairwise Order?
items.abstract: Structural-balance interactions are naturally defined on triads, but when pair affinities are themselves generated by continuous node attributes, it is not clear whether the resulting interaction remains genuinely higher order. Here we address this question for agents represented by unit vectors in an attribute space, with pair affinity given by their scalar product and a Heider product assigned to each triangle. For planar attributes, we show that the triadic interaction reduces exactly, at finite system size, to a pairwise Curie--Weiss XY model of the doubled angles. The ordered phase is therefore nematic and undergoes a continuous mean-field $O(2)$ transition at $k_{\mathrm B}T_c=J/8$. The same reduction reveals a local $\mathbb Z_2$ degeneracy: each nematically ordered state corresponds to $2^N$ polar assignments, whose binomial multiplicities make two nearly equal opposite groups typical at low temperature. Monte Carlo simulations support the exact critical temperature, the mean-field Binder-cumulant value, and the predicted complete-graph finite-size scaling. Finally, a tensor representation of the interaction shows that the planar reduction is dimension specific: in two dimensions the cubic invariant is constrained by lower-order invariants, whereas for $d\geq3$ it is generically independent. These results identify when attribute-induced triadic balance is effectively pairwise and when genuinely higher-order structure can remain.

items.title: Tracking the evolution of sub-Neptunes. II. The radius valley on gyrochronological ages
items.abstract: The radius valley separating super-Earths from sub-Neptunes is understood as a signature of atmospheric mass loss, but the timescale over which it develops remains poorly constrained. We investigate the age evolution of the radius valley and the super-Earth population around FGK stars using gyrochronological ages. We select $746$ planets around $510$ FGK hosts with reliable gyrochronological ages between $0.1$ and $4$ Gyr. A subset of $581$ planets around $404$ hosts, for which detection and confirmation completeness can be characterised, forms the reference sample. We measure the valley morphology and its locus in the period-radius plane, and infer the intrinsic super-Earth fraction with a selection-conditioned mixture model that accounts for stellar-age uncertainties. The intrinsic super-Earth fraction increases primarily during the first $\sim2$ Gyr, with no significant subsequent evolution. An exponential approach-to-plateau model places $90\%$ of this increase within $1.9$ Gyr at $90\%$ credibility. The radius valley is consistently resolved from $\sim1.5$ Gyr onwards, with no significant evolution in its depth or width. Its minimum may shift from $\sim1.5\,R_\oplus$ before $\sim2$ Gyr to $\sim1.8\,R_\oplus$ at older ages, accompanied by a change in the shape of the super-Earth radius distribution, although these changes are only suggestive. This evolution is consistent with atmospheric loss continuing up to approximately $1$-$2$ Gyr for a fraction of planets. The tentative shift of the valley minimum towards larger radii may indicate that planets with more massive cores complete envelope loss later, although the present data do not uniquely distinguish between atmospheric-loss mechanisms.

items.title: The maximum concentration of results in incomplete round-robin tournaments
items.abstract: The Herfindahl--Hirschman Index (HHI), a standard measure of market concentration, is widely used to quantify competitive balance in sports tournaments. To enable comparisons over time or across leagues, both its minimum and maximum should be known. The minimum is usually trivial. Our paper provides results on the maximum HHI in incomplete round-robin tournaments, where the set of matches is represented by a regular but not complete undirected graph. We prove that the lower bound of maximum HHI is reached when the tournament consists of independent round-robin groups, while the upper bound of maximum HHI is reached when the set of matches is represented by a bipartite graph. Maximising HHI is computationally difficult even for highly structured graph types corresponding to real-world tournaments, where the teams are partitioned into pots and play the same number of matches against opponents from every pot. The complexity of the problem does not depend on the scoring system or the number of opponents from a pot.

items.title: Ultra-High-Energy Tau Neutrinos as Probes of Lorentz Invariance
items.abstract: Abstract Neutrino telescopes have detected astrophysical neutrinos with energies up to 𝒪(100) PeV. Several current and proposed experiments aim to observe neutrinos at even higher energies, with the goal of detecting cosmogenic neutrinos. This increase in neutrino energy makes tests of Lorentz invariance violation (LIV) particularly appealing, since the effects of higher-dimension LIV operators on neutrino propagation grow rapidly with energy. In this work, we investigate the potential of the upcoming experiments GRAND and POEMMA to probe LIV in the neutrino sector through the detection of ultra-high-energy tau neutrinos. We generate the cosmogenic neutrino flux using SimProp and interface it with a calculation of neutrino flavor transition probabilities in the presence of LIV effects. Deviations from standard flavor transition probabilities manifest as changes in the expected tau neutrino event rates at GRAND and POEMMA. We first consider the case with a single nonzero LIV operator of various dimensions, and find that the projected sensitivities exceed existing limits from lower-energy probes by orders of magnitude. We then explore scenarios with multiple nonzero LIV parameters and show that their interplay can significantly modify the sensitivities compared to the single-parameter case. Overall, we find that upcoming observations of ultra-high-energy tau neutrinos will place some of the most stringent constraints on LIV.

items.title: The Effect of Field Line Tracing Height on Wang‐Sheeley‐Arge Solar Wind Predictions at Earth
items.abstract: Abstract A key component of the widely used Wang‐Sheeley‐Arge model is the tracing of magnetic field lines in the solar corona, as that largely determines the modeled open/closed field regions and in turn the predicted large‐scale solar wind structure. However, small closed field regions interspersed among the open field lines inside coronal holes (CHs) often hinder determination of the large‐scale open–closed boundary. Since most of this small closed flux inside CHs is confined to low heights, we demonstrate that by slightly raising the height from which magnetic field lines are traced from the photosphere (), we can improve the prediction of solar wind high‐speed enhancements (HSEs). We find a higher produces more accurate estimates of the HSE start time, duration, and peak speed, and enables the detection of HSEs that were missed with the standard . These improvements are primarily associated with changes in the great‐circle angular distance, while the flux tube expansion factors remain largely unchanged. A higher produces smoother open‐field boundaries and reduces small‐scale fragmentation within open‐field regions. These morphological changes lead to more stable magnetic footpoint mappings and consequently more robust GCD calculations. To assess the statistical relevance of these findings, we extend the analysis to 53 Carrington rotations and perform a multi‐metric evaluation of model performance. The results indicate that higher improves HSE predictions while reducing false alarms. We thus find that the choice of represents an important and previously underexplored parameter that can help enhance our ambient solar wind modeling and forecasting capabilities.

items.title: Can cosmic voids ease the Hubble tension? Local expansion in w 0 w a CDM
items.abstract: Abstract We investigate the effect of local cosmic voids on low-redshift measurements of the Hubble rate in flat w 0 w a CDM cosmologies. Using a hydrodynamical model for isolated spherical inverse top-hat underdensities, we compute the void-induced Hubble shift as a function of redshift, enclosed density contrast δ E and cosmological parameters. We find that the effect is mainly controlled by the matter sector, through δ E and Ω m,0 , while dynamical dark energy gives only subdominant late-time corrections. For a Planck-calibrated ΛCDM background, matching the SH0ES value requires a present-day void with δ E ( z = 0)≃ -0.44, substantially deeper than the KBC-like local underdensity. A KBC-like void lowers the SH0ES-Planck discrepancy to about 2 σ , but is not deep enough to fully reconcile the two measurements. Allowing for dynamical dark energy, including regions motivated by recent DES and DESI analyses, changes this result only at the percent level. We also show that the reported redshift dependence of locally inferred H 0 values can be represented phenomenologically by an effective enclosed matter profile. This reconstruction should be interpreted as a consistency test of local-structure effects rather than as explanation for an evolving background value of H 0 . Overall, local underdensities can affect low-redshift Hubble-rate inferences, but they do not resolve the Hubble tension within the spherical void setup considered here.

items.title: GLOW. I. Comprehensive Measurements of Gas-rich, Star-forming, Low-mass Galaxies in the Nearby Universe*
items.abstract: Abstract Gas-rich, star-forming, low-mass galaxies in the nearby Universe are powerful laboratories for studying baryonic physics in detail, including: stellar mass assembly, stellar feedback, chemical enrichment, and the interplay of the interstellar medium with star formation. Investigating these disparate yet interconnected processes requires data obtained by myriad observatories. Here, we present a comprehensive atlas of uniformly processed data on 37 low-mass galaxies within 6 Mpc. The atlas includes archival data on (i) the H i from the Very Large Array observatory; (ii) resolved stars from Hubble Space Telescope optical imaging; (iii) Spitzer Space Telescope 3.6 μ m imaging; and (iv) optical imaging from ground-based telescopes. We also compile measurements of (i) tip-of-the-red-giant-branch (TRGB) distances to the galaxies; (ii) direct method gas-phase oxygen abundances and nitrogen-to-oxygen abundance ratios; (iii) constraints on the local environment around each galaxy; and (iv) other measurements from the literature. We supplement the data with new observations where needed to complete the measurements for all galaxies in the sample. From these data, we find good agreement between stellar masses measured from color–magnitude diagrams and those estimated from 3.6 μ m imaging by assuming a mass-to-light ratio. We also provide the first mapping of the H i profiles as a function of structural parameters. These data sets and measurements are the foundation for the Galaxies Losing Oxygen via Winds (GLOW) project, whose main aim is to characterize the star formation−chemical enrichment cycle of low-mass galaxies by measuring the production, distribution, and retention of oxygen on a galaxy-by-galaxy basis.

items.title: Black Hole Astrometric Binaries in the Roman Galactic Bulge Time Domain Survey
items.abstract: Abstract The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope (Roman), NASA’s newest flagship mission, launched 2026 August 30. As part of its mission, Roman will conduct the Galactic Bulge Time Domain Survey (GBTDS), which will generate ∼50,000 epochs of high-precision photometric and astrometric data for ∼10 8 sources across 1.7 deg 2 in the Galactic bulge. Roman GBTDS astrometry is comparable to Gaia Data Release 4 in terms of number of stars, astrometric precision, and time baseline, and is highly complementary in terms of wavelength and sky location. In this paper, we investigate a synthetic population of GBTDS sources to characterize the detectability of unresolved astrometric binaries, in particular those with compact object companions. Assuming the occurrence rate of black holes (BHs) and neutron stars (NSs) in astronomical-unit-scale orbits around stars is 10 −7 and 10 −6 , respectively, and that Roman achieves an astrometric precision of 1% of a pixel, O ( 10 ) BH+star and O ( 10 ) NS+star detached binaries will be detectable. The BHs will have median mass measurement uncertainties of ∼25%, increasing the existing sample of detached astrometric BH binaries by a factor of 3. Together with the O ( 1 0 2 ) isolated BHs expected to be discovered by microlensing in the Roman GBTDS and an additional O ( 10 ) detached BH binaries in Gaia DR4, this will provide a representative view of the quiescent Galactic stellar-mass BH population.

items.title: Tectonics on Early Earth Driven by Earth's Changing Shape During Tidal Recession of the Moon
items.abstract: Abstract Few fragments of Earth's earliest crust have survived, and so this formative period of our planet's history is shrouded in mystery. To leverage the limited data available, it is important to understand all the processes that could have shaped our young planet. Here, I explore a previously neglected aspect of early‐Earth dynamics: rotation. Earth after the Moon‐forming impact was rapidly rotating with its rotation rate slowing significantly during the first tens of millions of years after the impact as the Moon tidally receded. Using planetary structure and tidal evolution calculations, I show that the initially distorted structure of Earth would likely have led to significant latitudinal variations in primary crustal thickness. Further, the subsequent changes in Earth's shape in response to its slowing rotation rate could have driven extensive tectonic activity and modulated the response of the crust to other forces. There was extension of the crust in polar regions and convergence in the equatorial regions at rates potentially comparable to those forming the Himalayas today in high‐angular momentum scenarios. Depending on the rheology of the earliest crust, such motions could have led to burial of hydrated and weathered surface material, extensive volcanism, and degassing of Earth's interior. Phase changes due to increases in internal pressure could have led to delamination of parts of the crust, producing early mantle heterogeneities. Hydrated secondary melting of the crust and the production of evolved magmas could explain the emergence of a diversity of rock types within tens of millions of years of Earth's formation.

items.title: Density-Gradient Modulated Dissipation and the Sunspot Temperature Deficit
items.abstract: The temperature deficit in sunspot umbrae (approximately 1700 K below the quiet photosphere) is conventionally attributed to magnetic pressure suppressing convective heat transport [1, 3]. However, a unified quantitative framework linking the macroscopic density gradient, energy dissipation, and the resultant temperature drop remains absent. This paper proposes a density-gradient modulated dissipation mechanism based on a steady-state, quasi-onedimensional axisymmetric perturbation model. We demonstrate that the umbra temperature is governed by three intrinsic factors: the suppression of the perturbation source due to magnetic convection blocking (RS), the geometric contraction of the magnetic flux tube (RG), and the density-gradient modulated dissipation factor (RD). By coupling the ideal gas scale height relation (Hu = HqTu/Tq) with the perturbation decay integral, a transcendental equation is derived and solved iteratively. Using observational boundary conditions (RS ∈ [0.45, 0.55], RG ∈ [0.40, 0.50]), the model yields an umbra temperature of approximately 4083 K (relative error < 5% against the observed 4100 K). Crucially, this mechanism shares the exact same underlying dissipation parameter (kα0 = 1/500 km−1) as the previously established coronal heating model. This unified scaling law quantitatively explains both the hottest and coldest regions of the solar atmosphere while maintaining a unified parameter set.

items.title: Microbial Syntrophy Drives Methanogenesis From Residual Hydrocarbons in Anaerobic Oil Sands Tailings.
items.abstract: Anaerobic oil sands tailings can generate methane for decades as residual naphtha-range and petroleum hydrocarbons sustain microbial metabolism, but how microbial interactions link hydrocarbon turnover to methanogenesis remains poorly resolved. To characterize these microbial associations, we analyse two naphtha-amended anaerobic tailings incubation series using 16S rRNA gene relative abundance, hydrocarbon consumption, and methane production data within a cooperative game-theoretical framework. The abundance-informed Shapley analysis attributes system-level variation to bacterial-archaeal coalitions, highlighting key syntrophic partnerships. Several taxa show inferred contributions to methanogenesis that are disproportionate to their relative abundance, indicating that model-based attribution can differ from abundance ranking. Sensitivity analysis shows that the main methane-attribution patterns remain interpretable across alternative abundance-weighted coefficient formulations. These interaction patterns shift across incubation phases, showing that microbial control over hydrocarbon-dependent methanogenesis changes through time. When incorporated into stochastic forecasting, Shapley-derived reaction intensities improve predictive performance compared with reduced microbial and non-microbial benchmarks. Together, our results indicate that methane production in oil sands tailings can be interpreted through abundance-informed bacterial-archaeal coalition structure, providing a coalition-aware basis for interpreting and forecasting methanogenic hydrocarbon transformation.

items.title: Seasonal and Environmental Influences on Microbial Community Dynamics in the Dunk River Watershed, Prince Edward Island, Canada.
items.abstract: Riverine ecosystems are crucial biogeochemical hubs, with their microbial communities playing a key role in nutrient cycling and overall ecosystem health. This study used shotgun metagenomic sequencing to characterize the seasonal and environmental drivers of taxonomic and functional microbial community structure (read depth between 1.91 and 30.44 bp) in four tributaries of the Dunk River watershed in Prince Edward Island (PEI), a landscape shaped by intensive agriculture and groundwater-dominated streamflow, where the seasonal and land-use impacts on the river's microbiome remain understudied. Although taxonomic composition showed no significant spatial variation among sampling sites, functional profiling identified subtle but distinct spatial signatures, primarily driven at the site with the least human impacts. Mass effects driven by above- or below-ground water dispersal pathways may override local selective pressures, resulting in a more uniform community structure across different locations. The study also identified significant correlations between certain rare microbial taxa and nutrient concentrations. This work provides critical baseline data on microbial ecology in PEI river systems, indicating that while temporal factors are the primary identifiable drivers among the measured variables, a substantial majority of the community variance remains unexplained, likely reflecting the inherent stochasticity of open riverine ecosystems.

items.title: Reproductive Parameters of Wild Female Hainan Gibbons (Nomascus hainanus): Implications for Conservation.
items.abstract: As a Critically Endangered primate species endemic to China, the Hainan gibbon (Nomascus hainanus) represents a conservation priority requiring urgent research attention. A study of its reproductive parameters can provide a scientific basis for the population recovery of this species. From October 2010 to December 2025, we recorded information on female reproduction and infant survival of the Hainan gibbon populations through direct observation. Meanwhile, we also integrated previously published reproductive data from November 2002 to June 2013. Based on 48 births of gibbons, we quantitatively analyzed reproductive seasonality, infant mortality, and interbirth interval. The results showed that gibbons reproduce throughout the year, and most births occur from November to March. Four infant deaths (i.e., within the first 2 years of life) were recorded, accounting for 8% of the total births during the 15‑year study period. Infants of primiparous females had 50% mortality, whereas the infant mortality of multiparous females was only 3%. The average interbirth interval was 29 months. Infant death resulted in a shorter subsequent interbirth interval. The year-round breeding patterns and relatively short interbirth intervals in female gibbons indicate that the current population has a moderate reproductive potential. However, emergency plans should be formulated to address the risk of infant mortality in females' first reproduction, so as to maximize the survival rate of infants and facilitate the population recovery of Hainan gibbons.

items.title: Arboreality in Wild Western Lowland Gorillas (G. g. gorilla) at the Mondika Research Center, Republic of Congo.
items.abstract: Although primates are typically considered arboreal, tree use varies widely. Among great apes, gorillas are the largest-bodied and generally the most terrestrial, yet arboreal behavior varies within and between species. We investigated arboreal behavior in one group of wild western gorillas (n = 1831.2 h of focal observation; 334 individual-days from 1 male and 4 females) at Mondika Research Center, Republic of Congo, to determine how tree strata use, activity, and food choice vary among individuals and fruit seasons. Compared with published studies, this group spent less time above ground than western gorillas at Loango, more than Virunga mountain gorillas, and approximately the same amount as Bwindi mountain gorillas. The four females were more arboreal than the male and spent proportionally more of their arboreal time resting/socializing than he did. Overall arboreality did not vary by season, but tree-strata use did, with seasonal patterns differing among individuals. Although less arboreal, the male frequently used high strata when in trees. As fruit availability increased, gorillas used lower strata more frequently and shifted from feeding primarily on leaves/bark toward fruit/flowers. These findings show that gorilla arboreal behavior reflects resource availability, forest structure, and individual characteristics, emphasizing that comparisons of vertical space use across primate populations must account for local ecology and within-population variation. Moreover, our results emphasize the importance of incorporating complex climbing structures into captive enclosures to support the health and welfare of western gorillas.

items.title: Comparative Analysis of Exonic SSR-Containing Genes in Three Diving Duck Species Reveals Shared Functional Themes.
items.abstract: Simple sequence repeats (SSRs) are ubiquitous components of eukaryotic genomes that contribute to genome evolution, genetic variation, and gene regulation. Although genome-wide SSR landscapes have been extensively characterized across vertebrates, the cross-species distribution and functional associations of exonic SSR-containing genes remain poorly understood, particularly in non-model birds. To address this knowledge gap, we performed a comparative analysis of chromosome-level genome assemblies from three diving duck species ( Aythya ferina , Aythya marila , and Netta rufina ) to investigate genome-wide SSR patterns and the cross-species sharing and functional characteristics of exonic SSR-containing genes. Comparative analyses of genome-wide SSRs revealed pronounced interspecific variation in SSR abundance and repeat composition, whereas exonic SSR abundance showed more similar values after normalization by total annotated exon sequence length. Cross-species comparison identified 4336 exonic SSR-containing genes shared among all three species, greatly outnumbering the species-specific gene sets. Functional enrichment analyses identified four broad functional themes associated with these shared genes: (i) gene transcription and epigenetic regulation, (ii) protein homeostasis and the ubiquitin-proteasome system, (iii) development, differentiation and morphogenesis, and (iv) stress response and cellular maintenance. The most significantly enriched categories were associated with transcriptional regulation, chromatin remodeling, RNA processing, and epigenetic regulation, whereas autophagy- and other cellular-maintenance pathways indicated additional associations with stress-response processes. These functional associations should be interpreted cautiously because they may be influenced by cross-species annotation limitations and gene-architecture differences. Collectively, our results reveal distinct patterns for genome-wide and exonic SSRs distribution among the three diving duck species and identify shared functional associations of genes containing exonic SSRs. These findings provide a comparative genomic framework for future investigations of exonic SSRs in waterfowl and other non-model vertebrates.

items.title: Climate-Driven Distribution Modeling of the Glacial Apollo Butterfly (Parnassius glacialis) for Biodiversity Conservation.
items.abstract: Understanding how climate change affects insect distribution is critical for biodiversity conservation, particularly in the case of range-restricted and ecologically sensitive species. The glacial Apollo, Parnassius glacialis (Lepidoptera: Papilionidae), is a high-altitude butterfly of notable scientific and esthetic value, yet its ecological response to climate change remains poorly understood. Here, we model the current and future distribution of P. glacialis across China and identify key environmental drivers shaping its habitat. We developed an ensemble species distribution model using 45 occurrence records and 10 bioclimatic variables, integrating outputs from multiple algorithms to enhance predictive robustness. Temperature-particularly seasonal variation-emerged as the strongest determinant of habitat suitability, followed by precipitation. At present, suitable habitats are concentrated in northern, southwestern, and eastern China. However, projections under future climate scenarios reveal a marked reduction in suitable range, with the habitat centroid shifting to lower elevations in Hubei Province. The direction and extent of this shift vary among scenarios, highlighting the species' vulnerability to both climatic and socioeconomic trajectories. These findings raise urgent conservation concerns, suggesting that P. glacialis may face significant habitat loss and range contraction under projected climate conditions. We recommend the establishment of targeted protected areas, the integration of insect responses into climate adaptation policies, and the implementation of long-term ecological monitoring. This study provides crucial insights into climate-driven range shifts in high-altitude butterflies and underscores the broader need for adaptive conservation strategies in a warming world.

items.title: Moult Timing as a Measure of Condition in a Northern Hemisphere Ungulate.
items.abstract: Many vertebrates that live in seasonal climates moult once or twice a year, with the effect of refreshing worn coat or plumage, increasing insulation or improving camouflage. The timing of moult may be in response to a variety of cues, but because it is costly, it is also likely to reflect the health and wellbeing of individuals, here referred to as their condition. Using the individually-monitored red deer from the Isle of Rum, in which summer and winter coats are easily distinguished, we (a) test for traits that are predictive of moult timing, (b) explore traits that moult timing is predictive of and (c) analyse covariances between moult timings and calving dates at the individual, annual and residual level. We show that adult female moult timing in July and November is associated with age, reproductive status and parasite burden, and has been getting earlier over time in November. A female's moult timing also predicts the overwinter survival of herself and her current calf as well as her future fecundity. Moult timing varies among individuals and years. Covariances between calving dates and the timing of each moult shed light on the temporal patterns of condition within individuals and across years, for example, across years, winter moult covaries with the following calving date but not the summer moult that occurs shortly after. The timing of moult appears to be a non-invasive measure of condition. Monitoring moult timing across years at the population level may shed light on year-to-year variation in population health and variation within populations is likely indicative of the relative conditions among individuals. Increased knowledge of population and individual condition may be of benefit for ungulate population management and conservation.

items.title: Raptor Models Alter Rodent Behavior During Acorn Dispersal.
items.abstract: The relationship between rodents and oak trees has attracted considerable attention. The interaction spans a wide range of outcomes, from extreme predation, in which rodents consume acorns, to forms of collaboration that approach mutualism. Acorn characteristics and the behavior of rodent species within the oak habitats are among the factors shaping this interaction. This study examines the influence of third species on rodent-oak interaction by using raptor models. The main objective is to determine whether raptors in the treetops can deter rodents from feeding on acorns, thereby reducing acorn dispersal. To achieve this objective, we monitored acorns' dispersal by four rodent species, Algerian mouse, wood mouse, common vole, and garden dormouse, in 10 m × 10 m semi-wild enclosures with oak trees in the four corners, two of them with raptor models. Beneath the 4 oaks, 60 acorns, 15 acorns per tree, were provided daily for 15 days, and the acorns in situ consumption and dispersal were tracked to determine whether the presence of raptor models altered the dispersal by any of the rodent species. The results show that species that are actively involved in acorn dispersion through transport (Algerian mouse, wood mouse) modify their behavior in response to the presence of raptor models in the treetops. The garden dormouse also modifies its behavior, although this species does not transport or bury acorns; however, it does move them around on the surface and consumes most of the acorns whole by preying on them. Therefore, it does not participate in the acorn dispersion process. The common vole typically occupies open habitats without oaks and does not modify its behavior, probably because raptor models are not perceived as a threat.

items.title: Effect of Gastrointestinal Helminths and Haematological Parameters on Flea Abundance in Small Mammals in Tanzania.
items.abstract: Fleas are important vectors of numerous pathogens, including bacteria, viruses, helminths and protozoa, and their abundance on small mammals may be influenced by various biotic and abiotic factors. This study investigated the associations between gastrointestinal helminth infections, selected haematological parameters and flea abundance in small mammals from three selected districts of Tanzania. Two wards and two villages within each district were purposively selected for sampling in Mbulu, Lushoto and Morogoro District Council. Small mammals were captured from households, fallow lands, crop fields, plantation forests and bush habitats and identified to species or genus level using morphological keys. Fleas, blood samples and gastrointestinal tracts were collected to determine flea infestation, gastrointestinal helminth infections, packed cell volume (PCV) and haemoglobin concentration (Hb). Associations between gastrointestinal helminths, haematological parameters and flea abundance were assessed using generalised linear mixed models. A total of 302 rodents and shrews were captured, with Mastomys natalensis (54.4%, n = 163), Rattus rattus (13.6%, n = 41) and Crocidura spp. (10.3%, n = 31) being the most abundant hosts. Overall gastrointestinal helminth prevalence was 71.2% (95% CI: 65.7-76.2), with Trichuris spp. (33.3%, n = 100), Hymenolepis diminuta (29.1%, n = 88), Angiostrongylus spp. (19.9%, n = 60) and Hymenolepis nana (15.2%, n = 46) being the most prevalent helminths. A total of 271 fleas were collected, predominantly Ctenophthalmus spp. (31.0%, n = 84), Pulex irritans (30.3%, n = 82), Dinopsyllus lypusus (28.8%, n = 78) and Nosopsyllus incisus (4.1%, n = 11). Overall gastrointestinal helminth prevalence was significantly associated with total flea abundance ( p p > 0.05). These findings suggest that coinfections involving gastrointestinal helminths and fleas are common in small mammals and that helminth infections may influence flea abundance. Understanding these host-parasite interactions may improve our understanding of pathogen transmission dynamics and inform surveillance strategies for zoonotic diseases in Tanzania.

items.title: Temperature Carryover Effect Revealed for Marine Fishes Using Spatio-Temporal Distributed Lag Models.
items.abstract: Understanding the impact of changing temperature on population densities is necessary to predict the likely impact of climate anomalies (e.g., marine heatwaves) or forecast distribution shifts under future climate scenarios. Population densities are often analyzed using spatio-temporal models (STMs), which typically predict densities based on local habitat conditions while also estimating latent spatial and spatio-temporal variation. Recent research extends STMs by also estimating density responses to habitat conditions at nearby locations using a "spatially distributed lag" (SDL) that averages habitat conditions in the vicinity of samples. Here, we extend the SDL by incorporating insights from diffusion-enhanced STMs to simultaneously estimate spatially distributed and time-lagged responses to nearby and past habitat conditions (a "spatio-temporal distributed lag" STDL). We then use summer bottom trawl survey data from the eastern Bering Sea (1982-2024) to measure whether spatial and/or temporal lags are parsimonious when predicting population density from temperature anomalies for six ecologically important fishes. Results show that time-lagged responses are parsimonious, positive, and substantial (correlation of 0.20-0.83 per year) for five species, and that density responses to temperature anomalies also diffuse outward over time for four species at 30-53 km per year. A self- and cross-test simulation experiment shows that model selection can identify the appropriate model and that parameter estimates are approximately unbiased. We therefore conclude that temperature carryover effects arise in marine fishes and implement the method in the R package sdmTMB so that future studies can estimate nonlocal and time-lagged responses when measuring density responses to habitat.

items.title: Zinc and Iron Homeostatic Interactions in a Mutant Lacking Nicotianamine Vacuolar Storage and Citrate Xylem Loading.
items.abstract: Metal homeostasis in plants relies on coordinated uptake, chelation and transport mechanisms involving, but not limited to, citrate and nicotianamine (NA). In Arabidopsis (Arabidopsis thaliana), disruption of the citrate exporter FRD3 (FERRIC REDUCTASE DEFECTIVE 3) causes constitutive iron (Fe) deficiency responses, altered Fe, manganese (Mn) and zinc (Zn) distribution, with Fe accumulation in the root cell wall. This ultimately results in oxidative and biotic stress responses, and impaired root development, phenotypes that are partially alleviated by Zn excess. In this study, we investigated the consequences of impairing both citrate loading into xylem vessels and NA partitioning within cells. The frd3 zif1 double mutant exhibits enhanced sensitivity to Zn excess, severe defects in root system architecture and meristem maintenance, persistent oxidative stress and compromised reproductive development. These phenotypes correlate with sustained activation of Fe deficiency signalling and marked defects in root-to-shoot metal translocation. Our findings reveal that coordinated citrate export and NA compartmentation form an integrated buffering strategy required to maintain metal homeostasis and partitioning, as well as redox balance and proper development, including root plasticity and seed yield, under fluctuating metal availability.

items.title: Relationships Among MHC Diversity, Parasites and Secondary Sexual Colouration.
items.abstract: Sexual selection via honest (costly) signals of fitness can generate patterns in immunogenetic diversity at the major histocompatibility complex (MHC). MHC diversity explains variation in immunocompetence-and therefore fitness-thus impacting the ability to generate honest signals. Differences in guppy (Poecilia reticulata) colour patterns can be driven by opposing selection pressures of predation and female mate choice, but the effect of parasitism has received less attention. By studying 21 wild guppy populations in Trinidad, we sought to quantify covariation among parasitic Gyrodactylus spp. infections, male sexual ornamentation (orange and black colouration) and genetic variation at the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) at both individual and population levels. We found population level support for a correlation between MHC diversity and Gyrodactylus prevalence, including an overall association between MHC supertype composition and prevalence. At the individual level, supertype (functional) diversity again emerged as a more informative measure than allelic richness alone. Predation was associated with Gyrodactylus prevalence and orange, but not black, colouration. Notably, some of these relationships differed between the individual and population levels. Further, much of this variation was explained by processes acting at a broader geographic scale within river drainages, which comprise divergent guppy lineages. These findings suggest that evolutionary history and processes such as genetic drift and gene flow contribute substantially to these relationships, but that ecological variation (i.e., predation) interacts with these processes. Our findings indicate that multi-trait relationships between colour, immunogenetic diversity and infection are best examined within their broader evolutionary and ecological contexts.

items.title: When Teeth Twist: Distinct Mechanisms and Patterns of Enamel Wear from Rotational Forces-A Preliminary Investigation.
items.abstract: Motivation Dental enamel possesses a unique anisotropic, heterogeneous hierarchical structure which enables a combination of high hardness and remarkable durability compared to other natural and synthetic biomaterials. Nevertheless, it undergoes mechanical degradation through fracture from concentrated overloads and/or progressive wear, both of which can compromise tooth function and longevity. Enamel wear is of particular interest to anthropology, as it is ubiquitous and enables researchers to discern the culture, behaviors, and ecologies of the study populations. Studies simulating dental wear in vitro often employ simplified loading configurations based on combinations of axial and lateral forces, which successfully reproduce the "classical" microwear features of pits and scratches, but do not capture the full complexity of in vivo loading conditions. Objectives To conduct a preliminary in vitro investigation of previously underexplored rotationally induced occlusal mechanical wear in enamel. Methods Cyclic contact tests combining compression (50 N) and rotation (30°) are applied to human enamel specimens using a testing machine with decoupled biaxial (axial-torsion) actuators. Damage is characterized by electron and confocal microscopy. Results Rotational forces produce abrasive wear with distinct microscopic damage patterns, involving transitions from quasi-plastic to brittle damage modes with an increasing number of contact cycles. After 10 4 cycles, the macrowear volume is 0.0023 mm 3 . Conclusions Rotational microwear differs from "classical" pits and scratches associated with axial-lateral loading. Findings offer a framework for interpreting curved microscratches and provide a basis for future investigations. More broadly, they contribute to improving models of dental microwear and provide new insights in biomaterials science and anthropology.
